reviews.text: A deliberate slow burn film in which the viewer experiences the world through the eyes of the notorious killer; the unsettling effect is amplified by Richard Attenborough's superb performance as the strange but ultimately submissive man who never breaks character, not even during the horrifying scenes in which he murders his victims. On the other side, a young and great John Hurt plays Evans, a troubled man, but you can't help but feel sad and hurt when you know how the story ends.Again, it's a slow-paced thriller in the vein of filmmaker Richard Fleischer's past thrillers, such as The Boston Strangler, where everything moves methodically, even documentary-style at moments.

reviews.author: MrPPeeps
reviews.text: I'm not sure how well-known the name John Christie is outside of the UK, or even England, but “10 Rillington Place” is a truly chilling depiction of one of Britain's most infamous serial killers, and the devastating miscarriage of justice that saw the innocent Timothy Evans wrongly hanged for Christie’s crimes. It’s a grim, haunting story, and the film does a remarkable job capturing the claustrophobia and bleakness of the events. The small, grimy flat where it all takes place becomes a character in itself, making everything feel uncomfortably real and intimate.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: What impresses me about this is how it makes its argument, without belaboring it, for the idea that Tim Evans is one of Christie's victims, and how it shows without belaboring the point where sexism enables Christie's predation. The former is fairly clear: manipulating Evans is simple enough, and the confusing web of compulsive lies only serves to entangle him deeper in the web. A use of relative privilege (simply being better educated, even if marginally) destroys Tim Evans, and Christie's actions are at the core of it.

reviews.author: 𝐋𝐢𝐩𝐞 🦈
reviews.text: "20 Feet From Stardom (2013)" is a documentary that goes deep into the history of backing vocals. There is this whole issue of injustices, devaluation and the difficulty of launching a solo career, even more so because they are women and black (although they could have gone deeper into this last issue). I liked the testimonies, it is interesting that almost all of them comment on similar experiences, I think because it is such a difficult and challenging profession. In some moments, I felt that it was too repetitive, because they touch certain points several times. But luckily, every time they brought up new information or some music scene (those voices are so surreal, I could listen to each one of them for hours), my interest immediately returned.

reviews.author: tromafiend
reviews.text: Giving voice to the (far from) voiceless, this doc follows in the tradition of Standing in the Shadows of Motown and The Wrecking Crew in shining a light on the lesser known contributors to some of popular music's greatest tunes. A profile of several artists with voices that can shake the very pillars of Heaven but who lacked the self-promotion and/or proper breaks in order to launch lasting solo careers. It’s an absolute crime that the singer of the greatest Christmas single ever cut isn’t a household name, so any doc that gives due credit to Queen Darlene Love is easily worth a recommendation in my book.

Certain conversations last as much as 3 lines and end there. It feels a little all over the place and I think that’s what I love. It works as a collection of details that, in some way, shape someone in the scene. The moments that shape you aren’t those that feel like that’s their main purpose, it’s those moments of true impulsiveness. This movie makes me want to make dumb decisions and get my shit together at the same time!

reviews.text: A docu-realistic human drama that portrays the existing life & freedom of women stuck within the conservative traditions and superstitions in a male dominated village of Northern Iran. What starts as a suspense drama going in search of a girl, Panahi slowly widens the genre horizon and turns it into an impressive observational drama, that engages you with enough subtlety and commentary. A good watch.

reviews.author: Lara Pop
reviews.text: Panahi's Life, And Nothing More but paired with his sharp social lens. I was enamored. 3 Faces is as much Panahi's ode to film as it is to life. The actors play themselves within a fictional story about a young Iranian girl's struggles to become an actress. She is hindered by a simple fact: she lives in an Iranian village where there are no such opportunities. The villagers look at her with scorn, calling her 'empty-headed' because she took the crazy notion of studying into her head.

reviews.text: A thematically rich film that probes strained solidarity and social repression between different generations of women. The mystery slowly reveals the suffocating cultural forces closing in around them. By focusing on Panahi rather than his wife, the film becomes too self-reflexive, keeping me at arm's length. The opening undercuts some of the depth before it can fully take hold.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Panahi playing around issues central to his work since his early days: power, class, the place of the artist, Iranian society’s sexism. It is a stronger imagined film than his recent output, milking a lot from Panahi’s position as distant observer/mediator as well as putting him in a position closer to patriarchy than usual.

reviews.author: Sam Jalali
reviews.text: In 3 Faces, Panahi continues his streak of "car cinema," but it’s understating how much this specific film grapples with the weight of tradition and the stifling of the feminine spirit in a way that feels both timeless and urgently contemporary.The film is all about where the Iranian identity is set to go, should it remain tethered to the rigid patriarchal structures of the past, for Panahi examines how these cultural expectations have been around for longer than the characters, or the audience, can fully reconcile.

reviews.author: Ben Neild
reviews.text: A famous Iranian actress receives a video message from a teenage girl announcing her intention to commit suicide, the recipient of this ominous dispatch compelled to locate its author by any means necessary in 3 Faces. Jafar Panahi’s compelling drama follows the real-life figure of Behnaz Jafari on a curious journey into the mountainous regions of Northwestern Iran, the actress playing a version of herself who is beset by various impediments upon entering a socially conservative community that seeks to quash the artistic ambitions of its young residents. The mystery surrounding the authenticity of the aforementioned video becomes a driving force for our concerned protagonist, a revelation surrounding the girl’s domestic situation dramatically changing the nature of the story being…

reviews.text: Farmer can't pay his mortgage so the banker sets his barn on fire. Nobody tries to stop him. nor does anyone seem to care about stopping a murdering bandit until the railroad (notorious cinematic totem of capital) gets involved. The railroad pays the farmer barely enough to cover his debts in order to risk his life and stop the guy stealing from the railroad. reviews.text: This has been on the watchlist for a while, and after watching it, it turns out to be a superb character-driven western that treats gunfights as secondary. Most importantly, the battle of wills is at the center of it. What starts off as struggling rancher Evans trying to transport outlaw Ben Wade to the train that will take him to prison morphs into a story about honor and masculinity and, ultimately, the price of integrity. It's the sort of modern western that just ticks all the boxes and works, and a lot of it's down to its leads' performances and sharp direction. reviews.text: hard to not see this excessive trash-noir as a fitting end to Hal Ashby’s legacy, a final film born from so much coke and booze that it had the (already) troublesome filmmaker pulled off of the film before it was complete, yet it still has his shaggy character DNA all over it, with its strong anti-authority stance and an empathy for people on the wrong path (and doing largely nothing to correct it) — you could credit the copious sex, drugs and violence to the co-writing of Oliver Stone and Robert Towne working from a source by Lawrence Block (!!!) but it also feels pure Ashby in his constant intent to provoke, pushing the envelope in the ribald 80s by further sleazing up and already tawdry genre much like he did for the road comedy with The Last Detail in the prior decade; an all around classless affair from a filmmaker who wanted no part of class

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: A messy, overlong, sunny neo noir that owns an ample amount of grime while offering up scene after scene of improv’d sleaziness, with Bridges just sweating and swearing his way through the back alleys, coke dens, and warehouses of LA. Surprisingly coherent, narratively speaking, given the numerous mishaps BTS, with Ashby slowly descending into a booze and powder fueled final state of being. One could view Scudder as an inadvertent piece of autobiographical pulp self-reflection, as he grappled with appetites that would eventually get the New Hollywood legend locked out of the editing bay (not to mention end his life). Still, the final shouting set piece is a marvel of bizarre staging, never feeling fully formed, but containing enough red faced rage to remain interesting. A real curiosity this one, that borders on being legitimately great, despite all its issues.

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: Sunburnt sleaze with a mile-wide mean streak and plotting that resembles scattered flashbacks from a three-day bender. With Oliver Stone writing and another dysfunctional cop at its center, 8 Million Ways to Die feels like an inverted Year of the Dragon, with Los Angeles substituted for New York and wartime trauma replaced by alcoholic self-loathing. Scudder is a perfect role for Jeff Bridges: he and The Dude could never be friends, but they each find themselves ambling their way through a noir nightmare, fueled by screwy optimism and various other substances. Tarantino's recent raving about the film makes sense, as so many elements and even some of the actors from his '90s output can be traced back to it. The unbridled cocaine histrionics of the warehouse climax must be seen to be believed.

Still, it’s perfectly watchable at just 84 minutes, and there’s actual plot here instead of the film running purely on make-believe vibes. reviews.text: "A Dandy in Aspic" is a 1968 film directed by Anthony Mann. Marked as Anthony Mann's final film, the director actually died in mid production. Although having completed most of the directorial work, lead actor Laurence Harvey took over completion on that front. The film itself is based on a novel written two years prior, and concerns itself on Cold War spy tactics, double crossing and betrayal. The gimmick in this feature is that a British agent by the name of Alexander Eberlin is tasked to seek out and kill KGB agent named Krasnevin. There is just one problem, as the British authority doesn't know that Eberlin is Krasnevin, a double agent playing both sides. This marks for an interesting…

All’s we can do is grab a piece for ourselves before some guy from outside comes and takes it all.” Or, more precisely, it’s twilight that Jimmy’s morally torn reporter inhabits, that moment right before everything starts to go dark, that hour when not everything is lost yet and maybe…

Ed Harris' character Jimmy is an unassuming newspaper man, a good guy who makes a poor choice and ends up strung along by a major local figure. once the wheels of politics start to roll downhill he puts everything on the line to jam a stick in the spokes; protect the people he cares about, preserve what precious little natural beauty there is left, mend his wounded conscience. he could be too late, but then again there could be something left to salvage. we're probably too late as a species to stave off the all-consuming glut of techno-capital expansion, postmodernity,…

As a young adult, I read the novel by John D. MacDonald, and saw other films by Nunez, and so had a retroactive fascination with this film even though my memories of it were dim. reviews.text: Absolutely my thing. Contemplative, open-aired, clench-jawed. Floridian southern-gothic-noir, shimmering like crystals on a blanket. Cracked pavement riverbeds and all sorts of low building mystery.theres a tone here that you just cant capture in words. grimy and quiet. worried but sparkling. Crepuscular and moody. Love recontextualizes every single thing. Nunez toes a razor-edged line and in return creates perfection. Highest recommendation possible from me.

reviews.author: dirtylaundri
reviews.text: Paradise is always already lost and now we're scrambling along. Although on the other hand, there's enough of the old, slow Florida left here to mourn its demise. At the center of it: a magnificent Ed Harris performance, which makes this sort of a companion piece to Romero's KNIGHTRIDERS. In both films he plays characters stuck in the past and faced with the challenges of an increasingly streamlined present. In the Romero film he chooses obstinate opposition and therefore romantic fantasy, here he chooses overidentification with the aggressor and therefore the melodrama of self-denial.

reviews.text: It's a shame this little American Playhouse production, based on the 1962 novel by John D. MacDonald, is all but forgotten; it's notable in several ways. First, it's simply a good movie. Second, director Victor Nuñez is one of America's finest indie directors; after this movie he'd go on to make two of the best films of the 90s (Ruby in Paradise and Ulee's Gold). Third, this is one of the movies that launched Ed Harris' career (coming hot on the heels of The Right Stuff and Under Fire).

reviews.author: Nick Dets
reviews.text: I’ve been a fan of Nunez’s relaxed, nuanced filmmaking for decades but only recently learned about this 1984 gem. Using an ever so slight daylight noir flavor, he tells this character drama about a reporter caught between abating his would-be governor friend with a shady land development scheme and aiding a romantic interest in fighting it. Nunez leverages these polarities to explore themes like grief, self-destructive guilt, ugly small town politics, and the sacrifices of loyalty. It’s a slow burn, but I found it easy to relate to Harris fighting to keep head above water amidst the mounting uncertainties of adult life. As he tiredly looks out onto a restoratively gorgeous coastal sunrise at the end, it feels like a hard won victory. (2.5/4)

It has a whole lot of shootouts and chases punctuated by a few gags, all of which are done in a fairly pedestrian way that doesn't take advantage of Keenen Ivory Wayans' talents particularly well. The plot here is a mess of clichés and the action is just okay stuff, and while the comedy has a few decent laughs here and there, it's mostly obvious jokes. At least the film has one really bright spark in Jada Pinkett Smith who really does a lot in a supporting part and practically runs away with the whole thing, though that's still not enough to make A Low Down Dirty Shame much of a great movie even if it is mildly enjoyable.

reviews.text: Filmmakers I thought about while watching this highly experiential work: Nicolas Windig Refn, Wong Kar Wai, Phillipe Grandrieux, Brian De Palma, Claire Denis. Also, features some long takes that would make Lav Diaz or Tsai Ming-liang blush. But here, the long take is applied to an anti-erotic, depressed, oneiric neo(n)-noir, with cuts to fauxpocalyptic cityscapes of Japan’s post-bubble urban decay. keenly observed psychosexual dynamics which are not always overtly sexual per se but come out in sublimated gestures. reviews.text: Doris Wishman cobbles together a slasher movie out of another, partially-lost movie; scraps of outtakes and stock footage; and whatever she had enough money left to film. Opens with a baffling montage of scenes and events from a film that doesn't exist, and goes from there. Padded with close-ups of various actors (notably the adult-film star Samantha Fox) doing Lou Costello 'fraidy-cat mugging faces. Continuity editing, eyeline matches, the 180-degree rule, all those rules you learned in learned in film school... you'd better forget about those for now.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: They say you can't polish a turd. Doris polishes many turds and accidentally explodes the slasher genre into microscopic pieces. Vicki comes home. A headline reads, "Teen survives rape & river, makes friends." Billy and Mary make it, but sometimes Billy isn't Billy. He has a Playboy bunny tattoo. Hold music plays while people navigate houses. I receive a phone call, like in a Godfrey Ho movie, to tie me in. Vicki dances for me, it's been a long time since she's received attention from men. Mary (or was it Vicki?) dreams of making love in flashing colors and being stabbed multiple times by her family. Billy likes scary masks. Vicki and Mary's dad gets stuffed into a refrigerator. Mary carries an axe in a briefcase. You may be wondering how I know all of this? They all kept diaries, and an old woman dubbed the story to BetaSP.

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: Doris Wishman was a boon to humankind. And A NIGHT TO DISMEMBER is her gospel, a photocopy of contemporary horror hits (THE AMITYILLE HORROR, HALLOWEEN) transmutated into a collage of psychic damage. Vikki Kent (adult star Samantha Fox) returns home after a stint in a mental institution. From there, the movie pretty much forges a genre of its own. Fists punch through chests. Negative ghosts interrupt make-out sessions. Wailing guitar solos overlap with mid-century library music. As the movie continues, pacing becomes more uneven. Established rules of structure and narrative are left behind. It's as if the dreamy abyss slowly engulfs us until there's no escape. A NIGHT TO DISMEMBER joins TETSUO: THE IRON MAN, SLEEPAWAY CAMP, and THE LAST HOUSE ON DEAD END STREET as a foundational horror film that eternally haunts my psyche. To quote Anton LaVey, a movie like this is "a beast that should be exercised, not exorcised." (Joseph A. Ziemba)

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: An unnerving, guilt-ridden and surreal silent era nightmare that is stripped of title cards that might help balance you and instead drops you head-first into the horrifying images of masked faces, expressionist dancing, torn photographs and literal dreams/fantasies trapped within concrete walls and prison bars. The uncanny use of non-linear editing and shifting, subjective perspective creating this stylish psychological fracturing effect as these past lives lost in time try to come to violent terms with the tangible reality of their current institutionalized surroundings. This should be as well-known and studied as the German expressionists.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: Okay, I’ll be very realistic about everything in this film, starting with its original context. This work was never meant to be experienced in total silence and full of confusion. In Japan, there was the benshi tradition, live narrators who guided the audience through the emotions, dialogues, and intricacies of silent films. They were an essential part of cinema, so much so that they were often more famous than the actors themselves. So, without a skilled benshi to provide narrative structure, anyone watching today, like me, is faced only with a succession of dazzling and feverish images. At times it’s captivating, but it’s also completely disorienting, since you’re caught in a fragmented storm of expressionist gestures, surreal compositions, and fractured…

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: It’s surprising to me that stories with such sentimentality surrounding physical or mental disabilities were box office hits in the 50s, 60s and 70s. Nowadays they are almost entirely read off as complete award bait and rarely hold the charm and emotion that is required for a heartfelt viewing. This is why watching A Patch of Blue felt fresh and compelling. It isn’t necessarily because it was innovative or daring but because it’s so genuine with its storytelling and excels in its simplicity. Each character arc and plot point are relevant and feel constantly engaging, allowing the filmmakers and actors to possess such sincerity. This is just a sweet yet never overly artificial piece of classic entertainment. Plus, no one deserved that sweet Oscar gold more than Shelley Winters that year.

reviews.author: sarah
reviews.text: My apprehension about films that deal with race or disabilities is completely justified considering Hollywood’s history (and even current status), so A Patch of Blue—a film that explores both race and blindness— made me quite nervous to start. To my surprise, this film actually shows a great deal of sensitivity to both matters, and presents the love story so sincerely and convincingly that I couldn’t help but be utterly charmed. This doesn't completely erase the film's problems, but I still really admire its effort (and Sidney Poitier’s smile).

Civilization, a structured relationship built on financial stability, a lifestyle that is sterile, claustrophobic and modern. Maybe Criterion or Cohen Media will clean it up and make it available, because it's low-key one of the best Merchant Ivories outside their top tier of stately period pieces, giving us a warm, totally charming adaptation of Kaylie Jones' autobiographical novel about growing up mostly in Paris as the daughter of novelist James Jones (From Here to Eternity, The Thin Red Line). The Jones analogue is played by Kris Kristofferson in one of his best roles, striking a perfect balance between crusty ex-soldier and literate, liberal-minded novelist-father,…

reviews.text: James Ivory’s A Soldier’s Daughter Never Cries is a poignant yet understated exploration of family dynamics and cultural identity. Loosely based on Kaylie Jones’ semi-autobiographical novel, the film chronicles the shifting lives of the expatriate Willis family as they navigate love, loss, and self-discovery. While it’s filled with moments of tender beauty, the film’s uneven pacing and lack of narrative focus occasionally undermine its emotional impact. The story is divided into two distinct halves, each reflecting a different stage in the Willis family’s journey. In the first half, we see the family in Paris, adopting Benoît (Leelee Sobieski’s deeply affecting younger counterpart, played by Samuel Gruen), a French orphan who struggles to integrate into their cosmopolitan world. The film’s second…

reviews.text: One tiny detail, ignored by most, in the diplomatic cables put out by Wikileaks in 2010 caused some confusion among international film critics. In it, Xi Jinping (then Party Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party, now President) talked about his enthusiasm for the films of Jia Zhangke, the director of films such as Still Life and 24 City. Jia's early films were made illicitly, without permission from Chinese authorities, and they were generally interpreted as being critical of his country's government. Subtly critical, granted, but certainly critical enough to preclude official approval. Or so we thought.

reviews.author: Doc Cortex
reviews.text: When I was commissioned by critically acclaimed blog, Obscurendure, to write a Viking season I was as happy as Larry. With the afore mentioned blog now on sabbatical I'm left with copious amounts of Viking based fodder to sit through, and at least 'The Darkest Day' is not the worst by a long way. The standard Viking film is full of historical inaccuracies and artistic license to say the least, however this offering takes a different approach. It looks like its been made by a group of over zealous museum employees who value authenticity above a story and entertainment. There's plenty of scenes where monks walk through the cold northern landscape, followed by Vikings who are equally cold and enjoying the Northumberland landscape even less. At times its gritty and disturbing, but it's never fun. I'd watch The Vikings box set instead if I was you.

reviews.author: AJ
reviews.text: I didn't know this was a Blood Simple remake until I was reading other reviews after I finished. It felt familiar, but, yeah, it's a point-for-point remake just carried over as a period piece to the Chinese west. While the Coen Brothers' film is a masterclass in suspense, Zhang Yimou leans heavily into a screwball/slapstick blend of comedy that effectively stamps out any suspense that could be carried through scenes. The lavish costumes and production design are nice eye candy, and I love the desert inn setting in historical China that draws the tradition of Dragon Inn to mind. I do like the non-international title more: A Simple Noodle Story, but both are great titles.

reviews.author: Calvin Kemph 🤠
reviews.text: I like to think I’m an ardent fan of outsider remakes of cultural cornerstone films. That is, one outside a dominant movie culture, remaking that work. So, when A Woman, a Gun and a Noodle Shop says in the opening credits that it’s a remake of Blood Simple, that is like an invitation for me. I like anyone outside the US remaking American films, far more than when the opposite happens.

reviews.author: Deven KB
reviews.text: An interesting example of cinematic cultural crossover, and honestly a pretty fun watch. The problem is it makes the fatal mistake of inserting very broad comedy into one of the least broadly comedic Coen stories, and Zhang Yimou doesn’t change the story or overall tone thereof enough to make it work. In the end, this mostly just reminded me how much I like Blood Simple.

reviews.author: braden
reviews.text: “Imagine that; the body, in all its delicious detail, fading away, leaving a skeleton with iron legs.”With exemplary world building and grotesque imagery; Peter Greenaway’s A Zed & Two Noughts is an arresting and masterfully built meditation on duality, life, and decay explored through the symmetrical grief of two widowed twins. Sprawling over a multitude of ideas surrounding nature, evolution, and humanity, the weird and often disturbing narrative is graciously complimented by striking cinematography, rich colours, an effectual orchestral score, and strange, unsettling visuals of real animals decomposing in stop motion; excelling in both creation of atmosphere and capturing of attention. It can seem kind of grandiose, but it doesn’t try not to be, and Greenaway’s artistic vision and Vierny’s eye for photography just bring the material to life so wonderfully.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: A zebra has stripes that are nearly consistent in their perfect symmetry, and yet no two zebra have an identical stripe pattern. Distinctiveness is in direct contrast to uniformity—disorder and order pitted against each other. I believe this is the core theme of A Zed & Two Naughts, a film which has a title reflecting nearly every aspect of its narrative. Beginnings are only beginnings if there exists a clear end, and there can be no endings without beginnings. Decomposition is seen as a way of deconstructing and reckoning with our delicate, feeble mortality, but in a turn of grand irony only Mr. Greenaway is capable of pulling off, it’s none other than nature itself that serves as a foil to this…

reviews.author: orson houellebecq
reviews.text: I find it ironic that Peter Greenaway has said that he wishes he could remake this, his "most troubled and troubling offspring", as he once called it, since not only is it one of my all-time favorite films, but I also think it is hands-down Greenaway's most singularly flawless achievement as a filmmaker. Appropriately, considering the film's preoccupation with symmetry, to me it feels like his most "balanced" work. It's thematically dense, visually immaculate, and above all, wickedly funny, something which doesn't seem to get mentioned often enough in relation to Greenaway's work. I've watched it too many times to still laugh out loud at every joke, but scene-for-scene I honestly consider it a brilliant comedy, on top of everything…

reviews.author: WraithApe
reviews.text: Film of a thousand cuts, tableaux rendered with an artist's eye for colour and composition. Rigorous formality framing meticulous reconstruction, an enigmatic master's coded fragments washed up on the shore of time. Girl with a red hat. The music lesson. The art of painting. Zoo ooz(e). Symmetry is key. Autogenetic transformation of unstable matter, apple to zebra. A menagerie of light, glass encased swan cadaver, inelegant in corpsed repose, fleeting signifier in the dark pool, temporary nexus, entrance to exit. Glass breakfast, siamese re-convergence, becoming one with unending putrescence and liquefaction snail mass. Compost rotting bodies, sweet oblivion in particulate re-configuration.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Interesting and in many ways quite accidentally dated; I'm not sure how stoked I am to see a story of journalistic ineptitude (certainly timely) represented by a naive girl reporter. It's more than a little sexist even setting aside her truly monumental -- almost implausibly so -- ethical lapses. And in the end she gets a stern talking-to from a grumpy old man. Did we, in 1981, need a relative corrective to the alleged reporter/cowboys of ALL THE PRESIDENT'S MEN? Do we still? Maybe that's an overreaction on my part but, you know, I'm just never sure the hidden dangers of a free press is always a good hill to die on. Still, Newman absolutely kills it as this quiet, sturdy dude who just wants to regain control of his life, and you just can't ever get enough Melinda Dillon. If Sydney Pollack was good at one thing, it was hiring Dave Grusin to make ruinous scores for his movies.

reviews.text: Director Sydney Pollack drew heavily on the visual aesthetic and atmosphere of All the President’s Men (1976) for his neo noir thriller Absence of Malice. Unfortunately it doesn’t have the weight and forward propulsion of the earlier film. Instead of playing out as a procedural it’s a wrong man story with a heavy romance subplot. Sally Field and Paul Newman are a good match and work effectively together. But my favorite actor in the film is young Bob Balaban who dominates every scene like a boss. On the whole it’s slow, somewhat bloated and brimming with breaches of journalistic ethics.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: I remember liking this when I saw it in college, but it is one of Pollack’s worst movies with a preachy overdone script and a Paul Newman lead turn that is not bad exactly but is pure unearned righteousness (the script and Newman got Oscars noms of course). The overdone plotting needs a very long climatic scene for guest star Wilfred Brimley to wrap up while screaming moral superiority. The Newman/Field relationship that is supposed to offer it a through line is loaded with bad ideas. Pollack's dramatic instincts fail him, but he does know how to smooth things over, Roizman makes it look far more inviting than it deserves and there are a murderers row of very good character actors to fill the screen.

Louis Koo heads a group of assassins that makes all their hits look like accidents—in one particularly fun scene we see him and his team brainstorming ways to take out their latest victim. When one of the group dies in what looks like an accident, Koo goes into Gene Hackman mode and starts suspecting everyone and everything around him as being part of a conspiracy. Koo is quite good here, underplaying everything while letting us read the doubt and fear on his face.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Paul Schrader didn't grow up watching movies and TV, reading comic books, listening to rock records, or fixing up old hot rods, so unlike his filmmaker peers he's able to tap into a level of misery and anguish in his work that is totally alien to mainstream entertainment. The fact that this was probably pitched and released as some kind of Fargo knock-off would almost be funny if humor could exist within its field of gravity. Just relentlessly bleak even by Schrader standards, but it doesn't feel like a rote miserabilist project, rather a sincere effort to try and exorcise a few demons.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Schrader translates his and his brother's own oppressive, abusive "Jesus freaks and candy asses" Midwest Calvinist upbringing to Russell Banks' pure dose of freezing cold, New Hampshire murder mystery as it slowly unfurls itself into a teeth-pullingly miserable familial melodrama. Has such a strange downbeat, funeral mood, and a very deliberately muted, snowy look that compliments the haunted, foggy-memory slow-burn editing structure and makes this feel like it's clumsily digging into and reopening festered generational wounds with a sense of lonely detachment.

reviews.text: So neo-noir it aches: Small cast of pungent characters brought to life with tremendous embodiment; visually enrapturing against the backdrop of a Palm Springs suburb, all dusty roads and sun drenched unease; sexiness infused with a search for oblivion in the body of another; everything points toward doom. Jason Patric is tremendous in this. A live wire of a man. Nervy, yearning, broken, caring. There’s a lot to dig in this movie but he’s the greatest argument in its favor. The ending is so devastatingly sad. This adaptation perfectly encapsulates the pulse of what makes Jim Thompson’s dark-hearted novels work so well.

Matthew Fox was the only one that seemed to care about the film, because he gave a really surprising performance. There’s the pleasure of ‘Hassan CHOP!’ But mostly I think it’s down to the fact Bugs and Daffy are talking to each other about each other. “What’s up, Duck?” There’s an easy shorthand and camaraderie with these guys – they’re going to Pismo Beach after having made like 100 cartoons together. Maybe that’s why they forgot to take the left at Albuquerque.

reviews.text: Interspersed throughout Susan Walter's All I Wish are a series of wildly jarring, totally inexplicable straight-to-camera monologues from the film’s various characters. One moment Sharon Stone’s Senna is flirting with Tony Goldwyn’s Adam, the next Ellen Burstyn is sitting in front of a black background talking about how every woman wishes for “better boobs.” These interstitials are demonstrative of an insecure filmmaker; rather than allow the film’s narrative to speak for itself, Walter has her characters simply state their feelings, philosophies, and theses. One might even hazard a guess that the film’s talking-head motif was developed in post-production, when it became clear that the film wasn’t coming together on its own.

It's a super-low-budget (reportedly about $20k) real-life-superhero story along the lines of Boy Wonder or The Specials, or to some degree, Alien Raiders. The seams and budget limitations certainly show, but leaving those aside, the usual problems of micro-indies are dealt with well — the acting is competent (Dexter's James Remar makes a fun cackling villain, the sound is fine, the superhero costumes look both handmade (like they would be in this scenario) and passably cool, and above all, the fight choreography is convincing. The film's biggest problem is that it can be hard to buy the characters as proper heroes when they're so easily pushed into apathetic resignation…

reviews.author: Zachary
reviews.text: Alois Nebel is a challenging little film set in the Czech Republic (then Czechoslovokia) at the end of the Soviet Union. Adapted from a trilogy of graphic novels, this striking work of black and white rotoscoped animation uses a dizzying, at times difficult to follow elliptical structure that weaves the viewer through the experiences of its titular character. With its shuffled timeline, the film is able to collapse history and present the chaotic period faced by many countries which filled the space between Nazi Germany and Soviet Russia. Some of the technique loses its luster for me after the first act, and it would be better to use the slight runtime to focus more tightly on the protagonist, but the movie is still both puzzling and evocative.

reviews.text: "Alpha City" ist unter den ohnehin oft schwer zugänglichen Filmen Eckhart Schmidts wahrscheinlich der schwierigste, weil er weniger fasziniert, als "Der Fan" (1981), "Das Gold der Liebe" (1983) und "Loft" (1985). Atmosphärisch dicht ist der gänzlich nachts gedrehte Film dennoch, und von fulminanter Eighties-Musik begleitet - tonangebend ist "Desire" von Yello. Zudem zeigt sich Schmidt erneut als Romantiker, im Sinne der Kunstströmung Anfang des 19. Jahrhunderts: hier sind es Gesetze der Nacht, die befolgt werden müssen, oder gebrochen und dann gesühnt werden müssen. Anspielungen auf Richard Wagner in anderen seiner Filme lassen vermuten, dass Schmidt bei seinem exzessiven Musikeinsatz Filme als Musikdramen denkt.

Neben ALPHA CITY gibt es zwei berühmtere US-amerikanische Nachtfilme, ebenfalls aus dem Jahr 1985: AFTER HOURS und INTO THE NIGHT. Eckhart Schmidts Version ist die künstlerisch-verkopftere, kühlere deutsche. Aber sie ist nicht besser, denn seine Vision hat nur Ideen und Szenen, keine echte Handlung. Toll anzusehen ist das aber allemal in der ALPHA CITY oben im Dicken B an der Spree und der Soundtrack ist mit Yello und Konsorten das coolste, was man aus deutscher Produktion damals auf Platte pressen konnte und das NICHT trotz sondern WEGEN der 3-4 Al Corley-Songs.

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: Anthony Waller's direction is nothing if not distinctive. In a different context, his hyperactive camera, dramatically overblown lighting, and penchant for finding over-the-top, wacky comedy in unlikely moments could add up to a singular vision. I'm reminded a bit of Jeunet inserting very French, farcical hijinks into the otherwise solemn Alien: Resurrection. That style is more at home here, given that Landis' original is certainly a funny film, but it still very much feels like the product of more than a dozen writers that it is, and its deluge of cheap CGI probably looked as bad in 1997 as it does now.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: What began as a personal project soon shaped cinema history especially when we talk about postwar popular cinema. At its core stood Brigitte Bardot, although not her first screen appearance, it unmistakably worked as the trigger for her public screen persona, consolidating the image that would come to define her career and propel her into international notoriety. Directed by Roger Vadim, who happened to be her husband at the time, the film became his entry into directing. It was born when intimacy, creativity, and professional drive overlapped unexpectedly. The film did way more than entertain the craving public of that time; it shifted perceptions across borders. Behind the camera, Vadim found both a beginning and a statement.

reviews.text: Animal is another creature feature crossed off the watchlist, and while it’s a decent enough watch, it’s not doing much to stand out in an already crowded subgenre. The characters are unlikable across the board, the story never fully pulls you in, and while the creature design has potential, it’s squandered by that all-too-familiar combination of jittery camerawork and formulaic structure. It’s one of those films that feels like déjà vu if you’ve seen enough of these—Feast, Splinter, The Lair, and so on. There’s some fleeting fun to be had, but the overall quality stays buried deep in the basement for most of its runtime.

A film about realizing too late that it’s too late, the fog clearing just enough to reveal to you more fog. It’s not all doom and gloom however, hope clings on. And, like a memory, no matter how badly you may sometimes want the contrary, you’ll have it forever.

reviews.author: Bob R.
reviews.text: Leslie Ann Warren is Lilly, a performance artist who creates an anonymous telephone-confessional called "Apology". The idea is to offer people a chance for guilt-free catharsis. Of course a bad apple named Claude decides he likes the sound of Lilly's voice on the answering-machine. Stalky, stabby, shooty shenanigans ensue. Warren, Peter Weller and John Glover all are in their fit primes, and Harvey Fierstein plays an unusually pleasant and well-laundered vagrant. Unfortunately, the talent alone isn't enough to save this one. An all-too-familiar police-procedural story coupled with a plodding pace and no surprises whatsoever make "Apology" the movie-title that writes its own indictment.

reviews.author: Jeff Williams
reviews.text: Early made-for-cable attempt to conceptualize and address the post-modern confessional obsession in the guise of a serial killer thriller. There's some occasional snatches of style in the music and art scenes but the film really needed less character hostility and arguments as it was hard to get behind anyone except for the Alpo-eating bum played by Harvey Fierstein. Lesley Ann Warren is suitably neurotic and easy on the eyes as the lead, and Peter Weller is well suited for his detective role, but no one is sympathetic enough to really engage. The supporting cast does feature some interesting, if limited, appearances by George Loros, John Glover, Jimmy Ray Weeks and Chis Noth and the story is involving enough even if the characters aren't.

reviews.author: David W
reviews.text: The last 30 minutes of Jackie’s ode to Indiana Jones deliver some gloriously creative and high-flying action set pieces. However, the first 60 or so minutes …well, the less said about that, the better. From its misguided homage to Raider's of the Lost Ark's opening, to some awkward exposition and gratuitously off-kilter music-video-inspired inter-cutting, to some rather lethargic screwball comedy interludes, Armour of God trudges through its first hour in unusually ham-handed fashion. Goofy montages, Chinese butter jokes, and a gratuitously effeminate waiter make for less than inspired Hong Kong action cinema, even of the comedic variety. And the one ray of hope amid this mess—an extended vehicle chase through picturesque European streets—fails to truly excite (at least this viewer).…

But this time it isn't just a brief moment and they start a life together until Asako once again has to confront her past.

reviews.author: ReAnimateMe
reviews.text: This movie doesn't deserve all the hate it's getting. A funny movie about two not-so-bright ladies is something I enjoy, because I think it's tougher to pull off effectively than it may seem. The two leads in this one also wrote the script, which is sadly not something you see too often these days. They're both talented comediennes with great timing and they play well off of each other. (Being friends in real life probably helps!) I was entertained and amused, and that's all that I wanted from this movie. It delivered; I was laughing out loud. So many reviews seem to be complaining that it has hints of Romy and Michele but that it's not the same. Do you know why that is? Because this is a different movie, you guys. See also: One of my other favorite movies featuring two vapid lady characters, "Dick."

I'd love to appreciate this for using the visual appeal of a video game cutscene to expand on a metaverse in fragile virtual reality, but the video game itself is dull, and while I love ladies with big guns I don't think the artifice of the digital world serves Oshii as well in live action without further manipulation of the image. I'm also not huge on the mallgoth aesthetic, the black feathered wings and scene fringe is a bit much, and while heightened archetypes are a key component of a distinct avatar, it quite simply looks ridiculous

reviews.text: There's nothing quite like the films of Nabwana: Mayhem distilled into its most bonkers components, both a parody and homage to American action flix. And it hurtles with breakneck absurdity, camp humor and outrageous no-fi SFX. Central is VJ Emmie's meta-narration: wickedly caustic, roasting every scene with deadpan zingers. Yet behind this is something candidly honest, a spirit of place, funny, almost tender, the reality of life in the ghettos of Kampala. Sometimes it takes an outsider to tell it like it is.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: One of Lee's most formally audacious and assaultive films, and as scathing a media satire as there has ever been. An angry, ugly, completely batshit reworking of Network and The Producers into a perversely funny and horrifying vision of America's historical racism maintaining itself in images/entertainment/industry and the illusion of choice that white money gives to black artists. "Look at what you contributed to!" "Keep 'em laughing." Not over the choice to film most of this in crummy DV (which make the bland office spaces and heightened Wayans performance feel even weirder, and make the eventual snuff and essay montage destination even uglier) and then the images of the modern minstrel show on this very colorful 16mm so that it uncomfortably pops off the screen! God Ellen Kuras, and Spike Lee who found the only good use for Michael Rapaport anyone ever will.

It's ultimately a jab at the money-grubbing Hollywood, and the faceless crowd hiding behind their invisible "black face" who feed off black misery as entertainment, whether knowingly or not. Technical wise this is as stripped down as can be. Thematically, however, Bamboozled is arguably Lee's biggest risk of his career.

reviews.text: White audiences were not ready for Bamboozled in 2000 and, to be honest, things have not really changed. This critical and commercial failure has now, widely, been reappraised as the masterpiece it is - but still upsets the right people (the sign of good political filmmaking). It is a film easy to describe as ahead of its time, but in reality a film that was so of its time (and continues to speak to this time) that so many could not handle it.

Film as self-justification and self-revelation; at first I thought this might be a case of 'mild interest but ultimate dislike' as with my response to the superficially similar Finisterrae but as the film continued my appreciation of Bressane's awareness of not only the function of the images but the literal images themselves (as enhanced by a steadfast refusal to place a cut without reason), images that analyze their own ability to counteract and communicate the weight inherently defined by that within them.

reviews.author: Yuri Deliberalli
reviews.text: Bressane afirma que este é um filme sobre o nada, o que não deixa de ser uma verdade e uma mentira. Isso porque o experimentalismo difuso do diretor pode afastar a lógica ou a continuidade narrativa, mas sem também transformá-lo em uma obra episódica. Ao mesmo tempo, há uma percepção sobre o humor, o imaginativo e o poder da imagem que incomoda (no bom sentido) pela clareza e consciência com que os planos são articulados.

reviews.text: Scots director Bill Forsyth's final American film starring Robin Williams was not well received by the studio or test audiences which resulted in the film, along with Forsyth's career, basically disappearing.It is a flawed film, but still retains many of Forsyth's signature stylistic approches to directing. It's tender, understated, whimsical and offbeat. It very ambitiously tries to tell the story of the meaning of (human) life, and does this by having Williams portray an ordinary everyman over 5 different historical periods covering about 6,000 years. It's deliberately slow and meandering, like life itself. I like it a lot.I would love to see a restoration of the film back to the way the director intended it to be but, for now, I'm quite content to watch the only version we have.

reviews.text: Bill Forsyth's Local Hero (1983) was the best film I saw in 2022, just a wonderful experience and one I urge everyone else to seek out. His follow up, Comfort and Joy (1984), was also very well received at the time, and so buoyed buy this Forsyth left his native Scotland to try and make it in Hollywood. However despite earning more critical success with 1987's Housekeeping and 1989's Breaking In, neither of them made any money. So after/despite that Being Human was his biggest creative and financial risk, a $40 million epic tracing the journey of humanity across the millennia as seen through the eternal recurrence of one man. reviews.text: Telling a child a story is a thrill. It’s a privilege to see wonder reflected in their eyes at the words they hear you say. I’m still that child who wants to be told stories that make me wonder. Some movies not only tell a story well, they do so in language that speaks to you as the child who first fell in love with being told stories. The best are those that achieve this without really trying. Then there are those movies that someone or group of someones believe they know how to manufacture language & story, with an end result that grates on the ears & the eyes. One such way this happens, is last-minute addition of narration.

reviews.author: Matt Neglia
reviews.text: Let’s negotiate, shall we? Imagine a more brutal version of “Argo” mixed with elements of “Bridge Of Spies” (Without the laughs and sentimentality) and you get BEIRUT. Jon Hamm gives his best film performance yet in the tense, adult thriller filled with twists and turns. Entertaining, paced well and it also features a good musical score. They don’t make adult thrillers like this often anymore which is another reason why we shouldn’t be closing the door on this one.

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: The sort of muscular, morally hazy pulp fiction for adults that I eat up for breakfast, lunch and dinner. Sure, it’s the very definition of middlebrow, but the numerous plot twists make up for any lack of ponderousness. Jon Hamm is the perfect drunken, haunted Tony Gilroy protag, always one step ahead of everyone in the room, regardless of how much he's had to drink or lingering melancholy from the past. There's some ham-fisted political commentary regarding Reagan era globalism in the back half that feels a touch forced, but the rest really sings as a tight programmer.

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: Seems to believe the standard nonsense that political conflict is born not of genuine disagreements but rather of simple misunderstandings, and the only bit of substance is the trite but true idea that you have to face your traumas rather than run away from them, but I'll be damned if Tony Gilroy doesn't write the perfect political thriller that you can pick up at the airport before a long flight, read exactly once, and buy a copy for your father before forgetting about entirely for the rest of your life.

reviews.text: Absolutely delightful regional early effort from Jay Woelfel that was filmed right here in Columbus! The budget is minuscule and the whole concept is almost too bold for the budget involved, but somehow Woelfel pulls it off and you get a beautifully surreal nonsensical dreamscape of a movie with things there one second and gone the next and monsters creeping in and out of frames. Some of the scenes are filmed inside OSU buildings and it works really well. Ever since my own college days, I’ve always thought old campus buildings were creepy as fuck.

reviews.author: belial_carboni
reviews.text: Beyond Dream's Door is a mesmerizing lofi odyssey of psychadelic proportions. A kaleidoscope of technicolour and surreal visuals create an ambitious low budget nightmare. I've been hoping for a proper release of this and today is the dang day!

reviews.text: Talk about a double downer, I watched Lars Von Trier's “Dogville” and Alejandro Gonzalez Inarritu’s “Biutiful” back to back. Despite the overload of misanthropic nihilism, it made for an interesting comparison between the two filmmakers. “Biutiful” is the kind of film Von Trier can only dream of making. Inarritu is everything Von Trier isn’t; he has his finger on the pulse of the human condition. Rather than telling gimmicky stories, he tells stories about deeply flawed people in a way that showcases some of the worst aspects of humanity, whilst always allowing them a small thread of hope and optimism that they can piece their lives back together, even though they seldom do, or if they do, it’s not for…

reviews.text: Linn da Quebrada está em obras e o transtorno é todo seu. "Bixa Travesty" é ofensivo, agressivo, subversivo, explícito e militante. É tudo o que o Brasil precisa neste momento. Seu discurso surge para desestabilizar, quebrar os padrões, chocar, desafiar a heternormatividade e o pensamento em linha reta. Sua função é muito menos organizar um pensamento ou uma filosofia e, sim, tirar o tijolo de baixo, sabotar o muro. Kiko Goifman e Claudia Priscilla não fazem apenas um retrato de Linn da Quebrada, mas, junto com ela, que é coautora do roteiro, realizam um filme-manifesto em que partem do registro de seu cotidiano para apresentar um universo incômodo porque fica restrito ao que a superfície chama de submundo. Este filme…

Using the brain of the man who caused the accident, a criminal in league with the mob, the operation is a huge success until character traits of the mobster begin over taking the friendly college professor and he heads back to New York to even the score with those who wished him dead including mob boss Bela Lugosi.

reviews.author: Ira Brooker
reviews.text: It's straight bullshit that this gets remembered as a minor Karloff/Lugosi vehicle. This is a Stanley Ridges vehicle through and through. Ridges kills it as the kindly professor who inherits the brain and personality of a vicious gangster after both men are severely injured in a car wreck. No disrespect to the marquee names - Karloff is fine as the colleague who pulls off the brain swap and tries to connive his way into a fortune in stolen loot, and Bela does what he can with a nothing part as a rival gangster - but Ridges is a revelation in a dual role, morphing believably and unrecognizably from mild-mannered academic to cruel sociopath with little more than a change of hairdo and a shift in attitude. Neither the story nor the direction is any great shakes, but Ridges is mesmerizing enough that I didn't much care.

reviews.text: 'Black Friday' is an underrated Universal picture starring horror icons Boris Karloff and Bela Lugosi (though Stanley Ridges actually has a much bigger part than Lugosi) that takes elements of previous horror classics and mixes them with what feels more like a Warner gangster film. There are hints of 'Frankenstein', 'The Wolf Man' and 'Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde' in the story about Karloff's gentle scientist performing a brain transplant to change his friend's life, only to give him the brain of a homicidal gangster that can take over at any moment.I really enjoyed this one for it's more pulpy tone and I loved Lugosi playing a gangster, while Karloff pulled off the perfect balance of a well-meaning but driven man. It's also a pretty good looking movie with some moody black-and-white cinematography.

reviews.text: The mystery beyond death is the central theme of The Black Pit of Dr M. This atmospheric Mexican horror film focuses on a pact between two doctors; the first to die will find a way to return and show the other what waits behind death's door. The style of the film was clearly influenced by the likes of German Expressionism and Universal Horror. Director Fernando Méndez makes grand use of light and shadow along with fog, creaking doors and a thundering foreboding score to give the film a real ominous ambiance. The narrative features a number of subplots which at first seem superfluous to the main theme, but eventually coalesce around the central thrust - delivering a story that would…

reviews.author: Liz
reviews.text: I can't get enough of these 50s Mexican modern-gothic horrors! There's no black pit here, but Méndez wrings every last drop of atmosphere out of the single clinic location which most of the film takes place at. These Mexican films are clearly cheapies, but I love how they make up for those budget shortfalls by ramping up the luridness of the plot, throwing acid attacks, flame stunts, and creepy doctor-student relationships into the mix. I didn't realize it until midway through writing this, but Ray Dennis Steckler's The Incredibly Strange Creatures Who Stopped Living and Became Mixed-Up Zombies totally ripped this off.

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: The first movie in the Indicator Mexico Macabre Box set is Black Pit of Dr. M. A super atmospheric and well-filmed late 50’s horror tale from director Fernando Méndez. I don’t have too much to say about it. It works well, looks great, has some very solid make-up effects and with just over 80 minutes runtime flows very smoothly. A perfect little movie for a late night Mexican Horror fix. The cinematography is definitely the star of the show. The female lead Mapita Cortés is photographed particularly beautifully and even though she’s not the best actress in the world, she fits the setting perfectly. We are off to a good start with the Mexican Horror set.

reviews.text: One of the most strikingly beautifully shot schlocky films I've ever seen. The black and white cinematography oozes gothic atmosphere and the shots of the moonlit sky with foreboding clouds are sublime. The film's basic lesson is don't muck around with death. I have a soft spot for these older Mexican horror films. This one doesn't disappoint.

reviews.text: A topical Canadian tax shelter quickie cranked out to take advantage of the 1977 NYC blackout, BLACKOUT has four psychos led by Robert Carradine terrorizing residents in a high rise during a massive storm that causes the titular event. It never gets as exploitative as its R rating would allow and other than a few instances of swearing, it could almost pass for a TV movie. Jim Mitchum is about as bland a hero as they could get, and it's doubtful that old-timers like June Allyson, Ray Milland, and Jean-Pierre Aumont were chomping at the bit to be in an exploitation movie by the director of CATHY'S CURSE.

reviews.author: Joe Wawrzyniak
reviews.text: A pretty nasty Canadian crime action thriller inspired by the infamous 1977 New York City blackout, this modestly budgeted picture manages to pack a really mean punch. Director Eddy Matalon gives the harsh premise concerning a quartet of vicious criminals terrorizing an apartment building during a blackout an appropriately rough and gritty tone. Moreover, Matalon generates a good deal of nerve-rattling tension as well as doesn't punk out on the ugly violence and raw brutality. On top of this, this movie earns extra points for its evenly balanced depiction of how a crisis situation brings out the best and worst in people.

reviews.author: Jeremy Milks
reviews.text: The producers of this film do a good job convincing us this takes place in the bankrupt grime of 70's NYC, but most of this was filmed in Montreal with a few establishing shots of Manhattan to complete the illusion. The main production team consisted of John Dunning and André Link, the Canadian duo who brought you slasher classics like My Bloody Valentine and Happy Birthday To Me. Director Eddy Matalon was responsible for the Canuxploitation brain-melter Cathy's Curse (which I'm still trying to process). There's plenty of sleaze and random brutal violence in Blackout, much like similar films Enemy Territory, Tenement and Siege, but it never really comes together as anything special. Shares a similar plot device to Alone In The Dark, which is a much better film, but this is worth seeing for Canuxploitation fans.

reviews.author: Ryan C
reviews.text: This gritty thriller started out great with a couple of really intense murder scenes, but soon devolves into a standard 70s cop thriller, very much like The French Connection but not as interesting. The reliable John Marley turns in a good performance, and there's a lot of familiar character actors in supporting roles, but the film is a bit sloppy. The camerawork is all over the place and the sound is utterly awful. I'm pretty sure they just shot the film in a functioning police station because you can hear people talking in the background while the actors are speaking their lines. The filmmakers probably felt this would add to the realism but it's really just distracting. John Cacavas' score is excellent, however; especially when his romantic theme is used to counterpoint the murders.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Some people never get to realize their full potential, or stick around long enough to do what they were so clearly put on this Earth to do. Maybe they die young, or maybe they just keep getting in their own way. Or maybe, if they’re anything like singer-songwriter Blaze Foley, they find a way to do both, burning out like stars that leave their light behind. But Foley never wanted to be a star, shining only for itself. He wanted to be a legend, and live forever. Thanks to Ethan Hawke’s slippery, whiskey-soaked biopic of the late musician — and newcomer Benjamin Dickey’s casually spellbinding lead performance — he’s closer than ever to getting his wish.

reviews.author: Kevflix And Chill
reviews.text: A music biopic that manages not to feel like every other music biopic. Told in nonlinear fashion, it highlights the life of “unknown legend” Blaze Foley, singer/songwriter/storyteller and pioneer of outlaw country played wonderfully here by Ben Dickey. The story jumps between three time periods, Blaze’s early romance with Sybil Rosen (Alia Shawkat), his later touring career, and a posthumous radio interview with his frequent collaborators Townes Van Zandt (Charlie Sexton) and Zee (Josh Hamilton). The early romance is easily the best. Dickey and Shawkat’s chemistry set the screen aglow as minstrel and muse. Sybil Rosen is credited with co-writing along with Ethan Hawke and I suspect that has something to do with the lovely handling of their romance. Blaze has this enigmatic way about him.…

reviews.text: ....Blind Detective presents a couple of interesting contrasts. The most obvious is with 2007's Mad Detective, which has a similar title and is also the story of a young cop enlisting the eponymous former cop to help solve a recent crime. Lau Ching Wan's Mad Detective approaches his investigations with the same techniques as Andy Lau's Blind Detective: he goes through the criminals' motions until he sees exactly what they did, and we see his vision of the recreation on-screen. These visions recall as well Running on Karma, in which Andy Lau plays a former monk who can see people's karma, the crimes they committed in past lives. Again, he's called in to help a young detective solve a crime.…

reviews.text: Apparently I watched this a couple of years ago but couldn’t remember anything about it. Usually that’s not a good sign, but I liked this a lot, probably more than the previous time. What’s most amazing about this movie, as with most of the films by the To/Wai duo, is the melange of tones. Suspense, police procedural, romance, slapstick comedy, action, even a touch of horror. This shouldn’t work and yet somehow it all does. Andy Lau is at his most charismatic when he’s playing a slightly goofy character as he does here—many directors make the mistake of straining to make him look cool in every shot, which tends to backfire. And nobody knows how to use Sammi Cheng’s awkwardness…

reviews.text: In London, tough, uncompromising, Sergeant Tom Brandt (Jason Stathman) is deployed to find a vicious serial killer who calls himself the Blitz (Aidan Gillen). His M.O. is murdering police officers. Brandt is assigned a gay partner Sergeant Porter Nash ( Paddy Cosidine) to assist him with the man hunt. The Blitz manages to elude Brandt and Nash at every turn as more police officers are killed.Blitz is based on Ken Bruen’s novel. The film is a fast-paced cat and mouse game between the police and the killer. The film explores how the police have to work in a modern society and the sacrifices they make.Blitz is a gritty and violent action/thriller with strong performances across the board.Stathman is solid as Brandt, the rough and masculine police detective. However Gillen is the highlight of the film as the sadistic serial killer. Gillen’s performance is energetic, intense, and crazed which made the Blitz a memorable psychopath.

The situations they encounter are more absurd than harrowing, while nevertheless solidifying the complementary nature of their newfound friendship. Parts of the film work well as broad comedy, but the quieter moments lack the existential heft typically associated with 1970s road movies. Still, I enjoyed it. The chemistry between the two female leads is effervescent. I like the Riz Ortolani score, too. The main harmonica ditty reminds me of Cisco Pike.

reviews.author: Michael Shawn
reviews.text: Few films plaster a smile on my face like this one did. The drop-dead gorgeous Monica Vitti (giving Cate Blanchett vibes to me) and Claudia Cardinale go on a wild road trip through several different film genres and basically non sequitur their way through the film. It's absurd and surreal and just plain delightful. There's no plot per se, so it relies heavily on the two ladies' personas, a challenge which they tackle with aplomb. The two have perfect chemistry and their personalities shine through encounters with the mob, and cops, and a kid on the run, and twin suitors. There's a lot of slapstick that may be a turn-off for some, but I enjoyed the high-energy and lunacy on display. It's a comedic adventure like only the Italians could pull off, and I loved every minute of it. Thanks to Andrew Black for recommending it to me.

It has to be said that the film looks rather nice considering the obvious lack of budget. The bright colours and well made costumes give it something of an unexpected opulence that doesn't really translate thrpugh to the narrative. It's slow moving but intetesting in places. reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Mario Bava's signature style of elegantly-crafted gruesomeness, artificial lights and painterly compositions meets its perfect material in this 60s pop art Giallo about a bunch of rich fashion designers and models who have surrounded themselves with an industry of beautiful surfaces and colorful images in an attempt to cover up their greedy, erotic, murderous impulses. Formally turning all their corruption and hollow beauty into this baroque dollhouse (as decadent in terms of production/costume design and lighting as it is sadistically violent!) as it moves through its many meticulous, technicolor funhouse murder machine setpieces. Honestly kind of astonishing how much of the visual vocabulary of the slasher was born right here in 1964, long before anyone who saw this at the time could've known what was coming. Alongside Suspiria and The Beyond, this is probably the Italian horror film.

reviews.text: An unknown killer is stalking and murdering gorgeous fashion models. There's no known motive, or reason behind the brutal attacks. The only common factor is all the potential victims work for a specific modeling house. As the bodies pile up, the police get more and more confused. Who's the killer? Is the killer someone very close to the models? What happens when all your suspects are in jail being held for questioning, and another killing occurs? Mario Bava's Blood and Black Lace is textbook giallo. It's one of the first, and it's been copied too many times to count.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: When the movie camera kills. Bava has always approached cinema as a cinematographer and not a dramatist, he regards everything in terms of shapes, light and color and not action and events and such post-human idea of film is pushed to limit here. The plot could be out of a krimi, but it is seen through a plastic surface: all shine sets, beautiful colors and actresses who becomes dolls to be butchered. The fashion setting serves it well, it is about evolving everything into this false surface and allow it to be destroyed. The images are beautiful and beauty equals death. The only empathy here is towards the murder's blade because Bava love those reds so much.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: A masterpiece of shadowed colors, of composition, and of tension, this film feels like it's at least ten years early. Classify it as the precursor to slashers, as proto-giallo, as Italogothic horror if you please, but what I saw with my own two eyes was a classic slasher, fully formed. A beautiful one, certainly, one that doesn't have the grit and gore of its children, but our faceless killer stalks women one by one until they are all corpses, iconically garbed, and with a plot twist under the mask. Amazing that this was derived from krimi as a reaction, as an artistic flourish.

I watched the theatrical cut under the title Blood Bath, which has been cobbled together from three or four different films from different genres. It eventually ended up being this story about a painter who also happens to be a vampire. He paints his victims before killing them and dropping them in acid. To be fair, the end result is probably a little more coherent story-wise than it had any right to be, but it's still something of a big mess. Much of it was filmed by Jack Hill, but then Stephanie Rothman was brought in and she delivered the vampire stuff. The visuals are way more interesting than the story anyway,…

I’m not sure you would describe the acting in Blood Bath as good or bad, but it very theatrical, exactly what you’d expect if you took a bunch of 1970s New York serious stage actors and put them in cheap horror movie. It’s nice that the stories do have that Twilight Zone / EC twist at the end.

reviews.author: Andrew Warren
reviews.text: Blood Feast is an impactful horror film, being the first Technicolor horror film with gore. While we did have films like Psycho three years earlier, this is the first film where we see red colored blood. And we get a lot of it. This is a wild “splatter” film, that sticks to what it tries to be, and that is a bloody horror film. The acting is terrible, and the story is confusing, but it seems like no one on set cared about making a good film, rather a historic film for the horror genre.

He is so overridden with grief he can't speak properly. It's horrendous acting, but there's something else happening here; the camera sits with him and that medium close-up for far longer than would be considered normal until his bad acting and his wailing, sobbing, grief goes from comedic to…

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: In his book SHOCK VALUE, John Waters summed it up perfectly: “I first saw Blood Feast at my local drive-in. When I saw teenage couples hopping from their cars to vomit, I knew I had found a movie after my own heart.“ After the nudie cutie trend had run its course, director Herschell Gordon Lewis, producer David F. Friedman, and (uncredited) writer Allison Downe decided that there was only one way to go—SPLATTER!! Erupting with pop-art brain-bludgeonings and pitch-black gallows humor, BLOOD FEAST is a cinematic riot that paved the way for everything from Sam Raimi’s EVIL DEAD to Peter Jackson’s DEAD ALIVE. A forever favorite and then some. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

All of the 80’s character stereotypes are here: the valley girl, the punk rocker, the crazy war veteran, the loyal girlfriend, the musically talented boyfriend... whose grandfather mysteriously disappeared off of a fishing dock seventeen years earlier. reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: Wading into this 50s teener turned out pretty well. A woman chemistry instructor at an all girl boarding school grooms one of the students to test a thesis she's trying to publish that the men in the male dominated field keep sending back unread. She's a serious scholar amidst the teenage girls but with mad scientist elements. It's pretty good concept-wise, as she exerts a mental and spiritual control over her teenage girl guinea pig converting her into a vampire in order to test the murky thesis that may save us from destruction if everything works. The relationship between them is pretty crazy, with some hypnotism and the power of an amulet that came from Eastern Europe. It exceeds its limitations at times, while at others it's full on teen fun, with the guys sneaking in for a dance party and one cheesy vocal number.

Naturally, the madder scientist hatches a plan to have the other one help him with…

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: Quite unusual if little antiquated but not uninteresting and kinda charming little (sort of) Vampire tale. It’s very similar in tone and style of the early Hammer films. For its time, it can be quite gruesome at times. I liked that. I also liked the setting, the atmosphere and Donald Wolfit performance as Doctor Callistratus. And of course, it’s always nice to see Hammer queen Barbara Shelley in anything. Dungeon chains suit her well.I wouldn’t call this a great movie or a classic but I had a surprisingly good time with it tonight. Fans of Hammer and old-school horror films could/should take a look.

reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: Ressurected after being executed as a vampire with a stake driven through his heart and now in charge of a prison for the criminally insane, the supposed vampire uses the inmates' blood for his search for a cure for his blood disorder. WTF is right. Blood of the Vampire is about the blood and finding the mix that will work with Dr. Callistratus figuring maybe he should use some blood from young women as well. His assistant Carl has a deformed face and yearns for Madeline Duval played by Barbara Shelley whose blood the doctor craves. Kind of wild at times with some nice atmosphere and Dobermans.

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: I recently bought a new German Blu-ray of the movie. And after checking out a few extras and listening to one of the three audio commentaries, my admiration for it increased. It's a really good looking film and the Hammer-like atmosphere is quite effective. The cast, especially Donald Wolfit and Barbara Shelley, is great and the uncut version is, for its time, refreshingly gruesome and with some nice sexual undertones. I still don’t think it’s a masterpiece but a film worth checking out for Hammer and old-fashioned Horror fans. And seeing a few busty women chained up in the dungeon is always a plus in my book. Just don't expect too many actual vampires!

reviews.author: Fint
reviews.text: The gushing blood in the prologue and the drama inherent in Donald Wolfit's eyebrows promise much but ultimately this is not one of writer Jimmy Sangster's better offerings. Though not anaemic, it could've done with a transfusion of chills and a stab of unpredictability in its tale of mad scientist blood research. Instead it keeps insisting on a pack of barking hounds being the most terrifying thing on the screen, several of which are far too disinterested to be remotely terrifying. Hunchback helper Victor Maddern's makeup is a constant source of pleasure, with one eye halfway down his cheek, but Donald Wolfit's performance is not half as full-blooded as you would expect from the old ham.

reviews.author: Grant McLanaghan
reviews.text: I’ve only seen one other of their films (1960’s The Flesh and the Fiends) but on the strength of these two alone, I can say that Baker and Berman’s horror output compares favourably with that of the House of Horror. And – here – this is despite a lack of a Cushing or Lee, though it features actors of a sufficiently high calibre. Okay, Sangster relies on narrative expedience a little too much for his own good but one can’t expect the moon on a stick from what is relatively low-budget but nonetheless well-crafted and enjoyably ghoulish yarn.

reviews.text: Pure black magick atmosphere. Mikels manages to conjure up something unfathomably dark (literally as well) as he put to celluloid 70 minutes of authentic feeling rituals. This kind of occult filmmaking is where low budget really excels--the lack of light, the sparse decoration, the dirty grindhouse feel--it all contributes to something that feels absolutely sinister. But also at the same time it's kind of cozy? Droning and ritualistic, I could very well see myself putting this on the next time I can't sleep.

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: With a personal life every bit as mysterious as his outrageous filmography, it’s no wonder why Ted V. Mikels’ productions often turn out so fragmentary. As Mikels states in Re/Search’s INCREDIBLY STRANGE FILMS, “It takes your guts and your entrails and your soul to make a film. You have to be as obsessed as a religious fanatic.” Give a consumed eccentric a canvas and he’ll show you the world. Take this one, for instance. Following up 1969’s ASTRO ZOMBIES and 1972’s THE CORPSE GRINDERS, Mikels presents BLOOD ORGY OF THE SHE-DEVILS: 78 minutes of plotless, PG-rated psychedelic abstraction in the form of an occult soap opera. Like any Mikels experience, you’ll either be bored out of your mind or drunkenly…

reviews.text: BLOODLUST! is a low budget, backlit filmed take on "the most dangerous game". In every way it is a generic retread of the oft told story. Or so I thought.It turns out that this film is an above average take due to its general weirdness. All of the flaws are there, cheap sets, hammy acting and a basic run through of the script. What makes it unique are the choices made.It is much gorier than I was expecting with an acid bath death that came out of nowhere. It is also more macabre than most of the telling with the trophy hunter aspect put way forward. The villain is played to suave, mustache twirling perfection and the group of young adults being hunted each have some fun with their stereotypes.It works better than I expected. It isn't reaching for greatness but by not attempting it rises. It's not a great film but certainly one I would recommend.

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: Shot on Super 8 in the back alleys of London by DIY superhero Michael J. Murphy, this is the Argento-lite of DIY trash-horror. When filmmaker Alistair’s latest slasher (also called BLOODSTREAM) is rejected by a scumbag producer, all seems lost. But when Alistair finds out that the rejection was a ruse to cut him out of profits, he does what any self-respecting weirdo would do: he dons a skull mask, calls himself The Angel Of Death, and embarks on a revenge-fueled bloodbath. This includes castration via barbells. Like the films of Fabio Salerno, BLOODSTREAM is an artful, barely-released passion project that's laced with autobiographical angst. It explodes with several movies-within-movies and a meta-enhanced commentary on the Video Nasties era. This is easily Murphy's most accessible work, and it becomes more and more layered each time I watch it. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

reviews.text: Video-terror trash, snuffing out the big man in an aggravated forced-reaping of what’s sown in isolated, SOV, rotting niche. The oscillation between couch-decaying delusions lost in VHS-taped trances and Super8-recorded murder — both with unnerving views of Patrick Oliver’s Alistair being lost in his own eyes — is realized incredibly well, conjuring the same grotesque sensation found in some of the genre’s greatest exercises in nastiness, bodily or cerebral—persistently bleak, but, with a taste of shame, just as amusing, charmed by its galvanized ugliness that feels like a death-dream fantasy only one final string away from becoming reality.
