reviews.text: YOU THOUGHT THE ACID at Woodstock was bad? A batch of Blue Sunshine LSD making the rounds of Stanford University in 1967 has a decade-delayed side effect that turns normal people into hairless, homicidal freaks. While this goofy horror flick could fuel MK Ultra conspiracies about current Silicon Valley fascism, it’s more fun to enjoy as a late entry in the drug-scare exploitation cycle. Creepier than any monster is the sweaty, bug-eyed man with random tufts of hair going berserk on a dance floor in what must be the first anti-disco protest. reviews.text: Everyone who loves bad movies - who genuinely thinks they're a form of outsider art, and have a passion and personal quality that is sometimes transcendent - needs to raise a toast every day to Edgar G Ulmer. His masterpiece Detour has all the qualities of a bad movie - the miniscule budget, the overreaching dream sequences, melodramatic plotting, and stridently one-note acting - but it remixes them into something brilliant, something that's been rightly admitted to the canon of Great American Cinema. Nobody talks about Detour as a guilty pleasure. It is pure pleasure.

reviews.text: Absolutely wretched sound quality on the copy on Tubi makes this one hard to understand, but what's there is a pretty basic serial killer narrative back before the term was in use. The misogynist backstory is both apt to serial killers and disappointingly played straight instead of used for any kind of commentary. The idea that finding out someone is a sex worker could turn someone into a killer is absurd, ignoring the pre-existing violence and attitudes that must exist for them to take that step, just as trans panic and gay panic defenses do; finding it as a running theme in old serial killer films is tiresome but not surprising. It makes this otherwise okay film much less sinister and much more pathetic.

reviews.author: Evelyn Rose
reviews.text: In 1938, Billy Wilder co-wrote a screwball comedy variant on the Bluebeard tale, produced by Ernst Lubitsch. In 1960, W. Lee Wilder made this cheapo macabre comedy variant on the Bluebeard tale, the closest Billy Wilder's smarter brother ever came to imitating Billy's brand. It's an interesting point of comparison. "Same business, just a different approach." George Sanders is perfectly cast as a goateed antique dealer hunting fortunes by marrying and murdering women. (In fact, Sanders plays Henri Désiré Landru, that real-life Bluebeard who also inspired Chaplin's Monsieur Verdoux.) Sanders is so charming in this that I regret to report that I'd definitely also have been suckered into giving him control of my life's fortune before he offed me. Corinne Calvet is memorable too as an amazingly accented and drawl nightclub singer, complete with a picture of Gold Diggers-era Ginger Rogers on her wall. How Would W. Lee Do It?

reviews.text: Body Waves is basically Hardbodies meets Wayne’s World, except instead of middle-aged guys learning how to score chicks, it’s the Three Stooges getting lessons from a SoCal Wayne and Garth. I mean that in the best way possible. It kicks off with one of the most striking openings in any sex comedy—silhouettes of flexing muscleheads against a blue screen, orange credits projected across their bodies. At one point, a muscle bro picks a wedgie so you can read the director’s name, all to a punk song about hemorrhoids (a relevant plot point), with the chorus: “I don’t wanna be in an original band!!” Unlike that band, this film—despite the familiar setup—is shockingly original, clever, creative, and way funnier than it has any right to be.

reviews.text: In what could have been a well-meaning but plodding B-noir/western in other hands becomes something special directed by Anthony Mann. A strikingly Wellesian, almost gothic, depth of field in most scenes but with a narrative rhythm that is distinctly Mann's. It begins like a newsreel, then becomes a slow-burning social-problem thriller, masterfully building in intensity until its stakes are almost primordial. Unlike other western directors, Mann did not move his characters from lawlessness to civilization, but would rather begin with civilization to gradually wear it down into much starker territory. His sophisticated but emotionally direct blocking of each scene gives the most innocuous exchanges a weight few other directors could muster. Violence is always exciting in his films, but rarely…

reviews.author: Evelyn Rose
reviews.text: "Don't cry, Mother. The boy's not going to Yale…" The third film of Rida Johnson Young's celebrated play, after a 1911 one-reeler and a 1918 feature (both by Selig), but apparently the only one to survive. Moving Picture World praised the ambience of the 1911 version, writing that "It is set in very appropriate backgrounds that seem very much indeed like Cambridge, Mass.," and it’s reported that the 1918 was partially shot at Harvard. No such luck here, which—save for a few touristy, stock footage-style shots of campus buildings—was confined to MGM's Culver City lots and location shooting in Sacramento. But the picture has other historical interest: it's the first star vehicle for William Haines, and it defined his persona as a harassing womanizer accompanied by a guy friend (here Jack Pickford) with whom he can't help but be a little gay.

This is one of Jones's very funniest shorts, one of the few times in his "mature" period where he went for a full-on Clampett-style "conveyor belt of absurd gags" cartoon. It's exceptionally fast-paced for Jones while still leaving room for the bull - one of the most exquisitely-animated creatures in the director's filmography - to have lots of stunned reaction beats, to shift its eyes cunningly, to contemplate this bizarre demigod-like rabbit who…

reviews.text: “You know what I think?" she says. "That people's memories are maybe the fuel they burn to stay alive. Whether those memories have any actual importance or not, it doesn't matter as far as the maintenance of life is concerned. They're all just fuel. Advertising fillers in the newspaper, philosophy books, dirty pictures in a magazine, a bundle of ten-thousand-yen bills: when you feed 'em to the fire, they're all just paper. The fire isn't thinking 'Oh, this is Kant,' or 'Oh, this is the Yomiuri evening edition,' or 'Nice tits,' while it burns. To the fire, they're nothing but scraps of paper. It's the exact same thing. Important memories, not-so-important memories, totally useless memories: there's no distinction--they're all just fuel.”― Haruki Murakami, After Dark

reviews.text: Beautiful cinematography and a great performance from Steven Yeun can't prevent this from being needlessly cumbersome and thoroughly exhausting to sit through. Strip away the pretty window dressing and arthouse veneer and you'll find a Manic Pixie Dream Girl, rote explorations of masculinity, and a lead character who is as blank of a slate as there can be — the last point is particularly problematic when your film is two and a half hours long. None of this outside of Yeun's character is interesting at all, and the occasionally obnoxious script says nothing of substance while trying to get you to believe it's deep. I just don't care about the lead or his problems, and the film doesn't do anything in the way of development to alleviate that. The climax veers on laughable as a result. Enough with these "tortured" piece of shit male protagonists already.

reviews.author: Edith
reviews.text: This movie dredged up some serious memories of loss, confusion, rebellion, and misunderstandings of youth. A coming of age story that isn't about the usual thematic contenders like sexual curiosity or finding your identity, but is parallel to the political struggles of the fifties using communism and conservatism through the eyes of children. How, in a fundamentally animalistic way, humans handle diversity and order. A parable akin to Animal Farm, Pan's Labyrinth, or Lord of the Flies, but definitely way darker. I honestly can't remember the last time a moment in a movie pricked my heart so hard.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Comparing the Red Scare (or an Australian equivalent) with the rabbit plague Australia suffered in the mid-20th century, this film centers the narrative on a nine year old girl who is caught in the midst of both by virtue of her affections. The film takes pains to develop all sides of both equations while quietly but firmly making it plain where it draws the line. To put another way, while the film makes a statement about fear, fear-mongering, and our responses to both, it remembers that there are human beings involved in it all.

The film explores all these elements through the child's perspective, creating her own way of dealing with them as her childish innocence ebbs away. reviews.text: I love Michael Fassbender but he sure does star in some rubbish! Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels meets Gladiator in Centurion; Neil Marshall's Roman soldier romp set in England and following some Romans who are caught behind enemy lines. The film is peppered with CGI blood, which goes well with the hard hitting action scenes that are fairly plentiful and well shot. However, the plot is an absolute muddle as it seemingly doesn't know what to with its characters or where the audience's loyalty is supposed to lie. The aesthetic is grey tinged dampness that doesn't look nice at all and to top it all off the narrative is overlaid with an annoying cringey voice over from Michael Fassbender. I love Dog Soldiers and The Descent. Maybe Neil Marshall should have just stuck to horror? Centurion had some potential but squandered it....one to forget.

reviews.text: Mostly noted for its absolute camp factor is probably the best realization of Vegas kitsch dystopia I've seen to-date: extension cord retro-futurism with many flowing neon lights, tubular Jetson kitchen decor, hidden underground bunkers, abandoned motel Hawaiian cults, and a plethora of Las Vegas glowing signs. This era between modern sci-fi and postwar atomic scares is the sugar-coated grimy sweet spot for dystopian candylands. So many impressive artistic details that elevates the escapism and isn't just a Mad Max clone. Even when I wasn't sold on Milquetoast protagonist, I see how it all fits together, dare I say I think the movie is rather feminist?

reviews.text: Leans a little too heavily on typical action beats (caveat: The crane/underground tunnel sequence is fantastic), but there's enough interesting stuff here to power 3 or 4 typical genre movies. Favorite part is Tim Thomerson's surfer-haired murder-cult leader, a hilarious depiction of decadent faux-individualism cult of personality hogwash mutating into something violent and fiercely territorial. Then there's the movie's unambiguous affirmation for humanity over machine, which is almost a complete 180 from how artificial intelligence is usually treated in stories like this - learn to love your fellow humans before you start shedding tears for fictional robots, society!

reviews.text: "Cherry 2000" is a 1987 film directed by Steve De Jarnatt. A science fiction film with dystopian flavorings, "Cherry 2000" was a film I caught once before many years ago and really flew over its lasting effects of potential connection. With its recent release on blu-ray from Kino Lorber, I found myself immensely drawn into the unique vision that the film is trying to portray. It's largely a quirky venture into the somewhat apocalyptic future not unlike the likes of "Brazil" (1985) or "Tank Girl" (1995) but its easily a feature that should be spoken about more in common discussion.

reviews.text: Much of the charm of Cecil B. DeMille’s Cleopatra is found in its recreation of a fantasy past, full of scantily clad dancing girls, elaborate mansions decorated with monumental sculptures, servants who move in choreographed patterns, and an opulent barge not unlike the TARDIS in its unlimited internal space. There is also, however, a bracing modernity to several of its key performances, specifically those of Warren William as a wry, reserved Julius Caesar, and Claudette Colbert, as the canny, seductive Cleopatra.

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: cecil b. demille's desert corridor emphasizes texture over narrative -- the shiny chestplates, bejeweled chalices, endless parades of decked-out extras carrying furbished banners through winding streets constructed of aluminum and balsa wood -- this is a level of cinematic luxury that ceased to exist after the 1970s and will likely never be seen again. sure, the story is just the bones of shakespeare's romania put into a pre-code microwave and set to 'nuke' -- but then those plot-bones are thrown into a pile of glitter-glue and lacquer and trimmed lace and i must tell you that i'm more than satisfied with the resultant dish.

reviews.author: noir1946
reviews.text: I’m sure there was excess in the cinema before Cecil B. DeMille, but he certainly refined it—if “refined” is the right word. His Cleopatra alternates dull, talky scenes with over-the-top ones. I like the sea battle, with CBD warming up for Reap the Wild Wind. One problem with Cleopatra, however, is that we’re supposed to care about the fates of Rome and Egypt, but screenwriters Vincent Lawrence and Waldemar Young come up with nothing to make us feel anything. Vinnie and Wally also write awful dialogue. When Cleo (Claudette Colbert) tells Marc Antony (Henry Wilcoxon), “I’ve seen a god come to life,” I defy you not to giggle.

reviews.author: sarah
reviews.text: I think the reason why I love this film so much is that it’s so unapologetic in the way it rejects any hint of cynicism. Cluny, so uncertain and so unguarded, is allowed to be herself the whole way through, and the story doesn’t try to change her in order to make her desirable to men. It doesn’t disparage her interests and hobbies, it doesn’t present her as an object to be mocked or ridiculed. The characters in the story either accept her, or they don’t, but she doesn’t change in service of a cheap punchline. She is, simply, herself.

reviews.text: A few years ago, I wrote the following about a monologue delivered by Greta Garbo in Ninotchka: "[I]t deftly combines pathos and humor, but doesn’t compromise either of them. It’s just as funny as it is sad, and it’s very sad." I added that Garbo "takes her role just as seriously as if she were playing Camille or Anna Karenina." Well, many of the same observations apply just as readily to Lubitsch's Cluny Brown. Star Jennifer Jones may have effervescence where Garbo had gravitas, but her character's internal life is allotted just as much respect by both actress and director as Ninotchka's was. Cluny's passions may be ridiculous, but they're still her passions, and the film takes them seriously even…

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: After the more epically scaled Heaven Can Wait, Lubitsch concluded his career with one of his most supple works, a perfect sublimation of his sexualized class comedies in which a plumbing-obsessed flibbertigibbet enjoys a sense of camaraderie with an anti-Nazi Czech. Along the way, Lubitsch mines their interests for double-entendre comedy, as ever, but he also demonstrates the somber aspects of hidebound class structures. The two scenes in which Cluny (played to earnest perfection by Jones) is humiliated for daring not to "know her place" are more savagely heartrending than anything else in the director's filmography.

reviews.text: A broken love story about broken people in a broken country, Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Cold War” is nothing if not true to its title. Barren even in its fleeting moments of joy, and emotionally inaccessible to the extreme, the film is dark enough to make the director’s Oscar-winning “Ida” feel like a frivolous comedy. And yet, as irreparable as these characters might seem, there’s something beautiful about watching them, in less than 90 minutes, try to fix each other over the course of 20 years — to become whole at any cost, long after they’ve forgotten what that really feels like.

Fairly good film, but a bit too forced in making the German's evil and honoring the bravery of us Norwegians. One of the biggest surprises about Commandos Strike at Dawn (1942) was the return of silent megastar Lillian Gish to Hollywood after a 9 year absence. Unfortunately they barely gave her any lines and she was mostly degraded to stand in the background reacting to what was going on, as if she was in a silent movie. Who better to do that, though? Still great to see her again!

reviews.author: Jeff DeLano
reviews.text: John Farrow directs this fairly standard wartime propaganda film about Norwegian villagers who rebel against the Nazi occupied force. There are few gripping moments, most notably a nighttime escape by boat to England, but the most distinguishing thing about this film is the presence of screen legend Paul Muni. Here Muni reins in his usual over-the-top persona to play a meek marine biologist who feels compelled to form a resistance group in his village after the Nazis kill one of his friends. The climax involves Muni leading a heroic charge with a British force to destroy a secret Nazi airfield. It’s an enjoyable watch for WWII buffs marred only by occasional lapses into melodrama.

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: Films featuring conmen and deception always think they are much cleverer than they really are. There are a few exceptions to that statement, the likes of Soderbergh's Ocean's Eleven, Russell's American Hustle, and of course, George Roy Hill's The Sting, which is probably the greatest the genre has ever seen. James Foley's Confidence isn't in the same ballpark as those films, but it is an entertaining piece of cinema nonetheless, with an intricate plot and a stellar cast embracing Foley's stylish direction. We get Dustin Hoffman, Andy Garcia, Paul Giamatti, Rachel Weisz, and Ed Burns at the centre of a con where up is down and black is white. There's a freshness about the script from Doug Jung, and a mixture of very different performances from Hoffman (creepy), Weisz (sexy), Giamatti (neurotic), and Burns (utter confidence), in a well worked caper with more twists than a pretzel.

reviews.author: teamgal
reviews.text: Powerful in what it depicts — the shooting of an innocent black kid, the subsequent intimidation of witnesses by the LAPD, the perjury at the inquest, the community failing to support their own — the film is, unfortunately, often hampered by the limitations of its blaxploitation budget. One senses the hurried production at almost every turn. The gaffes that we laugh off in urban crime pictures of the period are tragic in a film that actually attempts to seriously render the problems of black people living in an oppressive state. Still, for all its flaws, this is essential viewing.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: The tears of a mother at the sight of her dead son are filmed in grit and haze, in warm tones and city street grey, signalling clearly that this is a product of its era, 40 years old, but the statement has been made repeatedly since in a way that makes the moment not merely current but... instant, simultaneous, right now. Nothing has changed, nothing probably has ever changed, except that the narrative is somehow smarter on both sides. The lies are more nastily snarled, and the truth is more intricately presented. This is the story of gut-wrenching injustice, and it still works as a fairytale.

reviews.author: Quiller

In Cornbread, Earl And Me, two police officers (Bernie Casey and Vince Martorano) shoot the character known as Cornbread (future basketball legend Jamaal Wilkes) when they mistake him for a suspect they lost in the rain. The police department and city government quickly close ranks around them, insisting that Cornbread really was the suspect being chased, despite eyewitnesses who can verify the young man’s whereabouts before his death. When Cornbread’s parents (Madge Sinclair and Stack Pierce) hire attorney Moses Gunn to clear their son’s name,…

It could almost be an after school special (that's not an insult), but it really digs into the sadly still relevant issue of the police murdering black people for doing completely innocent things. Even better, this film focuses on the family and how they view truth-telling within their moral structure. It can be dangerous to tell the truth, but within the family unit it's discussed and given great worth. Cops may intimidate at every turn, but then there's 14-yr-old Laurence Fishburne making…

reviews.text: WWII thriller, about Russian and German soldiers trapped together under a collapsed building, verges on agitprop thanks to screenwriter John Howard Lawson's fondness for speech-making over action, but the setting and performances give it an uncomfortable intensity. The often hectoring dialogue acquires some emotional weight thanks to Paul Muni's frenzied performance as a soldier who's nothing more or less than the sum total of his exhaustion and hunger, while the stodgily schematic dramaturgy is granted some grace by James Wong Howe's way of photographing the players like a series of Rembrandt portraits made flickering flesh, flashes of light and terror waiting out an eternal midnight in the soul of Europe.

reviews.text: Considered one of Woody Allen's most mature and complex works, Crimes and Misdemeanors skillfully mixes drama and comedy by addressing philosophical and existential themes such as morality, guilt, love, death and the existence of God. The plot unfolds along two parallel story lines that intertwine in the film's final scene. The first follows Judah Rosenthal, a well-known and respected ophthalmologist whose life is turned upside down when his lover threatens to reveal their affair to his wife. The second concerns Clifford Stern, a documentary director in personal and professional crisis who is commissioned to make a documentary about his brother-in-law, a very successful television producer, whom he detests.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Curfew" is a 1989 horror film directed by Gary Winick. Ironically, the same guy bringing "13 Going on 30" (2004), the live action "Charlotte's Web" (2006), and "Bride Wars" (2009) into directorial fruition also directed a somewhat exploitation driven home invasion murder movie back in the late 80's. As many can laugh out loud at that concept, which it is funny, Winick is not nearly close to being the only one who has a career start in this manner, as many directors seeming "cut their teeth" through this kind of application. Just overall it's a funny factoid and acknowledgement that as you watch "Curfew" you every reason to bring up "Charlotte's Web".

Not quite, but it's super fun and there's a lot of great moments from classic WB cartoons. Among the many great WB characters, we get to see Daffy and Speedy, but also Bugs Bunny, Yosemite Sam, Foghorn Leghorn, The Tasmanian Devil, Tweety, Sylvester, and a slew of other regulars.

reviews.author: Will Menaker
reviews.text: The third entry in the Stuart Gordon/Dennis Paoli Lovecraft adaptations\ trilogy is a fun take on "The Shadow Over Innsmouth", but would have been twice as good if Jeffrey Coombs were the lead and not a younger actor trying to mimic his nervous, twitchy energy. An impossible task as Coombs is the only one who can make his unique brand of being repellent both endearing and charming. There's still a lot of fun stuff here. The location switch from the New England of the story to the Galicia region of Spain works well and there is no shortage of grotesque fish fucking mutant villager extras to make it work. There is also some pretty good gratuitous nudity and one truly horrific scene of a guy getting his face peeled off his skull.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Lovecraft stories are notoriously difficult to bring to the screen; but bless Stuart Gordon for trying! The film is based mainly on Lovecraft's classic The Shadow Over Innsmouth (but takes bits from elsewhere). Re-Animator and From Beyond are the Stuart Gordon films everyone remembers but this one is the most singularly Lovecraftian. The film triumphs over its low budget with a constant fantastical atmosphere. The central location of Imboca (substituting for Innsmouth) is quite the marvel with its rainsoaked streets, delapidated buildings and rather odd locals. The story encompasses many of Lovecraft's favourite plots, including alternative God's, weird cults/religion and cursed lineage. Unfortunately it does suffer from some spectacularly bad CGI and the ambitious plot does stutter at times but considering the lofty heights it reaches for; I'm going to forgive these problems and declare Dagon a flawed masterpiece.

reviews.author: Dave Jackson
reviews.text: I totally get, and mostly agree with, the criticism I've read of Dave Made a Maze. Yep, its lead character is more cardboardy than the titular maze. Yep, there's moments where it feels there's not enough happening to sustain a feature length. And yep, it straddles a strange line of tone and genre (I would argue this makes it more interesting). But god damn, this film is dripping with fucking creativity and passion. The detail of the sets, the beautiful, bizarre art direction, the design of the cardboard characters and creatures—it's hard to deny the talent and love that this film is bloated with. Dave Made a Maze is not quite satisfying on a narrative level, but it is very satisfying as a delightful and strange visual feast.

reviews.text: Franco Nero rocking the shabby raincoat, hat and moustache washed-up PI look unsurprisingly well in this. But it suits the late-polizio low-intensity gumshoe story going on here, which involves Nero’s character going back to Italy to settle an old score. There’s lots of time spent with him doing the actual leg-work, but that still leaves enough room for him to happily punch people in the face and get to know some ladies. The plot is possibly a bit convoluted, there’s lots of ‘he’s dead’ ‘no he’s alive’ going on, but Nero’s charisma carries you through most of it. And if that fails, you do get a very catchy Cobra theme song.

Luckily, there's enough else to take away from this. Franco Nero is ferocious as always. This role allows him to show his gritty side nicely. There's some fun scenes here and there too - best of which is a martial arts fight in a sort of disco arena. The soundtrack is particularly enjoyable - especially that title track…

reviews.text: You might be bored by DAY OF THE REAPER. You might hate it. But you’ll never see anything else like it. Shot in Florida for $1,000 on Super 8 by teenager Tim Ritter (TRUTH OR DARE), this is a psychotropic daymare as captured through the lens of a malfunctioning Kodak Instamatic. Waves of plastic Yamaha synthesizers and scratched emulsion roll over a landscape that feels like an adaptation of The Babysitters Club made by the Kuchar brothers while dropping acid. There’s also a killer wearing a black hood. If you want to leave the planet for 70 minutes, this movie is your best option. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

Plus, Danny Trejo and Danny Glover. The main dude has the charisma of a black hole, but he's surrounded by a ton of interesting characters and he fights well so it never really hurts my enjoyment. It was weird having Frankenstein actually being the bad guy this time around but it also made a nice change from the previous movies, being a devious psychopath with an army of Mad Max reject convicts following him like he's some sort of cult leader. I had a ton of fun watching this. I laughed out loud a lot and had a big, silly grin on my face for the rest of the time. It's full on entertaining crap and I hope they make another 20 of these.

reviews.author: Timcop
reviews.text: Predates "Robin Hood Daffy" by two years and features many of the same character dynamics as that one, but by that time they'd vastly improved the comedy timing and the inventiveness of the gags. Even so, this looks gorgeous, with the streets of London in beautiful green and yellow hues, and lots of dutch angled disorientating camerawork. The designs on the pub denizens and "costermongers", as Daffy refers to them, is also beautiful in its eccentricity and ugliness, like a British version of the Star Wars cantina dwellers. With those neon streets and the hideous caricatures of the London citizenry, if you told me this was an influence on Warren Beatty's Dick Tracy, I'd have to believe you.

reviews.text: Along with The Abyss and Leviathan, DeepStar Six was the third underwater “creature” movie in 1989. Last night I watch this one along with Leviathan as a double feature and I must say even though this one clearly has a lower budget I enjoyed it just as much. Not a great movie but a nice little deep seas creature feature with a good cast of characters (Miguel Ferrer is the clear highlight) and a dense atmosphere. Destroyer пытается что-то сказать при кино на мета уровне, но поскольку он в руках людей не особо умных, хватает его лишь на воровство чужого, и эксплуатейшен, который снимают персонажи интереснее самого фильма. Забавляет разве что несколько моментов со стероидным культуристом, играющим маньяка, среди которых сжигание из огнемета в туалете, шалости с отбойным молотком и срезание у жертвы волос с последующим их поеданием. Перкинс в роли режиссёра уверенно едет на автопилоте и в меру эффектно умирает на электрическом стуле. И всё это под неплохой саундтрек от музыканта их группы Фрэнка Заппы.

reviews.author: rotch
reviews.text: Como bien señala Luis, La libertad del diablo es un finísimo ejemplo de ese subgénero poco estudiado que es el documental de horror. Everardo González toma el talking head, el lugar más común del documental, y lo pervierte. Oculta a todos los sujetos detrás de una máscara claramente inspirada por una tradición de máscaras del género que inicia en Les Yeux sans visage y pasa por La piel que habito y Goodnight Mommy. Y luego los envuelve en la oscuridad más tenebrosa que ofrece el cine digital. El resultado es hermoso y aterrador a la vez. Fácilmente pudo haber escogido un tono de desesperación o de denuncia. Pero en vez de eso eligió asomarse al abismo.

reviews.author: Olevar
reviews.text: Vaya programa doble que me aventé este sábado en Ambulante. Después de ver el infierno que viven los rescatistas en Alepo, tocó ver el horror absoluto que se vive en México causado por la violencia, los secuestros, la impunidad, y sobre todo, la ambición desmedida.

reviews.author: Aarón García del Real
reviews.text: Las cifras de la violencia en México son alarmantes. Los 10 años de la guerra contra el narco han dejado más de 100,000 ejecutados, entre 30 y 50 mil desaparecidos cada año, e innumerables víctimas indirectas: padres, hijos, parejas que han perdido a alguien. A pesar de ello, la sociedad se ha vuelto –aparentemente- inmune a estas noticias, viéndolo como algo cotidiano y normalizando lo que es una realidad atroz que deberíamos estar negándonos a aceptar.

reviews.author: Rigo Ayala
reviews.text: Everardo González ha sido capaz de retratar explícitamente (sin mostrar ni una sola imagen explícita) como la violencia ha llegado a todos los niveles de manera inesperada, sin distinguir edades, razas, géneros, hasta volverse cotidiana y parte de la realidad mexicana. Ya uno como espectador imagina los terribles alcances de las anécdotas de víctimas y victimarios y como la brutalidad los ha devorado. De visionado obligatorio.

reviews.text: la mejor película mexicana reciente de horror no es vuelven, sino este documental --claramente inscrito en la escuela incipiente pero fructífera del documental de horror--. todas las decisiones estilísticas aquí están tomadas para construir una atmósfera de opresión, de horror, pues, un horror recalcitrante que solo termina subrayando el horror de los testimonios, de la realidad de este país donde vivimos y morimos. el uso de las máscaras la coloca en otro nivel. de verdad brillante.

reviews.text: Well there's about a thousand films with Django in the title, but this is the only official sequel to Sergio Corbucci's masterpiece and the only one that sees Franco Nero reprise the title role. Django Strikes Again begins with the famous gunslinger having abandoned his violent life to live as a monk, but he's forced back into action when he discovers his daughter has been kidnapped by Hungarian bandits. This film is a completely different animal to the original. It's less a western and more of a Rambo style action film, while the muddy desert is replaced by water and jungle. reviews.author: Daniel Shillito
reviews.text: Having spawned nearly 30 unofficial sequels, it's rather funny that the only official sequel to the original would take 21 years to come out, long after the imitators had died out, and would see our beloved gunslinger Django going full Commando. Nero's engrossing performance and return to his most famous role manage to trump the rather lacklustre production values and often flat direction, while Donald Pleasence's amusing turn as Ben Gunn helps provide the movie with a bit more star power in the filmmaker's attempts to revitalise the spaghetti western genre. It's very much a movie for the fans, chocked full of explosive action, occasionally stylish and hard hitting imagery, that despite Django Strikes Again's unfortunate shortcomings remains a very fun and noble attempt to bring back a waning genre.

reviews.text: The official two decades later sequel to Django. It is much more of a 80s action movie than an Eurowestern, although the all over the place plotting do suggest the latter and while I’m sure the starting point was someone noticing that Nero with a machine gun fit nicely with those Rambo days, it riffs around far more eclectic. It was shot in Colombia instead of Spain (one of these days I’d like to find out why Italian cinema of this period liked South America so much). Lots of twilight of the Italian exploitation to it, some of it even deliberate. Nero does put a good amount of effort. The action isn’t very memorable, but it feels less cheap than many Italian movies from the late 80s, too bad that it is hardly inventive. A very inessential movie, but far from an embarrassment the context suggests, which counts as a win.

reviews.text: Subtle as a great dane, and less convincing than a show poodle that’s trying to pretend she’s an untamed stray, “Dogman” is an obvious and strained little movie about an Italian groomer who’s going through life with his tail between his legs. Another severe consideration of Italy’s criminal underworld from the director of “Gomorrah”— albeit one that hews much closer to the margins than it does to the mob — Matteo Garrone’s latest film might present itself as a cozy revenge saga, but that’s only because it’s trying to throw you off the scent. Alas, it isn’t long before the neutered cries of a three-legged allegory start to come from all directions, the barely hidden subtext barking its head off…

Doch während er sich in der Welt der Vierbeiner souverän und auf Augenhöhe bewegt, scheitert er an der Welt der Zweibeiner. Marcello will einfach nur von allen gemocht werden – darüber definiert er sich und seinen Wert für eine Gesellschaft, von der er immer mehr spürt, dass sie ihn und seine Dienste immer weniger benötigt. Daraus entstehen immer wieder berührende Szenen voller tragischer Komik – die gesamte Bildsprache von Regisseur Matteo Garrone taucht tief in jenen klassischen Humanismus ein, dem sich das italienische Kino mit seinem Neorealismus schon so oft…

reviews.text: Chuck Jones' own The Great Piggy Bank Robbery. I love how tenacious Daffy is in this one--he doesn't sulk after ripping his pants off, he doesn't demand that the patrons of the bar pay attention to him; just immediately moseys on up to the bar for his yogurt chaser with the utmost confidence. There's a charming innocence in his obliviousness and delusion. Again, very Duck Twacy-esque in him roleplaying as this fantastical authority figure he sees himself as. The later ones are crafted around Nicholson acting persona and, in many ways, try to respond to perceptions of it, Drive He Said might say to do the same without his actual presence as the shadow of Bob Rafelson is all over it (instead there’s a very inexpressive lead pretty much by design, although one might question if it is wise). At its worse, it can suggest Nicholson trying to emulate the popular counterculture movies that he himself was for a short while identified with, but it is far more ambivalent than most of those. The…

reviews.author: Camel Camel
reviews.text: It feels like overcompensating[1] for something, Nicholson casting somebody so anti-electric in the lead role of this, his first directorial effort. But if it’s like playing basketball with one hand tied behind one’s back, then the result is about what you’d expect. I’d love to be sincere in an effort to make a counter-intuitive case that this is, in fact, a brilliant satire about what boring horrible people professional athletes (and by extension, actors) are, but I think any revelations or insights along those lines are inadvertent.

Henry Jaglom who plays a politically charged professor here, you might remember as Warren the freaked-out painter in Psych-Out (1967), also with Nicholson and Dern. M.A.S.H. star David Ogden Stiers cameos as a professional owner, while Cindy Williams (Laverne and Shirley, American Graffiti) briefly appears as a manager's girlfriend. Jack himself cameos as a bearded guy in dark glasses during the campus military draft scene. There's lots of trademark "Dernsies"…

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: The game of filmmaking is played with a cast and crew, who hope to achieve a singular goal, whether it be one of aesthetics, thematics, or spirituality. The object of the game is to create a set of rules to which one must adhere, unless your name happens to be Mr. Peter Greenaway. For this fellow, rules are determined —by him on whim— and made to be subverted; playing with structure is a lot like playing with friends or playing with animals. And just as abraxas casts beams from above, so too is his name equal to the numerical value of the calendar year : three-hundred and sixty-five. Why bring this up here? Because I want to; does one need a better reason? Making your own rules, and breaking them cheekily, seems to me the most fun.

reviews.author: madeline
reviews.text: A genuine monolith. The 'Hunting Trilogy' is one of animation's finest feats, and its ending note is superb. Set in a snowy landscape, the now-iconic 'Rabbit Season/Duck Season' bit is taken to its logical extreme. Daffy is tricked into identifying as a number of non-fowls, as Bugs continually gives him the slip and redirects everything dished out ten-fold. Poor Elmer is left to go insane in the cold, jerked between the two tricksters, unable to discern reality and left chasing a baseball into the snowy tundra. Jones et al manage to infuse life and warmth into this frozen mise en scene to terrific effect.

reviews.author: nick
reviews.text: Peter Greenaway's outrageous Eisenstein biopic is a hot mess but admittedly a fun one. Chronicling Eisenstein's 10-day stay in Guanajuato where a gay romance changed him forever, this gives a spotlight on the Soviet enfant terrible with a tortured life. I'm unfamiliar with actor Elmer Bäck, but he played a memorable, dramatic and dedicated Eisenstein, probably the project's best aspect. Greenaway also wasn't afraid of showing his hearty stylish tributes to Eisenstein as a filmmaker. However, these tricks may not be impressive enough to counterbalance the at times dull, ultimately too on-the-nose script. Overall Greenaway is good at making us look, but not at making us care.

reviews.author: Enfant du Siècle
reviews.text: Eisenstein in Guanajuato is the provocative and demystifying portrait of a mythical figure in the history of cinema. It chronicles the misadventures of the Russian filmmaker during his visit to Mexico and, in particular, focuses on his relationship with the intellectual Jorge Palomino Cañedo. In addition, we find a series of anecdotes about Eisenstein's time in Hollywood, and reflections on death and sex, embellished with Greenaway's mannerist and exuberant style. Unfortunately, it really falls short when trying to explore Eisenstein's interests in a country as sui generis as Mexico, a place that fascinated foreign artists and intellectuals during the first half of the 20th century. There is also nothing about the creative process behind the unfinished ¡Que viva México!, and even personal relationships are barely sketched out. Greenaway simply does not achieve a balance between the personal life and the work of the biographed character, who ends up lost among aestheticism and ramblings.

reviews.text: Huh. I mean as with all Moore you have to accept a certain amount of condescension and oversimplification and honestly the overt Trump stuff here hardly registers in the early sequences but when he turns the camera towards specific grassroots movements surrounding the Flint water crisis, West Virginia teacher's strike and local elections he begins to paint a genuinely effective picture of the class-based weariness that undemocratic, capitalist institutions (very much including the DNC, that Obama water clip...) create and benefit from. Consider me genuinely surprised at how little of this was the ~wild, crazy Trump movie~ promised and how much of it was a pretty straightforward and damning critique of all the historical precedent for his views, policies and tactics. Pouring one out right now for all the #Resistance-adjacent folks that are gonna turn this on expecting the former and have heart attacks every time this highlights the failures and corruptions of the Democrats that got us here.

Being older I don't dislike them, and the comedy still holds up very well! But the lack of talking always makes the cartoons feels so much longer, and the gags used are usually much shorter than other Looney Tunes bits. Very fun, but I prefer other things. I'll give this cartoon specifically more credit since it is the first Roadrunner and Coyote appearance together, and the comedy is iconic like painting the rock or the highway bridges with the dots.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Many dismiss this early Cronenberg because it's very obvious it's one of his few films he didn't write but the redneck drag racing drive-in script he got his hands on isn't terrible and Cronenberg does a perfectly fine job retooling elements of Frankheimer's Grand Prix and Jack Hill's Pit Stop: romantically dramatizing the men crazy enough to get into one of these perpetual fireball machines and the brutal oil industry men (played by John Saxon!) that organize themselves around exploiting them. It's a bit limited by the budget but this is basically Canadian Days of Thunder. Nice Alberta location work, solid grit-textured photography by Mark Irwin, the Bruce Springsteen knockoff theme is hilarious and adorable, and so many explosions lol. Was not at all expecting the very last one.

reviews.text: Fast Company is surely the biggest departure of David Cronenberg's career compared to the film he's best known for. This one focuses on the drag racing circuit and the drama between the racers, mechanics etc. It's all pretty simple stuff - fast cars, girls, machismo and a soundtrack full of driving tunes. While the film doesn't break any new ground, it's mostly entertaining throughout; mainly thanks to the characters. The action is split between racing scenes and character drama, with more of a focus on the latter. The ensemble cast is good enough, with a standout performance from John Saxon as the villain of the piece. The film moves at a steady pace, with a few explosions etc here and…

reviews.author: nick
reviews.text: No other director understands the inevitable pain of fate better than Takeshi Kitano. In his masterpiece Fireworks, Kitano played an impassive police officer, Nishi, who is a superman capable of everything -- rob a bank, repaint a car, kill a bunch of gang members without hesitation, yet the only thing this superman couldn't do, is save his dying wife from cancer, or bring his long passed daughter back to life. In this pessimistic tale, everybody hurts, and everybody struggles to survive the cruelty of life, by relishing the scarce moments of happiness, even if they are as flitting as the fireworks in the sky.

reviews.text: A lot of Kitano's genre work leading up to this is defined by a sharp contradiction of his more poetic, tranquil filmmaking sensibilities and the frequently ugly realities they are suddenly and painfully interrupted by. There's something different about this one. He's developed his formal control to the point where he's effectively merged the two in an attempt to capture the experience of trying to persevere with those things living inside you simultaneously all the time; constantly aware of the beauty and the horror, the sentiment and melancholy. It's hard not to connect this idea with Kitano's own near-death experience and recovery process via art (the paintings drawn by his injured, suicidal friend are actually his own paintings), and though…

Deeply intricate - at first it impresses because…

reviews.author: Neil Bahadur
reviews.text: Among the most underrated films of the 2010s, the museum as a space of magnificence and/yet something quietly fundamental to the continued existence of a state. Something which connects us to all of history, where art connects us to the world of the past and yet at the same time a deceptive space that hides the stories behind the artworks - not of their making, but of their journey. All the lives lost in the military campaigns through history that brought these artworks there. Perverse in the same sense - that the human search for the ineffable and the human addiction to war are one and the same.

reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: Bonaparte is the funniest thing in the film, naturally enough. He's vexed at the Prussians who appear to be in his museum (the Nazis from the recreation) and he loves standing by the great paintings and declaring "It's me" like a megalomaniacal twitter meme. A comprehensive look at the museum and its history is of course impossible, so Sokurov focuses on the areas that interest him most: a collection of Assyrian artifacts, a 9,000 year old sculpture of a human figure from the Jordanian desert, paintings of the museum itself, of people touring its galleries and observing its works, a myriad of human faces in portrait. This latter section inspires the film's most fascinating rumination, as he speculates about what he (incorrectly) deems a uniquely European obsession with portraiture, and whether our ability to see what people look like hundreds of years ago changes our view of ourselves.

reviews.author: Mike Kennedy
reviews.text: I liked the idea of Russian writer/director Aleksandr Sokurov’s essay film more than I did its execution. Sokurov uses live action, animation, archival film footage and photographs, and CGI sequences to illustrate his voiceover thoughts on the significance of Art and, in particular, pre-20th century European art history. “Where would we be without museums?” Sokurov asks at one point.

As with classic Hollywood comedy stars such as Cary Grant and Jimmy Stewart, you get the distinct feeling that he was having F-U-N fun playing his role. Kotto in Friday Foster is a joy bomb, lighting up the screen in every scene he shares with Pam Grier (gosh, if only they were in twenty more movies together...) and even the ones in which he isn't ("What am I doing here?"). My happiness while watching this performance is only diminished by the regret that Hollywood didn't trust black actors or white audiences enough to give he and Grier more leading roles...what could have been!?!

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: The late Renee Harmon is completely overlooked for her tireless work on otherworldly exploitation and horror movies like LADY STREET FIGHTER and JUNGLE TRAP. In FROZEN SCREAM, a scientist (Harmon) invents computer chips that turn people into zombies on Halloween night. And she does it all in the name of answering life’s most important question: love or immortality? Filled with disconnected dubbing, experimental soundscapes, and a refusal to do anything by the rules, FROZEN SCREAM is a delirious DIY slasher that feels like it was filmed by a committee of brilliant dementia patients. It's frustrating because there's some vague hints at interesting ideas here, with themes of immortality and religion enthused with plenty of tedium. reviews.text: Frozen Scream and Don't Go in the Woods are like the KISS solo albums of the Harmon/Bryan partnership, each a demonstration of what they both brought to the table, but lacking that other extra dose of scrappy weirdness that makes their movies so endearing. Here, Bryan's sense of humor is gone, allowing Harmon to turn out what feels like a 'luded out version of Phantasm, reaching for Halloween but inadvertently creating something else entirely more interesting and original. If Run, Coyote, Run represents a complete disruption of the space/time continuum, then this is one of the first cracks. Love and immortality.

See this movie came out in September of 1990 and Gene sadly lost his wife and the world lost a very funny lady about a year earlier, Gilda Radner. So the whole movie being a love story involving Gene is hard to root for from the get go, knowing his personal life must have felt shakey after losing such an important part of it. If you look even deeper into her death, she actually died of Ovarian Cancer so this movie would seemingly be very personal to Gene. Which makes it's subpar score even harder to give.

reviews.author: Comicbookfan
reviews.text: A documentary about the British comic 2000ad that was the home of judge dread. It's your standard talking head documentary but filled with some legendary comic artists and writers who worked on 2000ad. It doesn't reveal anything new but as a comic fan I enjoyed hearing these guys talk about ther creation. It features pat Mills who was the founder and whose rebeliousness and honesty comes through with hilarious moments. It sadly doesn't have Alan Moore though, it would've gone up more stars if he was interviewed.

reviews.author: Geoffrey Broomer
reviews.text: The Story of 2000AD features sit-down interviews with everyone you would want to hear from on the popular British comic (home of Judge Dread). After setting the stage for the publications creation, and offering insights into its initial run - the documentary soon takes a sidestep away from chronology, instead introducing popular characters with brief overviews by their artists. Future Shock eventually gets back on track, but for legal reasons never names the corporate executives causing problems even as a large portion of it is dedicated to listing grievances against them. While highly informative, having a large degree of knowledge going in helps (I do, but still found aspects hard to follow) - when they lament the Andy Diggle years,…

reviews.author: Cinema_Strikes
reviews.text: This documentary on the history of 2000AD - the British comic anthology that gave us such amazing strips as Judge Dredd, Strontium Dog, Slaine, ABC Warriors, and Nemesis the Warlock, and continues to deliver with new classics like Grey Zone, Shakara, Zombo, and Brink, as well as launching the careers of many of the pivotal figures of modern comics like Alan Moore and Grant Morrison - makes for a terrific introduction to the storied mag and its history.

reviews.text: I was a big fan of 2000AD as a kid. I’ve never been into super heroes, but the worlds of Dredd, Rouge Trooper and Slaine were rich and appealed to me as a youngster. I’d been excited to see this film since I heard about it a year or so ago. It’s basically a talking head piece, but it’s filled with interesting characters and stories. There is also a ton of amazing artwork on display from the comics and is a real feast for the eyes.

reviews.author: mrbalihai
reviews.text: Although I was vaguely familiar with Judge Dredd in college, I first became fully aware of 2000AD comics through the Shriekback song, "Nemesis", which was a minor dance hit back in the 80s. My friend Steve used to hang out with the band, and he bugged Barry Andrews incessantly, trying to get him to explain what the song was all about. Barry would just smile and say nothing. It wasn't until a couple of years later that I figured out it was, at least in part, referring to the 2000AD character, Nemesis the Warlock, and his battle against Torquemada the Inquisitor. The lyric, "Everybody Happy as the Dead Come Home" was lifted right out of the comics, and someone wearing…

GOKÉ, BODY SNATCHER FROM HELL (Kyūketsuki Gokemidoro, 1968) is a phantasmagoria impulse of political allegory and nightmarish landscapes, one of the best late 1960s Japanese genre films, as David Kalat writes in his Turner Classic Movies essay, “is one deliriously pole-axed masterpiece that haunts the memories of all those lucky enough to have seen it”. reviews.text: Gordon Scott’s first sword & sandal movie is a mostly fast-paced and action-packed but always comfy and charming Italian fantasy epic co-directed by Sergio Corbucci (who also co-wrote it with Duccio Tessari). There are some pretty good set pieces involving different worlds and creatures, some early 60s gore and spectacular action scenes for this type of movie (and some scenes and story elements that would still be repeated until way into the 80s). I always like these movies best when they throw in some horror and fantasy elements, such as Mario Bava's 'Hercules in the Haunted World' or 'Goliath and the Dragon' (though it's also Hercules in that movie, but the changing names of these peplum heroes are a topic for another day).

reviews.text: Based on the 1934 short novel by James Hilton, this movie deftly counterbalance's moments of amusement with heartbreaking sadness. Directed by Sam Wood, who helmed the Marx Brothers' classic A Night at the Opera four years earlier, it follows a school teacher of a boarding school who recollects his vocation and private life between the years 1870 to 1933. Robert Donat portrays the protagonist with a shadow of gloom never faraway while Greer Garson is thoroughly endearing; delightfully counterweighing Donat’s performance, which won him a Best Actor Oscar over Clark Gable in Gone With the Wind.

Hale County This Morning, This Evening is messy and discontinuous, threads are picked up and put down, people are born, people die, people go to school, people go to work, people go to church, they hang out and just spend time with each other.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: The primary function of a great documentary is to capture life authentically without influencing its subjects with the presence of the camera or the documenter. Expansive, contemplative and intimately pensive, filmmaker RaMell Ross takes us on a wistful wandering into the lives of a two Black American men and their families in Hale County This Morning, This Evening. Taking a close look at the past, residing in the present and striving for a better future; the film is equal parts a work of vérité realism as it is meditative sublimity. Ross gives us a glimpse into the lives of people too often disregarded in the realm of documentary filmmaking and he paints a portrait of an entire racial and geographical landscape,…

reviews.author: Josh Larsen
reviews.text: A very particular sort of camera is at work in Hale County This Morning, This Evening. It peers from unconventional angles, lingers on images longer than they at first seem to deserve, and generally offers a perspective that is at once unremarkable, given the everyday subject matter, and revealing.

reviews.author: Allison M. 🌱
reviews.text: A contemplative film that explores Hale County, Alabama from director RaMell Ross. With Apichatpong Weerasethakul as the creative advisor, we know how things are going to play out. Personally, it's not my kind of movie, as I prefer more of a story (and a point). For instance, the Sandra Bland documentary was extremely strong and moving. Hale County had some great moments as well as some good photography. My favorite was probably the lightning storm which was poetic. It captured other moments in the lives of a tight-knit community.

reviews.author: Brother Bro
reviews.text: RaMell Ross has a wonderful eye for beauty and great editing / filmmaking sensibilities all around. There’s no real narrative here to latch onto but I enjoyed losing myself in this community and letting the images wash over me. Taking narrative out of the equation in this way seems to elevate truths that are otherwise glossed over or fabricated. There’s no need to make meaning out of a person’s struggles, or justify a lengthy take of a toddler cheerily bumbling around a living room.

reviews.text: Whenever someone proposes the idea of a person of color playing a classic character like James Bond, Batman, or Superman on the big screen, I cringe a little on the inside. And I've really struggled to figure out why. I'm sure that it would be the opportunity of a lifetime for any POC who would be chosen for the role. And there are more than enough capable non-white actors to fill those roles and deliver a performance worthy of those characters legacy. But it just doesn't sit well with me. And that's the power of motion pictures in a nutshell. They have the ability to project your image onto the screen and give you something to look up to. But…

reviews.author: Tim Brayton
reviews.text: Putting Elmer back into his green coat and smart little hat makes it irresistible to consider this Chuck Jones's apologia for earlier cartoons like Elmer's Candid Camera and especiallyElmer's Pet Rabbit: we've figured out how to do these right, let's go back and correct the boring old ones. It fits the overall impression that this is a metacommentary on what it means to be "a Bugs Bunny cartoon", thought it's not necessarily that subtle about it otherwise. At one point, Bugs literally says out loud that he's not going to let the plot end yet, since there are still gags he can play. I find interesting but in some ways kind of stiff; Jones in 1945 isn't at his peak…

reviews.text: Bugs avoids becoming Elmer's dinner through a simple, typically smart-alecky move, but chooses not to escape Elmer's house because, as he tells the audience, it's a set up too good to waste. So he stays and tortures Elmer (who, after all, tried to make rabbit stew out of Bugs). Cue a series of hilarious gags constructed out of physics defying animation, Carl Stalling's music score and Mel Blanc and Arthur Q. Bryan's (he does Elmer) voice acting. They liberally reference pop culture (Stalling's score riffs on well-known pop songs and classical music) and frequently break the fourth wall, including the elaborate final joke where Bugs tries to convince the audience they have Rabbititus. Bugs pretends to be 'Dr Killpatient' and, in another scene, Elmer's reflection in a sequence inspired by the Marx Brothers' mirror sequence in Duck Soup. It's rich, heady stuff delivered at breakneck speed.

There's barely any suspense and the central plot idea is not made use of (which is a shame after a reasonably good start). Jeff Goldblum delivers an entertaining performance as always; but Jeremy Sisto is terrible as the central antagonist. The soundtrack is decent but really I'm not surprised that this has faded into complete obscurity.

reviews.text: near-parody of this kind of completely miserable, deliberate, portentous "men… nature… violence… animals" stuff. At least The Grey tapped into a deeply wounded Neeson at the time, recognized that as the most compelling on-screen energy and ran with it. This has got career-worst performances from most of its major cast (except James Badge Dale, who somehow comes out looking good in everything for whatever reason), who are almost uniformly operating in the exact same brooding, whispery "this has Themes" register. Frequently comes alive in the action at least, there's an exceptionally brutal shootout about an hour in, but almost all of it is actively deflated by the slow, methodical style Saulnier seems to think provide this with meaning. Huge step down from the passively anxious, unpretentious Green Room imo, that managed to say—and make you feel—way more by simply diagnosing a vicious situation and then brutally sustaining it for 90 mins.

reviews.text: Down here shivering; everything smells rotten accompanied by the deadly sub-zero air. A pure white sheet of snow will soon be covered in thick scarlet fluid, deformed corpses and body tissues as there is an unbearably clogged sensation in the chest and a queasy churning in the stomach. The savagery of conflicts between nature and man, native mysticism, Alaskan landscape of frigid cruelty all comes down to a kettle-boiler that certainly takes a decent amount of time to simmer but subsequently never able to blow. Wolves’ spirits approach along with imminent darkness. The atmosphere is invigorating yet it becomes even more palpable when the lifeless light of permanent winter shone directly into the rural, unnerving menace.

reviews.author: Tim Brayton
reviews.text: By 1950, the Chuck Jones unit was so powerfully dialed-in that it's a little startling and even disappointing to find a short that is just blatantly a practice round. There are a lot of impressive and cool techniques being noodled around with here, particularly in the background paintings: in one particularly bold layout, we follow Bugs as he's swept up in the bucket of an excavator, and the skyline of New York swings behind him in a dizzying path so extravagantly angled that I can't even really visualize what the background painting must have looked like. Elsewhere, we see some extreme examples of Jones's comedy of goofy-looking still poses, in some cases spiced up by the human in question having…

reviews.author: Zachary
reviews.text: If the bunnies in Watership Down had handled their human interlopers like this, that story would've been very different. And also needed a new title, I guess. This is quintessential Chucky Jones here in two senses. First by spotlighting Jones' take on Bugs as noble defender of the home front. Along with writer Michael Maltese, the pair believed the rascally rabbit should never be the instigator, but only unleash war on those who trod on his soil first. The second is that once in the fray, the short unfolds as not one, but two Rube Goldberg setpieces that would make the man himself sweat under the bowtie with their intricate interlocking pieces and spatial mastery. All hail the Looney Tunes GOAT, doing what he does best, and better than practically anyone else.

reviews.text: Red Sparrow is an eye-opening documentary that never fails to leave an impact. It does an amazing capturing the many human rights violations and corruption that occur within China. And it made me rethink my understanding of China’s government. It’s a miracle that the filmmaker, Nanfu Wang managed to get all this footage to the US without getting arrested. Her sincerity and honesty helped to make this documentary feel more personal and authentic. Having it through her perspective makes the movie all the more impactful. I don’t want to be much more at risk of spoiling it, but I highly recommend seeking out this documentary as soon as possible.

reviews.text: The weight of the camera, the propulsion of the filmmaker - how much responsibility should we accept? To what lengths must we go for the sake of peace? What is irreparable? For freedom has never been the absence of discipline. Though media is now tethered to us in utero, the questions remain the same and equally as important. Technology cuts out steps to the daily routine but it adds more to the before and after. Vigilance is a mighty cost when politics will be politics yet what will you do when your hand is on the lever? What will be the action that defines you? Your version of good is just as violent and haphazard yet you know something still must be done. And something will be done - a witness offering conjecture - an omniscient power coupled with being small, lowkey, out of the way.

reviews.text: Was in a bad mood - more tired and achy than actually angry - and this had been added to my brother’s Plex server - probably at the request of my Mom, who keeps asking for uploads movies she already owns on DVD. I’ve long considered this to be one of Allen’s best movies, and maybe his last genuinely great one, with maybe his most inspired aesthetic conceit - that restless, roving documentary camera, which turns the conversations into endurance contests without the breathing room you get in shot-reverse-shot cutting. Obviously, the best performances are given by Judy Davis and Sydney Pollack, whose relationship to the material is professional but feels acidly, viciously personal as a result of their mutual talent; Allen and Farrow, who are using the shoot as a kind of therapy, aren’t “good” exactly, but it’s impossible to not be fascinated by their scenes, and especially the one where their characters reminisce about better times.

reviews.author: Rick Burin
reviews.text: This bruising, brutal slab of social realism was made during that brief period when Hollywood had the opportunity, and the inclination, to take aim at the nation’s ills. In 1932-3, films like Heroes for Sale, Wild Boys of the Road, The Mayor of Hell and Gold Diggers of 1933 (ostensibly a throwaway musical) held a mirror up to Depression-era America, in all its cruelty, drudgery and despair. Packed with righteous rage, these explosive movies went off like dynamite, helping to set the national agenda and changing laws and lives. Then the Hays Code came in, and the mainstream simply wouldn’t touch progressive pictures (with the very rare exception, like Ford and Zanuck’s The Grapes of Wrath in 1940).

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Exceptionally dark and angry pre-code crime drama/prison escape/social realist pulp movie that was designed to raise awareness of the brutal conditions of American labor camps but is also a sprawling, tense piece of Hollywood entertainment as well. Paul Muni is incredible at doing the desperate, wiry routine required here as the movie stacks horrifying, dehumanizing physical punishment and absurd, “legal” injustice against him one after the other until they’ve become completely entwined. The explosive breakout car chase climax in this is insane and the ending is about as bleak and sad as they come. “We need their permission to sweat.”

It also, however, effectively highlights a number of blind spots that were present at the time even at socially aware studios like Warner Bros. — studios sincerely interested in education, and highlighting injustice.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: I Am a Fugitive from a Chain Gang is a brutal and tragic melodrama which was also one of the first of Warner Brothers’ movies to depict a social conscience. It stars Paul Muni as a wrongfully condemned criminal on a chain gang who finally breaks out and heads to Chicago. It’s adapted by Howard J. Green and Brown Holmes from Robert Elliott Burns's autobiography and directed by Mervyn LeRoy, who delivers an authentic and straightforward film. It recognises the dreadful consequences of the Great Depression and evolves to assume an aggressive look at the unjust and cruel treatment of prisoners in the penitentiary system following World War I.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Val Lewton tasks Jacques Tourneur with a Haitian voodoo/plantation slavery Jane Eyre and—instead of turning in the exploitation B-picture that premise suggests—makes a genuinely lyrical, haunting gothic horror melodrama. One that reckons with the psychological and spiritual ramifications of that colonial history, as well as our broader relationship to the past (and the dead) in such a sad, unsettling and dreamy way that it rivals the best Henry James adaptations and is as heartbroken as it is eerie and ominous. Wind and drumbeats have never been used to such atmospheric effect and the supernatural, tropical locale lends itself to all the incredibly elemental tone poem imagery that is designed to force its rational and scientific white protagonists to reckon with…

reviews.author: reibureibu
reviews.text: External cultural artifacts made malleable so as to always fit within the parameters of the colonial, the foreign made just familiar enough to curtail unease to tolerable levels: tolerable as opposed to none at all because it is inherently contradictory and thus the malleability required to minimize such necessity, and tolerated to begin with because it is massively profitable of course. The land becomes a backdrop for white anxieties to play out but all the while reminding them of their abject hypocrisy. The wrongful inheritance of Saint Sebastian's suffering; the wrongful annexation of Haitian voodoo. A land of contradictions naturally breeds more: the living dead are born.

reviews.author: Alice Stoehr
reviews.text: So lyrical that watching it is like running your fingers through gossamer. Howling wind blows through stalks of sugar cane. Ceremonial drumming is audible far off in the night. Moonlight pours between the slats in the window shades, inscribing a broken pattern of horizontal light onto every surface in the room. (Noir lighting in the middle of the Caribbean.) The horror lies in these and other sensory details, gradually amassed over the film's slim run time. The plot is someone dreaming Jane Eyre, twitching in their slumber as intimations of romance give way to voodoo rituals. Unlike the bulk of Hollywood's 1940s output, I Walked with a Zombie acknowledges (if only marginally) the legacies of colonialism and slavery. But then, a Lewton/Tourneur collaboration isn't really like anything else. It's wind and drumming and moonlight and then you wake up.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Spare close-ups merely cap the overwhelming sense of unease, even dread, that Tourneur can put into long and medium shots. He begins the film with shots of empty rooms, static but active with tropical humidity, and the sense of misery and stagnation of those shots is only expanded when he finally turns to people. Tourneur filters ambiguous supernatural forces through the more visible effects of post-imperial interaction, wherein whites feel as trapped as the indigenous population they continue to control, in some cases literally. It always upends expectations, particularly when it reaches a Wizard of Oz-esque revelation of the person controlling the island's voodoo. Tourneur's crisp films work best for the unknown shaded into the crystal-clear frame, and none of his films is as troublingly unknowable as this.

reviews.text: I wish I had more to say about Beale Street, but all I can call it is heartbreaking. It filled me with a tension that so many black films fill me with, where I’m waiting for an ultimate, inevitable cruelness to set in, and so paralyzed by that waiting that I watch it more like a horror film. But there is no cruel twist coming. It’s all there from the beginning. And although it is more than anything a story about love and the lengths we go to see that love through, it’s a story about how much longer that length is when your very existence denies you to the right to live a peaceful life.

reviews.text: I honestly went into this last night thinking I'd have to downgrade my rating, but it continues to work like (pardon) gangbusters with an audience, and even if the script and gags aren't at the highest notch for the genre the involvement of real blaxplo heroes like MVP Bernie Casey, Isaac Hayes and Jim Brown plus that unbelievably infectious Gap Band theme song -- I seriously couldn't get to sleep last night because it was stuck in my head -- elevate it into something really special. It feels smarter and more relevant than a typical spoof because of the angle of time having passed these guys by, but it never ever lets whatever serious things it has on its mind get in the way of its consistently goofy, fourth-wall-destroying tone. This probably holds up better than a lot of much more revered 80s film comedies.

reviews.text: Depicting the very influential Wheeler family and their part of the 19th century US expansion into the western territories. A hefty miniseries that spans the generations: 1825 - 1890; height of US turmoil over civil war, native American genocide, slavery, gold rushes and the transcontinental railroad. Glamorized as Spielberg's pieces are, it concentrated heavily on the first people's displacement and assimilation by the white man; as well the hopelessness to stop the cycle of violence because of warmongers on both sides. A huge talented cast minus a couple that chewed the scenery... cough Skeet Ulrich cough cough... Sean Astin cough. Overall, a decent watch but AMC's Hell on Wheels did it better.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: A very strange, existential French art drama about one of France’s greatest historical figures (who has made it to film more than a few times in the hands of some of their best filmmakers) and also an electro-metal musical featuring mosh head-banging. Pretty fun! Director Burno Dupont captures the spiritual and patriotic awakening by placing the young Jeanne in wide, careful framing, while the indifferently elemental landscape contrasts the raw emotions of her expressive singing, intentionally amateur choreography, and intense bass drum kicks. It implicitly echoes the final words of Terence Davies’ Sunset Song “the land endures” as we watch some of humanity’s biggest struggles (war, religion, labor rights, personal and national duty) unfold through the emotions and moral devotion of a child. She also has an uncle that raps.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: A very Hollywood trying to catch up with current trends in late 60s youth romance. Dustin Hoffman plays the male lead, and except from Midnight Cowboy it is his first studio movie after The Graduate, and it is easy to imagine an executive thinking this was the perfect follow-up vehicle for him. It is also Peter Yates' follow-up to Bullitt, which is much funnier. It is at heart a very conventional two people spend some time together and fall in love fiction, only they meet in a one-night stand and there are new wavish aesthetic tics. What works is none of the stuff that gives it a pleasing time capsule quality, but how the movie is good at setting up a private world for its main characters.

reviews.text: This is a surprisingly fresh take on the time Michael Jordan tried his hand at professional baseball—a chapter of his career often glossed over or drenched in myth. Normally, ESPN tends to paint its star athletes as untouchable icons (looking at you, LeBron), thanks to the cozy relationships between sponsors, networks, and the athletes themselves. But this time, they actually dig into the reality: Jordan, for all his otherworldly talent on the court, simply wasn’t quite good enough to make it in baseball. He gave it everything, showed flashes of potential, but ultimately, he belonged on the hardwood.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Wolf Gremm’s Kamikaze 1989 stands as Rainer Werner Fassbinder's final acting role before his death, and it is a film infused with his spirit. Not only is he in nearly every scene, but by the side of his character throughout the film is Günther Kaufmann (as MK1 Anton), Fassbinder's frequent collaborator and onetime lover, and familiar face Brigitte Mira, too, makes an appearance. In addition, the film's vision of the future overlaps considerably with that found in Fassbinder's World on a Wire in terms of the presence of all-powerful corporations, and the mysterious, sterile offices in which they dream up and conceal their secrets.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Kamikaze 1989" is a 1982 film directed by Wolf Gremm. The film is most noted for being one of the sendoff endeavors for Rainer Werner Fassbinder who died that very same year. Based on the 1964 book "Murder on the Thirty-First Floor", the world dynamic (or at least Germany) is one of seemingly an absolute central power. Without the freedom to choose, the belief is that the conditioning to commit crime will decrease. Yet even though this process is put into place, there is an underground opposition force by way of the" Krysmopompas" who single out corruption in a passed out literary comic dubbed "The Blue Panther". This is where the entry point of Police Lieutenant Jansen (Fassbinder) comes in,…

reviews.author: Justin LaLiberty
reviews.text: wild german future jam with Fassbinder owning the frame decked out in some leopard print swag while laconically navigating some arcane crime shenanigans that puts this into singular genre amalgam territory, like if Inherent Vice and World on a Wire became one -- nothing else like it

reviews.author: DavidNeedToKnow
reviews.text: A very weird, stylish and special film. Crime mixed with sci-fi, which works surprisingly well and feels like a comic book adaptation. In the middle are the legend himself, here in his last film role shortly before his death and Günther Kaufmann as his sidekick. But surprisingly, Franco Nero is also there. You can clearly see and notice here that Rainer Werner was very exhausted from all the years of obsessive filmmaking and that the many drugs, alcohol and little sleep didn't make it any better. Even though Wolf Gremm directed this on paper, it is definitely Fassbinder's film with its vibes. The title Kamikaze also fits the filmmaker's hectic life very well. Essential for fans.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Spaghetti ends in a mournful ballad, packed with religious imagery and gorgeous scope compositions. Keoma is violent and cruel, but its sweep isn't very usual for the genre. Like the following year's California, it is a twilight of the Eurowestern movie, made by longtime Italian industry craftsmen who knew the well was pretty much dry by that point and decided to just go for it. A very strong cast, Castellari can be counted to deliver action, but the large swings in it, a mix of constant punishment and regret, are more unexpected. It is a very physical movie that seems to constant trying to pull back, positioning its violent gestures on a larger canvas.

reviews.text: I was already annoyed at the amount of puerile horniness in the first Kizumonogatari film and this one just upped the ante. Half the movie is just unrealistically large breasts jiggling and the protagonist drooling and stammering over lacy panties. I'm certainly not against eroticism in films, but there's nothing erotic about this. It's just childish and annoying. There is so much potential in anime, but creators keep going back to the same tired trope of an audience surrogate teenage boy awkwardly lusting after a teenage girl in a completely over-the-top manner. It's not only tedious, but it's such a tonal mismatch with the dark, violent material in the other parts of the film that it makes both feel worse by comparison. Even the fights are a letdown, all predicated on the protagonist discovering some heretofore unknown power that instantly wins the battle for him. Nothing like a good anticlimax to really get your blood pumping.
