reviews.text: I'm rather torn about this movie. On the one hand, it's lit and shot quite brilliantly and in a way that I find severely lacking in most of the movies I see today. On the other hand, I found the story to be a bit shaky and hit-or-miss, with some scenes really hitting it out of the park and some missing their mark entirely. Donald Sutherland and Jane Fonda give pretty great performances, and Fonda's character is interestingly complex. There are some hints at themes of surveillance and paranoia and the psychology of love. The problem for me was that ultimately it didn't feel like it all added up to anything coherent. I would definitely recommend this to anyone interested in the 70's noir revival aesthetic or anyone interested in hooker-with-a-heart-of-gold characters, but for me it was definitely the weak link in Pakula's paranoia trilogy. Good but not quite great.

It also includes a pretty great cast and a pretty damn good performance by Vin "500 Fights" Diesel. Knockaround Guys is definitely worth a once over if you're a fan of the mobster movie genre. One last thing, I think the moral of this here story is: don't use cocaine while committing a crime. reviews.text: Antonioni makes almost the perfect stereotype of what European art films are. It is instantly apparent from the opening credits of La Notte that this will be an art film above anything else. It is film of mood and ideas over story. It is a journey into the night, destined to go towards a perfectly open ending. La Notte is a film about how we value life and the questions death gives us. It presents broken, detached people with nowhere to go if they want to escape their situation. Responsibility depresses us and compresses our lives, we want irresponsibility so we can live freely but our head tell us not to pursue that path. We are alienated from each other…

reviews.text: Sex happens in the shower, love happens in the bath. Among its other virtues, Gillian Robespierre’s “Landline” is the rare movie that appreciates the difference between the pleasure of standing in the water and the satisfaction of soaking in it — the difference between trying someone on for size and swishing around in their dirt until your skin prunes and the water runs cold. Almost everything that a second feature should be, the film is bigger, richer, shaggier, and more satisfying than Robespierre’s “Obvious Child,” though obviously a product of the same irreverent imagination. It’s that most elusive of indie dramedies: An honestly told story about the messiness of human relationships.

reviews.text: I really love films that tell you a story almost solely through visuals. For the first thirty-seven minutes of this film there is not a single line of dialogue. Save for the odd muffled announcement being made over the loudspeakers at the Circuit de la Sarthe, every aspect of the narrative in this opening stretch is communicated purely through expressions, gestures and the raw sound of motor engines. It’s a smart and streamlined audio-visual language that tells the viewer everything they need to know in the most straightforward of formats. Towards the very start we are presented with a simple shot of Steve McQueen’s character, Michael Delaney, staring blankly at a crash barrier; his strained, glazed-over expression immediately telling us…

reviews.text: On paper Le Mans should have been a winner. It stars the iconic Steve McQueen, a petrol head known for his love of racing and made for such a film. The action is authentic, featuring real-life footage from the previous year's 24 Hours of Le Mans. Both the excitement and peril involved in such high-stakes competition is captured.

reviews.author: Anna Imhof 🌸
reviews.text: Steve McQueen was in love with realism. When he had his hands in a project, you could be sure he would insist on as much authenticity as possible. It was his idea for example to use real nurses and doctors instead of actors in the hospital scenes in Bullitt, and you will find the same meticulousness here: People of different nationalities aren’t played by Americans, we don’t recognize the Italian driver by the way he’s making dramatic gestures or the Frenchman because he’s carrying around a baguette. We recognize them because they speak a foreign language, and it’s not important that we understand what they’re saying. Clearly McQueen’s priority was to capture the atmosphere of the world of car racing…

reviews.author: Channing Pomeroy
reviews.text: As a film about racing, it’s simply unrivaled. If McQueen’s goal was to "remove the barrier of film” and show what it truly feels like to race a motor car against the best in the world, it’s an unqualified success that’s never been duplicated. It combines footage from a camera car driving in the actual 1971 Le Mans, three months of recreation filming at full speed using the same drivers, and scenes that captures the longueurs of a 24 hour race in the drivers’ trailers between racing shifts.

If Jeremy Clarkson hasn’t masturbated while watching this film at least once, I’ll eat a sock. (I would even bet big money that he can finish before the first word of dialog. To be fair, that arrives about forty minutes in, but he’s a septuagenarian, so he deserves a sporting chance.)

reviews.author: Brian 🐒
reviews.text: Rosenbaum was right. Pornography of the nihilistic sublime. The big joke of the title is that there are no actual “lessons”, just Herzog’s usual pompous neo-German romantic shtick. He shoots Kuwait as an alien planet so he can bypass understanding or analysis and instead wallow in the monumental beauty of destruction: epic blasted wastelands, apocalyptic plumes of smoke, every human figure reduced to a fossilized vector of pain or of greed. All the Wagner needledrops and portentous recitations from Revelation were absolutely insufferable. That the filmmaker had the temerity to liken this to Goya (whose images of war present atrocity in all its horror, absurdity, pathos, and—perhaps most importantly—specificity) only throws his idiocy into starker relief. A pile of fascist kitsch.

reviews.text: (Her standards are so inexplicable to me, but then, she's actually connecting, even if it is with people who are reprehensible, beneath her, scum of the earth. She's alone but not alone; so part of me still envies her odyssey. The enigma here is her; we see the tears in her eyes, we see the pain in her face, but when she is not hurt all we see is a blank slate. The men are cold, contemptuous. Not a single one shows any companionship, kindness, or sincerity. This is a scathing film, and its moments of humor are undercut by its bleakness in retrospect. It looks cold, feels cold, shimmering darkness of a city night or sunny days blotted out by thin fabric, it's all sharp but limited, always moving.)

reviews.text: In the 1960s the western began to reflect on the discrepancy between reality and legend through the introduction of increasingly older, tired and disillusioned heroes. However, it is only following the climate of social protest and cultural revolution that emerged in 1968 that Hollywood radically questions the myth of the Frontier. This profound revision overturns the foundations of the genre and dismantles its consolidated conventions. The romantic western definitively fades away, replaced by a crude visual and verbal realism, combined with a clear moral condemnation of the role of violence in American society. In Little Big Man, Arthur Penn adopts a reformist perspective on the complex relationship between whites and Indians, reinterpreting American history in light of contemporary events such…

reviews.text: An extraordinarily controlled piece of work. A slapstick comedy so dark, so icy cold, that it's been miraculously stripped of every single joke. reviews.author: Dubthrone
reviews.text: A beautifully composed minimalist slow-burn about the perception of miracles within the context of institutional ritual, commercialism, Church equivocation, and questions around piety. Sylvie Testud plays Christine, a woman suffering from severe MS, and a regular visitor to locations of Marian apparition. These trips, we learn, she makes less out of faith or hope for a cure than for the cultural benefits, and the opportunity to travel and be active.

The first half of Madeleine is really interesting, with some tender romance that eventually peels away to reveal a cynical world where love doesn't have a say and no love is truly pure. reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: “The emotions you are having are not your own, they are someone else’s. You are not the cat — you are inside the cat.” So begins Josephine Decker’s “Madeline’s Madeline,” an ecstatically disorienting experience that defines its terms right from the start and then obliterates any trace of traditional film language, achieving a cinematic aphasia that allows Decker to redraw the boundaries between the stories we tell and the people we tell them about. The result is an experimental movie with the emotional tug of a mainstream hit, a fragmented coming-of-age drama that explores the vast space between Hollis Frampton and Greta Gerwig in order to find something truly new and ineffably of its time. This is one of the boldest and most invigorating American films of the 21st century.

How does a hoe work? How long is a planted row of seeds supposed to be? Only 25 reviews on Letterboxd. reviews.text: Extremely Canadian artifact of 70's aimlessness. Alexis Kanner is nice to look at and gives a humorous Brando-like performance as a shiftless mumbling Thoreau wannabe. Maud Adams shows up and fucks him in a barn. I didn't even recognize Sam Waterston as his freeloading best friend. The plot is an afterthought to character.It's a deceptively deliberate film and sort of defies criticism. But it's also bleak and ponderous. I wouldn't enjoy sitting through it again. It plays like a proto-Stroszek. I do find it interesting that Harvey Hart went from being a veteran of the Universal backlot to making something that feels so experimental and in tune with the youthful avant-garde of the early 70's.

reviews.author: Trudes
reviews.text: This French documentary that focuses on the details of a 77 year old woman's life is everything that is pure about filmmaking. It's simply a person picking up a camera, with no idea what she's making, filming someone and even declaring at the end that she does not know what it is. A portrait, a diary, an experience? The segmented structure of it is beautiful and Sofia Bohdanowicz's direction is the definition of free. Shot on 16mm film, the vignettes are full of nostalgia. I think it could've been cut down a bit, but this represents what I believe to be the true beauty and purpose of all this movie stuff.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: As a general rule I try to avoid comparing women directors to other women directors, especially the handful of names typically batted about cinephile circles, but it is difficult not to think of Varda while watching this. But it's intended as a compliment; Bohdanowicz brings the same kind of open, humble interest in others that supersedes any urge to assert her own aesthetic vision onto real people or places, instead sitting back and listening. And what she gets is an inexhaustible fountain of charming anecdotes, recollections and relaxing routine from Juliane, the benign goofball septuagenarian, whose cheerful verbosity never comes across as inane prattle based on the care with which Bohdanowicz shoots the woman and her surroundings. With limited film stock, the director captures the daily bustle of the film's setting (here, the 18th arrondissement and Montmartre) in a series of almost still lifes, unfussy yet ebullient images that reflect the area and Juliane's contrapuntal talk of herself.

reviews.author: Harrison Wade
reviews.text: It's a pleasure to see a film so carefully attuned to small artifacts. While presenting Juliane's routines, Maison du bonheur offers a way of understanding history through habit and memory through images. Most segments, the image lags just behind the audio as if clarifying and specifying. But the images always fail to reach the depths of the dialogue. How can a cup of coffee capture Juliane's memories of her childhood? How can images of geraniums teach us how they keep away mosquitos? There's power in how Bohdanowicz makes each segment feel like the everyday through a composition defined by slight ellipses. That tension uncovers the artistry in living, which is, to me, what Maison du bonheur is about; Juliane explains how, for her, putting on make-up is a daily form of art. I see that generosity in each segment. I think it's a worthwhile way of living.

Much of that is because it's an adaptation of a novella by Prosper Mérimée in Carmen (1845), about a vixen who brings nothing but sex and death.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: I love movies where the filmmakers aren’t trying to impress the viewer but rather engage the viewer and make them feel that they are at the same level as the movie. What I mean is that Marty perfectly exemplifies human interaction and relationships in a very realistic way, so much so that over 60 years later I can still relate to it. If I were to describe it in one word it would be human. Ernest Borgnine plays the character of Marty with such realism and depth but the role is neither flashy nor crazy. The way he speaks and his tone of voice, his simple facial expressions, and body movements he makes are so believable and human in every sense. I couldn’t help but feel like Marty a lot because of this. What a stunning film, and it’s so easy to watch and enjoy.

reviews.text: A good standard spaghetti western that gets the job done, Lucio Fulci showcases that he always comes in clutch regardless of the genre he is pursuing. "Massacre Time" is something that I would consider a "meat and potatoes" standard meaning that its pretty straight forward but fills you fill and is satisfying in the process. There isn't a whole lot of plot details to keep tabs on when Franco Nero's character of Tom Scott wanders into Laramie Town, just simply that he is searching for answers when it comes to his past. All is revealed through purposed arcs within the narrative, but more importantly the film is just a mass gathering of western gun battles throughout. Naturally some other spaghetti westerns are more prolific in their stature, but "Massacre Time" is incredibly accessible and well-rounded within the genre.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: I don't understand the fashion world, but McQueen made me appreciate it like never before. Clothing as pure art, Alexander McQueen's work possessed the most primal, urgent, emotive beauty. The film McQueen shows how the myths he presented onstage derived from his reality. He brought his personal pain out in his designs and it takes real talent to represent the inner self in such an external manner. McQueen's story, of a humble working-class genius not interested in bullshit, makes for a tale both awe-inspiring and ultimately tragic. He wanted art above all else and that purity of vision seems extraordinary. McQueen never delves into an explicit consensus on how his genius worked, but it provides an overview of the struggles…

Some interesting dresses are featured; some are even to the point of insanity. He had a modest upbringing and became a huge name in his youth. With a lot of responsibility to bear, he turned to cocaine. He also became HIV positive and suffered from great depression which stemmed from abuse as a child (from someone not in his immediate family).

Entretanto, o filme deixa claro a quem pertence essas memórias. Não me entendam mal, assistir um filme é mergulhar no olhar do outro, mas esse me transmitiu tanto pedantismo, que mal senti vontade de molhar os pés. Além disso, a característica que mais me marcou nesse filme é o quanto consegue ser arrastado, cansativo. Na metade já estava exausta.

reviews.text: Is it possible that MJ was better at basketball than anyone has ever been at anything else???? That's such a wild claim but it feels right. This doc has some great footage of that last season (a story told in greater length in the new Netflix docuseries) and that's extremely enjoyable of course, but it's also a fun example of "the Omni movie" as a format-- it's spectacular and that's the main thing. Opens up with a shot of MJ dunking from the free throw line and they do the Matrix freeze-and-spin trick-- looks a little eh nowadays but it's very easy to imagine watching this projected 30 feet high in a planetarium and losing your fucking mind. Narration by Laurence "Morpheus" Fishburne really adds to the messianic feeling. With music by Fat Boy Slim and Soul Coughing. Man I hate Fat Boy Slim as a person but you have to admit that his music is IMAX as hell.

reviews.text: This is hands down the best documentary I’ve ever seen– and I’ll admit that I don’t watch them frequently, but it’s also one of the best movies I’ve seen in ages, and easily the most affecting film I’ve seen in a long, long time. Bing Liu made a beautiful, sobering Boyhood of his own life, about the trauma we adopt from our parents and our surroundings and how something as small as skateboarding can act as an escape from the pain of an unfulfilling life.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: Like most kids of my generation, I tried skateboarding. I had a buddy who had several boards and he always wanted to skate, so when I went over to his house I'd try it. I wasn’t great, but I wasn’t bad, either. Still, it never took the way it does for some kids. I sometimes wondered why.

reviews.author: demi adejuyigbe
reviews.text: As heartbreaking as it is life-affirming. Made me cry again. Just as struck with how affecting it is to see my own life reflected in these kids as I was the first time. Watched this with a new friend I've been skating with and we talked about how freeing it is to move through the world on wheels; it's not just a sport, it's a miracle. To glide over the ground like a bird– it's an affront to physics, a level of control over natural laws that can be mastered like nothing else. When you're a kid burdened with a lack of that control in every other part of your life, sometimes it's nice to know you can just take flight.

reviews.text: It's not very promising in the beginning, but once it jumps forward and everything starts to unravel, it's truly something to watch. So many things I can relate to, so many things I'm happy not to be able to. It's morose, but elegant. There are some hackneyed elements inherent to black family dramas, but this has all the nuance and authentic writing those films typically lack. Wish there was more compelling dialogue, not to say it was bad, though. The script is expansive, yet it handles many characters so well, more showing than telling. So bittersweet.

reviews.text: The title of Modern Times holds a double meaning to the film. It comments on living during the depression-era, but it also comments on Charlie Chaplin’s career during the transition of talkies in cinema. Dropping this silent masterpiece when the silent-era was in the past and where the modern times had talkies dominating the theaters, Chaplin proved to the people that silent films weren’t just a technological constraint in the medium — they held unique merits of storytelling that deem them both viable and irreplaceable.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Melodramatic disintegration of the female mind is a subgenre that rarely rises above its misogynist roots. Even the best examples often suffer from the sexist assumptions, implications, and themes; when these films are at their best, they tap into something true about patriarchy's impact on women by accident. Many of them, like Symptoms and Morgiana, pit woman against woman in a tired format of womanly jealousy. And yet, even in films like this with problematic portrayals and stereotypes, there is power in these performances, in seeing a woman carry a film, in sharing and empathizing with her pain. The horror is internalized violence and misery. In spite of themselves, films like this resonate.

reviews.text: Anxiety-riddled porno writer/dog walker (Gould) misplaces himself in one of his novels and loses touch with reality. He butts heads with the institution at every turn when he attempts to move from one NYC apartment to another. The movers are some mystical, shadow organization. The police cite him for every malfeasance. The telephone company is something like a team of Navy Seals. Cigar-chomping voice on the telephone surveils him and reports about the activities of his wife. Every woman becomes some form of a sex-kitten/truth-teller. Now. Filter all this through the early 1970's-era Gould filmography where "evil" modernity becomes a disruption in being human.

reviews.author: proofrock
reviews.text: Figured out how to see an uncut (if not properly OAR’d) version of this allegorical steamer, with Elliott Gould as a dogwalker and porn author who’s getting the runaround in life from the moving company set to take him and his wife (Paula Prentiss) and all their problems from one Manhattan apartment to another. Lotta Philip Roth phonemes, lotta fantasy, lotta hoo-hah and nonsense but I enjoyed it more than Little Murders (don’t @ me). Cool opening shot of the Deuce, with visible marquees for Russ Meyer’s Finders Keepers, Lovers Weepers, and Umberto Lenzi’s Paranoia (Orgasmo). Movie is fine, watch it or don’t, but Gould fanatics won’t be let down.

reviews.text: The first half of this film was really good. Although it was set in the 30s, it had more of a 60s feel to it and wasn't too dissimilar to Goodfellas. Peter Falk dominates this half of the film as a superb villain in the vein of both James Cagney and Joe Pesci. May Britt was good too and added an interesting dimension. It was fascinating to see her as I'd previously only known her as being Mrs Sammy Davis Jr. The music's great and at one point there's this really good nightclub singer whom I didn't realise until the credits was Sarah Vaughan! But suddenly someone flicked a switch and there was this voiceover talking about how great the police were and it becomes this rather dull procedural film. Right at the end, the murders return but it wasn't enough to redeem the second half. Still worth watching but it could have been a lot better.

reviews.text: "Murphy's War" is a 1971 WWII war film directed by Peter Yates. Starring Peter O'Toole in the starring role, the film begins with strong imagery focused on the aftermath of a German U-boat attack in the tropical region of South America. The boat attacked is that of the "Mount Kyle", a merchant ship which the U-boat found could be a hinderance in displaying the secrecy of their location. As it seemed that all of the personnel onboard the boat found their demise, a lone crewman named Murphy somehow survived. After miraculously being saved by a pacifist doctor down river who is part of a Quaker mission, Murphy plots his revenge to on the U-boat by any chance he can get.…

reviews.author: Wade Garrett
reviews.text: What a strange little film. It moves at a steady pace even though not much happens for the first hour or so. It's an action movie without that many action scenes, a dramedy without any real laughs, and a character study that never forces the characters to take a step back and breathe. This kind of in-between status of genre and execution keeps it surprisingly entertaining throughout. Murphy's War defies categorization, much like the weird energy of its titular actor, Peter O'Toole. Definitely recommended for all, even if just for the batshit, nail-biting conclusion.

reviews.text: In the waining days of WWII, Murphy (O'Toole) finds himself the lone survivor of an attack on his merchant vessel by an elusive Nazi U-Boat and its vicious commander. He winds up in a Quaker's hospital in Venezuela with no witnesses to the submarine's presence in the canals. So as the radio announces the domino effect of disarmament across the European front, Murphy devises a plot to find and destroy the sub. Duty mutates into revenge and gets slapped with a ticking clock, and both Murphy and the Germans get embroiled in a needless pissing contest when both parties could much more easily wait for an armistice. The "last word" mentality is as significant an allegory for war in general…

reviews.author: dwtyre
reviews.text: The best documentaries are those which capture something that you yourself could never see. They replicate the perspective of another person, someone you have never met and will never understand. And yet, through the film, you can feel their love and their loss, their joy and their sorrow, their humor and their pain. Just for a moment. And then you shut the film off and you're closer to understanding that person than you could ever have dreamed. My Flesh and Blood is encapsulated in that description perfectly. Brilliant, not so much it its cinematography or its artistry, but because of the beautiful lives toward which it calls us to bear witness. Truly a one of a kind experience.

reviews.text: One of the movies that started it all for me. Fresh out of high school, the extent of my knowledge was limited to what was in my local video store and the Troma catalog. Not a bad start but it was 'Mystics in Bali' that propelled me into the absolutely insane world of South East Asian horror. The tone of the movie is pure magic and the flying headed witch inspired not only an interest, but practically a lifestyle. If there's one thing that connects me to my teenage self it's movies and this is a canonical example of everything I desired from a film. Self defining, other-wordly, colorful, exotic catharsis. It might not be the greatest by many standards but it will always be a first love.

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: Materializing from Indonesia, MYSTICS IN BALI is an unforgettable interpretation of the Krasue/Leyek ("witch with the flying head") folklore of Southeast Asia. Cathy and her boyfriend travel to Bali so that they can investigate occult phenomena for a book project. But they never expect to encounter a witch who haunts the night in search of fetuses to eat. Directed by H. Tjut Djalil (LADY TERMINATOR), MYSTICS IN BALI is a sweaty hallucination that’s awash with Technicolor landscapes, rumbling synths, and an avalanche of lo-fi body horror. It's a slowburn, but not a no-burn. Prepare for lots of witch cackling. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

Loose, naturalistic dramas about trendy people in a trendy city, leavened with a hint of comedy before drifting towards Serious Issues that aren’t taken all that seriously. For most of its first half, it holds pretty closely to the formula – if that’s the word – before a dramatic third act twist derails it from its sub-genre path altogether. Without delving into specifics, this isn’t a “Baumbach” kind of ending.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Arguably Albert Pyun's best-looking movie, with its multinational backdrops and business-suits-and-machine-pistols aesthetic, deftly mixing location work and low-budget plastic production design. At its occasional peaks of true inspiration maybe the most successful attempt to make a William Gibson cyberpunk knockoff movie. If it lacks Gibson's ingenuity and terse elegance, at least Pyun wasn't above stealing whatever else wasn't nailed down (Gruner's anti-hero lead is basically a wholesale lift of the Turner character from "Count Zero", just as a for-instance). Even once it mostly turns into a chase movie with robots it's still packed with outstanding animatronic and prosthetic work and terrific stunts. Under-appreciated.

reviews.author: Yves Bouwen
reviews.text: Nemesis is a genuine genre-bender. It starts as Blade Runner and quickly becomes RoboCop. From cyber-noir to a Westernnetics style shoot-out and back to cyber-noir. Throw in a conspiracy thriller plot. Don't ask me to explain it. I will get lost for sure. I have to say I find LAPD cop Alex - more machine than man - a bit gullible. He seems to trust anyone he bumps into. The action is adrenaline inducing, with big guns, bigger explosions and the demolishing power of an atom bomb. In the third act we are treated with a jungle-punk adventure. This is all topped off with a terminator dancing on the edge of a volcano, Ray Harryhauser style.

reviews.text: "Nemesis" is an early 90's cyber punk endeavor directed by Albert Pyun, who unfortunately passed less than a month ago as of the writing of this review. With that being said, Nemesis fits the build of Pyun auteur-based style in delivery, proceeding forward with a pure experience to deliver a fun fan experience and clearly wearing that energy on its sleeve. The film absolutely has its moments of being goofy in some of its own elements, but it's like it doesn't care because its frankly too busy blowing shit up. A with that, you respect it even more for…

It's a film that's drenched so deeply in the process that Rembrandt gets himself involved in as he's coming up with a painting, to create a statement about art in and of itself - then indulging themselves within it. In some sense, it's maybe the best way for a director like Peter Greenaway to tell Rembrandt's story, because it's a habit that perfectly suits him too.

reviews.text: Only Peter Greenaway could dramatize what’s essentially an art history dissertation and make it this narratively and emotionally captivating. Not my favourite by any measure, but still remarkable. Portrait painting (and art in general?) as a site of conflict—financial, artistic, and in this case, also moral. The murder mystery at the core of the film is dense and complex, and critical information is delivered without the film ever signalling that it’s especially important. But even if you have trouble following the plot, Greenaway’s formal choices and all the great performances keep it so reliably watchable.

reviews.text: Thank God for independent cinema. It's refreshing to see something that is confidently its own thing; it stands out, it challenges form and, in those moments where all its elements come together, it really connects. Notes on Blindness is hugely inventive, sensitive and wholly imaginative film, so much so that, that I'm almost left regretful that it didn't connect for me throughout. The combination of stunning imagery and poetic prose are captivating, but something in it contemplative nature allowed my mind to wonder -- I dipped in and out of immersion -- yet I walk away thankful to have seen it, ready to push people to watch it and eager to revisit soon.

reviews.text: A fascinating formalist experiment that didn’t quite work for me like it should. The filmmakers take the audio diary of a man who has to cope with the loss his eyesight, and pair it with visual recreations, having actors lip sync to the audio tapes. Hearing the story told firsthand is absolutely moving, but I can’t help but feel that it would be much more effective as a purely auditory experience, as I often found the visualization distracting. Even though it doesn’t work conceptually for me, there’s a great deal of care and sensitivity put into the film; I still found it beautiful, poetic, and innovative.

Determined not to give in to his disability, he continued teaching, and started recording for the next 10 years on cassette tapes his musings about life and his experiences as a blind person. This documentary featured these audio tapes as sound track and script, while having actors re-create the scenes on film, utilizing dubbing and voice-over techniques to bring the tapes to life on film. reviews.author: BrandonHabes
reviews.text: The attempted rape of a woman afflicted with cerebral palsy by a man presented as mentally offbeat is extremely uncomfortable to watch, but it’s also precisely the point. The perverse and extreme nature of the scene challenges even the most sympathetic viewer to draw a line, proving that judgment plays a critical role in society for what is considered socially acceptable, and what is not. In a film where people are just as handicapped by their prejudices as the couple is by their differences, the near-rape scene crosses the threshold of what is “neurologically normal” and pushes the man even further to the outskirts of society, leaving him more alienated and marginalized than before.

Admittedly I am one who needs to catch up on South Korean cinema but I've nevertheless been rather highly impressed with the different sorts of films that I've come across from such a country. I feel like South Korean cinema is also ignored way too much these days and especially with a film like this, they continue to stun myself.

reviews.text: This was a strange experience because I didn't want it to end, and yet every minute I wished I wasn't watching it. A movie you definitely have to be in the mood for, but if you are, it's a hilariously intense comic tragedy. The opening scene sets the stage pretty well, and surprisingly, it gets MORE stressful after that. It was like if Revolutionary Road was set in the present and was a batshit insane comedy. Recently I was pontificating about how improv is generally a bad idea in film, but this movie definitely shows that it can add so much to a film if utilized correctly. So many great lines, and a brilliant balance of naturalism and histrionic character work. Worth a watch if you have the stomach for the "Stresssploitation" subgenre of dark comedy.

reviews.author: omarpierce
reviews.text: How do I tap into Croatian Letterboxd? I wanna know what the 100,000 people who attended Drazen Petrovic‘s funeral really think about this doc. I truly believe Vlade Divac feels deep love, loss and remorse around Drazen, but I kinda feel like he doesn’t understand the layers beneath it any better than I do, which is to say not at all. The way locals look at him and talk behind his back when he returns to Zagreb is crazy to see and maybe the most compelling part of the film even though it alludes to a much bigger conversation that we never get.

reviews.text: Before Magic, Larry, and Michael, basketball was...kind of lame. Especially the world of college basketball as portrayed in 1977's One on One, one of the earlier films to delve into college basketball. Our focus remains on Henry Steele (Robby Benson), a freshman from a small town who's attending the big city university Western (everyone's favorite Los Angeles institution) on a b-ball scholarship. We're supposed to sympathize with the underdeveloped Henry as coeds throw themselves at him, he gets an easy job overseeing lawn sprinklers for the rich salary of $4 an hour, and cops let him off in exchange for tickets to the Notre Dame game.

reviews.author: Miguel
reviews.text: Bugs Bunny Ranked (#91)Leave it to Jones & Maltese to totally reinvent a character they'd only used ONCE beforehand, and somehow pull it off with flying colors. Mel Blanc gives this retooling of the Coyote (now named "Wile E.", which wouldn't become his official name across all media until decades later) a voice that's oozing with smug pseudo-intelligence. He's book-smart, yet dumb in every other regard. That personality plays beautifully against Blanc's nonchalant line reads as Bugs, who's at his most ambivalent in this short. One of the best in the series, and a perfect example of how to properly rework a pre-existing character.

reviews.text: Has night ever looked both so cool and hot at the same time? It does in Pale Flower, an amalgam of noir and gangster/yakuza genres. It's not just Shinoda's visual aesthetic but also the content and the actors. Ryo Ikebe is the epitome of cool. We all want to be like him, secretly. Mariko Kaga is the epitome of hot. We all want her, even though we know it won't be good for us. These two shouldn't be compatible, but they are. They were made for each other. But the bond they share has no name. Beauty in destruction. That's what Shinoda is after. Gambling dens, night clubs, racetracks. The film is situated in this world. Toru Takemitsu amazing score suits it perfectly.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Much of noir is about symbols — symbols and moods. Wet streets and dark nights; hungry women and malleable men. The march of fate; the desperation of the helpless. It's about the way men wear hats, and the way they look at women in black dresses, whose shoulders glow in dim light. And it's about the inevitability of death, and the pointlessness of faith.

reviews.author: Angelica Jade Bastién🪼🌷
reviews.text: A film that on its surface has that endlessly cool posture of noir. Its aesthetics are endlessly rich and fascinating. The pulsating score. Characters wearing sunglasses at night. Smoke elegantly billowing toward ceilings. The soundscape of heated gambling. Characters curse, bleed, drink, smoke, gamble, kill. But most importantly they yearn. This is a film that is essentially about incredibly lonely people doing what they can to feel and capture joy. But they do so in ways that ensure their own ruin. Pale Flower is a reminder that sometimes all I need to really deep down dig a film are impeccable vibes, piquant characterization powered by intelligent performances, a commitment to cool, and a vibrant understanding of loneliness within a cityscape.…

reviews.text: Nothing changes. Times passes, old faces are replaced by new ones; bets are laid, money is exchanged, luck switches hands, but nothing changes. The streets stay soaked with the same rain; the same cards are turned over, over and over again. It’s a cycle. It never changes. There are horses to be raced—more money to be lost and made. Same old same. Then, up out of the crowded streets through crepuscular corridors buds a flower. Unwavering in graceful mystique and beauty, the flower tries to anchor its roots among the shadows of this cyclical world, but a flower can’t bloom underground. Many have come before me and many shall come again, attempting to restart here anew, but only this wicked game…

It does grow on you (if you have no standards) and for nostalgia purposes, it's a prime example of USA Up All Night material. reviews.text: It’s a silly sex comedy, but has the audacity to treat the romance between thirty-year-old Sylvia Kristel and a fifteen-year-old boy (played by an actual underage actor) semi-seriously. With age gap not even being the central issue, and not shying away from rather risque scenes of sex and nudity with the boy present. I imagine that if anyone wanted to release this today, or god forbid show it publicly, would be facing demands for their head, but I won't lie to you, I was quite entertained. And the main credit for that goes to the great Sylvia Kristel who, as per usual, effortlessly makes her character sympathetic. The most uncomfortable thing for me here was that it put me in the position of rooting for the disgustigly rich and privileged against working class people.

reviews.text: Well this definitely plays differently now than it did in the early eighties, in fact I'm surprised they're showing it on Prime.Back then it was another light, silly sex comedy....and every teenage boy's fantasy.The plot is preposterous with 15-year-old rich boy Philly (Eric Brown) being seduced by immigrant housemaid Miss Mallow (Sylvia Kristel) as part of a blackmail plot, but things get weird when they actually start to fall in love. Kristel's acting is not great, but Howard Hesseman has fun as the slightly depraved chauffeur, Lester, who has come up with the plot.This would certainly not be made today, at least not played for laughs as it is here, but I quite enjoyed the inappropriateness of it in a nostalgic kind of way.

reviews.text: Upsettingly clever Elio Petri commentary, about an accountant who is allergic to money. Embracing theft as a philosophy and a lifestyle, he quits his job and dedicates his life to torturing a corrupt capitalist butcher. It's the third part of Petri's Neurosis Trilogy, (which of course I am watching out of order, le sigh.) I don't have much to add to Gentry's great summary, except to say that all of the performances were superb-- especially Daria Nicolodi in an early role as the butcher's mistress. She's such a presence. Her sexual antics got the film censored for a short while. Petri delivers the expected misogyny but not without comment. Our hero Total (Flavio Bucci) cannot resist using Nicolodi as an…

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Elio Petri sees fit to take apart a society based on possessions in this truly absurd sort of crime film come strange comedy. The plot focuses on a lowly bank clerk who, upset about living in poverty, decides to start stealing from a wealthy butcher - who in turn uses the crimes to own advantage by claiming insurance. The film is very oddly paced but makes its point in such a unique way. There's always so much going on - not least the central conundrum, the dichotomy between "to be" and "to have", and the fetishistic way money and property are portrayed. Flavio Bucci (best known for his role as the pianist in Suspiria) is perfect in the lead role…

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: A transgressive cross between Bertolt Brecht and Karl Marx, Property is No Longer a Theft is the kind of film I so often crave, but so seldom receive. It is a film that is iconoclastically self-aware and so darkly comedic. It is scathing in its critiques of bourgeois power structures and capitalist deregulation. It is, despite being as left-leaning as a film could possibly be, not a blindly loyal Marxist piece of cinema; it asks tough questions, challenging both the morality and practicality of the philosophy behind itself. The main question posed however is this: who are the real thieves? Is it those who burgle in the dead of night? They steal for pennies and when compared to those who raid…

reviews.text: There is a striking scene in the middle of Elio Petri's Property is No Longer a Theft where a famous thief is given a funeral by the cream of Rome's criminal underclass. His eulogiser exhorts the gathered mourners - and we the audience - on the value, nay, the essential need, that society derives from crime. Like the film surrounding it, it projects the surface appearance of absurdism but, also mirroring the entire piece, it strikes at a surprising and counter-instinctive truth. As this man lists all the various institutions and hence professions and hence support services and hence livelihoods that rely on the presence of crime to exist, we realise that what he is saying is not exactly false.…

I would've liked this movie more if it didn't have a "Women. Amirite?!" attitude about it, which also extends to a mean-spirited portrayal of the lesbian couple at the heart of the movie, a movie written by two men. Joe Swanberg, the mumblecore director and actor, stars in the film's second half and turns in arguably his best acting performance to date. He is intense as hell in this. reviews.text: Two kisses and a crossdressing sequence were enough. To any queer woman, Christina could not be more queer, even if she does spend most of the film in love with a man. To any trans person, Christina is a fountain of dysphoric behaviors and triggers. This film, with its tragic hetero-romance, is as openly queer as it probably could be. Two kisses, and a crossdressing sequence. It somehow manages to convincingly have two women be in love, and two men, but with only three characters, because subtext can isolate moments and spin them into whole universes. In reality, she was in love with a woman and left not for a man but for herself. Hollywood tries in their own ways to honor that, but it's still laden with this unnecessary connection. (The film itself, all massive old Hollywood-built sets and snowy landscapes and that low angle on the coronation scene is just stunning, truly stunning.)

Every gag is perfectly constructed, with an emphasis on slow build-ups to big punchlines, like the Sheriff of Nottingham slowly realizing that he's been had while in the middle of doing construction work on his new home, and Bugs methodically baking a cake for the Sheriff to fall into after he's been repeatedly clobbered on the head. Then there's the Errol Flynn cameo at the end, which is just icing (cake again).

reviews.text: Honestly, I don’t think this is nearly as bad as people seem to think it is! Obviously, it’s filled with issues in both the mediocrity of its story and lacklustre execution, but I found it’s core character motivations to be surprisingly solid. Every character has a personal problem to overcome, and even if they are small-stakes, I actually found that to be really wonderful because when you’re at the age of these characters, overcoming those small challenges can feel like lifting the weight of the world. Having those problems find resolution through the unlikely bond of a middle-school basketball team brings a lot of charm to the movie for me! Combine that with a healthy dose of nostalgia points, and all the film’s problems largely fall to the wayside because of just how breezy and light the movie is!

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Ride in the Whirlwind" is mid 60's independent western directed by Monte Hellman. Looking back at the time of its releasement, it is one of the founding western films with the wave of New American Cinema that predominately made its impact known throughout the 1970's. Uniquely enough, in probably what was a budgetary effort at the time, Monte Hellman shot this film piggybacking of another one of his efforts "The Shooting" (1966). They are both different within the narrative context, both now they are considered companion pieces of each other in addition to the application of being able to be viewed on separate terms.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: there's something here about short-term thinking (look at the way they idly play checkers, a game of strategy, while complaining about how futile of a game it is), and then something else that suggests these characters are trapped in a behavioral loop (endless pursuit, capture, and escape), and it seems to be pointing at something spare and existential. but deliberate inertia is still inertia, and even at 80 minutes i couldn't wait for this to either get moving or wrap up.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Ostensibly more straightforward than The Shooting, though Hellman's idiosyncratic use of close-ups and the suffocating use of interiors hints that this is every bit its companion's equal as an unnerving formal experience. If the other film was a John Cheever-esque exercise in quiet surrealism wherein the taciturn western hero ultimately confronts only himself, here the contents are more explicitly political in their deconstruction, noting that in a time where the only evidence was circumstantial evidence, being in the wrong place at the wrong time is tantamount to guilt. In a brutal yet oddly subtle and understated way, the film shreds the genre's morality plays by illustrating how posses of outlaws and of their victims ultimately look the same to an…

reviews.text: the certified copy of westerns. monte hellman subdues everything monumental and cliche that has been building-up in the genre since 1939 while still honoring the symbols themselves, snatching them by the scruff amidst the chaos of billowing dust and blaring gunshot. ostensibly it is as 'back-to-basics' as any normal b-western, yet the enervated tone transforms each scene into a study of its inception & dispersal. the closed-circuit logics of ride in the whirlwind and the shooting are analytic without being compact, and the pointed denial of personal masculine agency in both works seems like a necessary rebuttal to a century's worth of narrative altars erected to guns, trains and stetsons.

reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: A perfect companion to/inversion of The Shooting. Instead of wandering through wide open spaces, the heroes are trapped in increasingly confined ones. Instead of chasing something they don't know for reasons they don't understand, they're being chased by perfectly logical (if extra-legal) pursuers for perfectly logical (though mistaken) reasons. In The Shooting, it's Warren Oates's fate to chase himself through an endless wilderness. In Ride in the Whirlwind, it's mere chance that ensnares Jack Nicholson and it is luck, the randomness of bullets fired into the brush or a pretty girl catching the eye of a lonely man, that allows him to escape.

reviews.text: Lavish sets, amazing scale, hundreds of extras, and plenty of romance and drama, but the fun really starts at the halfway mark when Robin Hood shows up and we get 40-year old Douglas Fairbanks shrugging off the chain mail and bouncing around like a kitten who’s been into the catnip.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: The most striking part of this were the sets. Huge castles and grand forests made up most of the film, and they were of a scale that gave the whole thing an epic feel, even if it is was one of the slower Robin Hood tellings I've seen--until the last act. The last act becomes a huge, sprawling battle that would not be out of place in something Tolkienian, but without the orcs. The effects are all a bit basic, but the size of things made up for that remarkably.

reviews.author: Jim Dooley
reviews.text: For audiences in 1922, ROBIN HOOD generated as much excitement as RAIDERS OF THE LOST ARK did for my generation. It starred the tremendously popular Douglas Fairbanks who was known for his acrobatic stunts in thrilling adventures. The pre-release publicity promised spectacular sets filled with an epic-sized cast. Even its premiere was one for the record books. There had been filmed versions of the Robin Hood story before, but nothing approaching this.

reviews.text: Over the years I've seen so many different interpretations of the legend of Robin Hood that I can't quite remember whether he was a cheeky chappie in green tights, a forty-something year old with a Californian accent, a beefy Kiwi with an even dodgier accent, or an animated fox? I can now add this strange amalgam that seems to toss bits and pieces from folklore and every other film about Robin Hood into the mix too. To say this was far removed from previous films I'd seen would be an understatement, because this was all over the place tonally from the off.

reviews.text: Each Robin Hood film seems to have a variation of the primary story. In this film, we don't have a Sheriff of Nottingham or Guy of Gisbourne. Instead, we have Baron Roger Daguerre who plays the role of collecting taxes from the people. The baron is initially the friend of Robert Hode, another modification to the story that establishes the common name of Robin Hood. As Hode and Daguerre fall out of favor with one another, we see the conflict Daguerre endures attempting to serve Prince John while maintaining some interest in Hode.

reviews.text: This is the only “heavy metal” horror movie you’ll ever need to see. Jon Mikl Thor and his bandmates end up in an old house, which was the site of a brutal satanic killing. Soon evil beasties possess groupies, three full Thor songs are performed, and everyone makes love for a very, very long time. The creatures may or may not look like penises with googly eyes and wigs. The practical effects of ROCK ‘N’ ROLL NIGHTMARE are only eclipsed by Thor’s hairless, ripped bod. You will see more Thor than you are comfortable seeing, but the leather studded banana hammock is so worth it. In true Canadian form, ROCK N’ ROLL NIGHTMARE is polite, generous, and cares deeply that you are comfortable and have a good time. There is only one true Thor. Long live his reign! (Annie Choi)

reviews.text: Harold Lloyd, often referred to as “The Third Genius” of silent cinema in deference to Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton, is seldom mentioned in the same breath as his seemingly immortal contemporaries despite the fact that he out-earned The Tramp and The Great Stone Face during their heydays, and made more films than the two of them combined. Revisiting Lloyd’s fourth feature / his masterpiece, 1922’s “Safety Last!”, it seems that Lloyd may not be remembered as one of the silent era’s greatest screen comedians in part because he may not have been a comedian at all.

reviews.author: Branson Reese
reviews.text: Harold Lloyd is often considered the third great silent comedian behind Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton but whereas Caplin was a sentimental clown and Keaton was a deadpan surrealist Lloyd's angle was that he was just a guy who kept almost dying. This shocked audiences in the 20s for whom dying had fallen out of fashion. Nowadays the Jackass boys fill the cultural niche left by Lloyd's death in 1971 from being struck by lightning as he cleaned the top of the Chrysler Building. And if I'm being honest, they do it a lot better due in no small part to their ability to speak. Who said there's no such thing as progress?

reviews.text: This biblical epic from Cecil B. DeMille is a lush visual pageant. The lavish sets and costumes sport every color of the rainbow in all their bright and shiny technicolor glory, as if the Middle East never saw a speck of dust. Some beautiful location shots add to the grandeur. The script does a fine job of elaborating and expanding upon the biblical story of Samson and Delilah, turning it into a great twisted romance for Victor Mature and Hedy Lamarr. The thrilling finale is a marvel of 1940s special effects, with an explosive magnificence that rivals much-later sword-and-sandal movies like Clash of the Titans.

reviews.text: As the movie started, and I sat through about ten minutes of company logos, I thought to myself, I bet this movie is going to start with the opening credits on a black background with the audio of the opening scene playing over them. Unfortunately, this wasn't the only prediction of mine to be proven true, including the one concerning how the film ends. Girl loves boy, but girl is set to marry another boy in an arranged marriage, parents disapprove, etc., etc. Classic boilerplate plots are fine, provided they offer something else that's new or interesting. This doesn't. The director shows little understanding of visual storytelling or spatial sense; I never did figure out where the two houses where most of the action takes place were in relation to each other. I also kind of hate the title, which is meaningless other than as a puerile metaphor.

reviews.text: A movie that asks the question, "What would happen if Scoob and the gang ran into something real and horrific?" This movie is pretty funny and then it's pretty violent and gory. The first hour had me laughing and enjoying the journey well enough. The last half hour becomes a bit of a blood bath and most of the humor takes a backseat at that point. It was still fun to watch though. This movie is definitely flawed and far from perfect, but anyone who enjoys horror comedy can find something to like with this film. It's a good premise, it knows how to have fun with it, and by the end, you'll see plenty of blood and guts.

reviews.text: I urge everyone, sincerely, to take some time out of their hectic lives and watch this gem of a movi...no, film. Everything from the writing, costuming, and score is first rate. Did I weep at the final montage? Sure. For "to weep is to make less the depth of grief." As the credits rolled, I found myself huddled in a windowless room, embroiled by emotions made raw by the stinging poinards of truth, and forced to face those transitory realities of life we only consider quietly in the honest solitude of the near-dawn hours, the ones we never dare voice aloud. This is a truly marvelous cartoon, succeeding in every register one of these can succeed: the backgrounds are thick with creepy atmosphere that gives even the silliest jokes a macabre energy, the timing of gags is absolutely airtight (the scene of Porky walking blithely through a room while sharp blades keep missing him by centimeters is, like, perfectly timed). reviews.author: Eliza
reviews.text: Easily one of Chuck Jones’ best and my personal favorite of his three Porky and Sylvester cartoons. It has a tendency to be on the talkier side, particularly Porky’s repeated noting of the house’s charm, but it’s by design and follows the Tex Avery philosophy of repetition—drill an idea into the audience’s head and immediately refute that in any and every way possible. Gorgeous posing, atmospheric layouts, clear and concise storytelling that is funny first and foremost. I adore Claws for Alarm for its layouts and appreciate the minimalism, Jumpin’ Jupiter has its own share of moments, but I definitely feel this is Jones’ most sincere, focused, and unadulterated if you will entry of the bunch—even if the ending is a lame throwaway caricature. Really a shame we only got 3 of these!

reviews.text: Jolting, chockfull of discoveries, blasting your expectations. Searching for Sugar Man is a documentary on a genius musician that even most rock jocks have never heard of, that of Mexican-American singer/songwriter Sixto Rodriguez from Detroit. The producer who discovered Peter Frampton declares to this day that Rodriguez was more talented than Bob Dylan or Bob Marley. Two albums were produced, “Cold Fact” in 1970 and “Coming From Reality” in 1971, and both flopped commercially in the U.S. Testimonies suggested that the crushing blows of failure drove dissolute drifter Rodriguez to suicide. Dead or alive his music bootlegs found their way to Cape Town, South Africa which made Rodriguez godlier than the Rolling Stones and a catalyst for political revolution.

It is a really well pieced together documentary and thematically rich one peppered with the wonderful music made by a wonderful human being, and it all just breezes past in a runtime of 85 mins. Also featuring one of the most emotional concerts I've seen. Highly recommended, but make sure you go in knowing nothing about it.

reviews.text: When you’re doing one of these subtext-heavy allegorical movies, the critical thing is that you get the “text” of the movie right. Meaning: the movie’s surface story — the characters and plot that you’re using to deliver your allegorical messages — needs to be interesting and compelling by itself, subtext aside. And that’s the problem with Shadows And Fog. It arguably has worthwhile subtextual things to say about death looming over our shoulders, our role in the universe’s “plan”, the value that children bring to our lives, etc. (even though Allen had already been saying similar things in his films for at least 15 years by this point). But the story is dull, the characters are bland, and the humor…

reviews.text: Though its schtick and story wear thin and result in a middle-of-the-road narrative experience, Woody Allen's "Shadows and Fog" is too good-looking and well-cast to be written off as an average film. Filmed in inky black and grainy white, Allen executes his film as a reflection of the German Expressionist directors of the early 20th century. The plot, dark comedy, and typical social commentary may ramble on a bit too long, but the film's aesthetic keeps things appealing.

reviews.text: Naked women in pods, James Hong as a mad scientist, and mutant monkeys - what more could you ask for? It turns out, a lot more! "Shadowzone" is a mash-up of every sci-fi and horror film that came before it, borrowing ideas from better-known films. The most notable example of this is "Alien," as "Shadowzone" is a cheap knockoff that lifts entire scenes. Unfortunately, much of the runtime is spent inducing sleep rather than building suspense, as the film swaps tension for pure boredom. Maureen Flaherty is naked in a see-through pod for 85% of the film - does that make sitting through the rest of this dull affair worthwhile? I can't say it does.

reviews.text: Burt does De Palma—and it's almost as good as that sounds. It's so close! Between an action-packed opening and conclusion, there's the bulk of the movie, which could be charitably described as 'meandering,' but it's also home to some of the film's most interesting stuff—like Reynolds as a vice cop who, like any good pervert, has way more chemistry with the film's love interest when he's watching her through binoculars than he does when they finally exchange dialogue (I love the scenes that contrast Burt's working-class cop swilling Budweiser with Rachel Ward's high-end escort pouring herself expensive red wine)...or Henry Silva's PCP-powered hitman, who seems to take genuine pleasure in slaughtering people with his shotgun.

reviews.author: Justin LaLiberty
reviews.text: Burt doing De Palma, similarly aping Hitchcock (there’s not very subtle shades of Vertigo here) but also trading in voyeurism and paranoia, not unlike the same year’s Blow Out — it’s easy to accuse this of being overlong and erratic (it does change vibes every 20 minutes or so) but, despite Burt’s claims that it’s “Dirty Harry in Atlanta”, that only adds to how weirdly European this all feels, as if Fernando Di Leo and Jean-Pierre Melville co-directed an Atlanta set vice squad thriller full of hookers, nunchucks and a fittingly bonkers Henry Silva

reviews.text: Probably the only movie of its kind – a real-life couple capitalizing on their fame by portraying the story of a jerk falling for the girl he leads a slut-shaming campaign against after he thinks she falsely accuses his friend of rape. The romantic angle definitely feels contorted just to give its stars some sexy scenes that are easy to promote during Must-See TV, but the more serious aspects of the movie work shockingly well. The idea of an entire school, teachers included, blaming a girl for her own rape and being hesitant to punish “good boys with a bright future” is unfortunately no less relevant 25 years after it premiered. Even though Tiffani Thiessen and Brian Austin Green have chemistry (admittedly I preferred David with Valerie over that dishrag Donna on 90210), this movie would have benefited from focusing solely on Tiffani’s character getting justice.

reviews.text: Osamu and his wife Nobuyo can’t afford to have sex anymore. Middle-aged and marginally employed, the Shibata couple is crammed into a ramshackle apartment on the outskirts of Tokyo, along with a pre-teen son named Shota (Jyo Kairi), Nobuyo’s younger sister (Matsuoka Mayu), and the frail grandmother whose monthly pension keeps everything from falling apart. The musty hovel can hardly fit all of the life that’s stuffed inside of it; random boxes and old toys are scattered in every direction, as if everyone would rather live in the mess they’ve made than dare to remember all the things they’ve lost. And it's those ridiculous moments that are almost always her best — she can be vulnerable, sure, but so can nearly everyone else. reviews.author: Chris Hughes
reviews.text: A late period silent and transitional film, Show People has a lively score and jokey sound effects but no spoken dialogue. It’s a spoof of the boilerplate “milkmaid to movie star” plot and based, according to some, on the meteoric rise of Gloria Swanson. Marion Davies stars and she’s in her element. She has advanced comic skills that don’t show in her dramatic work. She has a whole arsenal of funny facial expressions and goofy postures. King Vidor directs with his emblematic confidence. The pace is perfect and the jokes all land. The story is charming too. And the cameos! So. Many. Cameos.

If it had an ounce of supernatural element to it, I'd say Hal Hartley had just made his own pilot to an alternate Twin Peaks series. Instead, it's just an independent film indebted to Lynch's weird amalgam television masterpiece that happens to capture the zeitgeist of its era--or at least, the appearance of it--deftly.

reviews.text: The most unnerving moment in 'Sledgehammer' doesn’t even involve typical horror-movie horror of any kind. Just as the group of soon-to-be slasher victims arrive at the haunted cabin they will be staying in, there is an extended slow-motion shot of one of the couples walking across a field set to bright and cheery music. They embrace and laugh throughout their long journey across the short distance. At one point, the man tries and fails to balance a beer can on his girlfriend’s head. They seem to be without a care in the world. This moment is so goofy, innocent, and sugary that its mere presence within a movie called 'Sledgehammer' is enough to send bad vibes out to all your…

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: SLEDGEHAMMER is the first shot-on-video horror movie ever made for the home video market . . . and so much more. Ted Prior (DEADLY PREY) leads a cast of self-loathing party animals who face off against a dimension-leaping ghost with a fondness for homicide and wearing a flannel. By the end, guts, brains, and beers are splashed across every inch of the haunted condo walls. Directed by David Prior (KILLER WORKOUT), this is a feel-good collision of slow motion abuse, unintentional surrealist art, homoerotic pathos, and slasher video-barf. The old saying will always ring true: if you survive SLEDGEHAMMER, you’ll never, ever forget it. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Sledgehammer" is a 1983 SOV horror feature directed by David A. Prior. The film focuses on a revenge plot scenario, where years before a boy witnesses his cheating mother and her lover killed with a sledgehammer. The boy, who was hiding in a closet during the ordeal, goes missing and it is ultimately assumed by authorities that his disappearance was due to the murders as well. Fast forward a decade later and sledgehammer related deaths are occurring again, leading to the audience playing a guessing game with the cast of characters if it is the young boys return, possibly the original killer, or something else entirely all together.

I especially like how 30-somethings with visible age lines and beer guts play horny teens whose only interests are "getting wasted" and getting laid.

reviews.text: Watching this and Space Jam in the same day should honestly be a crime.My thoughts and approach to this film shifted throughout its duration. At first I was totally approaching it as an experimental film, which it is to a certain extent, but the further into it I got I realized it's actually just a really unique horror film. Not only that but it's one of the most terrifying horror films I've seen. But it's also, in some ways, a drama, maybe even a romance. Sleep Has Her House is so abstract yet so focused that it can really fit into any genre depending on how you look at it, although calling it a comedy is definitely a stretch.…

reviews.author: Eli Hayes
reviews.text: Lit and shot in a manner that allows dimness to completely envelop the majority of each long take, so that the focus on the landscapes & the exploration of space feels like you're observing the remnants of an isolated or even forsaken region. The cocoon of darkness that the life exists within is so murky that it's less reminiscent of shadows & earthly lowlight, and more reminiscent of a distant location in which earthly sites sprout from deep space; a galaxy trapped somewhere between ourselves and an inky infinity. For me, this is a "science fiction" film, through and through -- a portrait of an Earth, or an adjacent reality, that has become alien, invaded not by extraterrestrials but by a slow, persistent decay. A knowledge that, eventually, the nightfall will become permanent and places such as these will only exist in the memories of a blind universe.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: More "slow cinema" should take a stab at horror. Like watching the Night on Bald Mountain segment of Fantasia on slo-mo, Sleep Has Her House presents the unmolested beauty of nature, then slowly twists and gnarls it using little more than almost imperceptible pull-outs and a slurred sense of time communicated by fading light. The film's elements are, well, elemental, using subtle movement of space and time to radically alter the tone. Consider how the opening shot of a waterfall begins so tranquilly. Then the shot starts to expand, pulling out until the cascading water, at first gossamer waves of falling mist that fills the screen, gets smaller and smaller as a colossal landscape emerges around it. Eventually, the roar…

reviews.text: Nocturnal snapshots of heaven descending into Earth. There is a primitive aspect to Scott Barley work, his movies tend to play around some very basic elements, light and all enveloping darkness, the wind on the trees, water, clouds, the movement of the camera (whose material presence is always felt) as it relates to those. Less a return to nature than a return to essential things and the manner filmmaking can render them. It is never just pure admiration, but also contains a good deal of trembling, a horror like quality that is hard to shake. Sleep Has Her House, his first feature I’ve seen, makes this relation more explicit even before moving towards pure near abstract horror in the final…

reviews.text: Nature is a force. It is both ruthless and beautiful, a scourge and a blessing, vicious as it is soothing, isolating as it is holistic, tangibly earthly as it is so elusively transcendental. Bewildering, impossible to demarcate, its power to harm and to heal is as omnipotently inexorable as it is pulchritudinously abstract. Lambent hills awash with light; river and wood oscillating flawlessly like a pair of licentious lovers. The hand that rocks the cradle is the same manus that starts us to reckon. A storm is coming. And something greater still, even less discernible, totally metaphysical. No wonder we created gods.

We're witness to colossal waterfalls and massive trees that extend beyond our heads. I got this sense that this movie could be taking place long before humans came into being, or long after we're gone. It drives home the idea that whether we humans evolve to the point of leaving to other planets, or we all bomb each other and end the race, the…

reviews.text: Time has not been kind to Alfonso Cuarón's debut feature, a rather simple and ridiculous comedy. The fact that it is considered one of the best Mexican films of the 1990s is not necessarily a compliment if we take into account that, in the last two or three decades of the last century, Mexican cinema was going through a profound crisis. Sólo con tu pareja is a collection of clichés, not very funny implausible entanglements, an insufferable protagonist, and a sense of humor quite basic and now dated. In addition to this, there is the musical accompaniment with pieces by Mozart, some pseudo deep dialogues, and various epigraphs that endow this work with a certain youthful pretension. As it has…

reviews.author: Deckk
reviews.text: 100-word review: Cuarón's feature-length directorial debut is a dark romantic comedy that blends quirky humour with moments of existential introspection. The film's premise is undeniably bold, but its execution somewhat uneven. The tone oscillates awkwardly between farce and earnestness, making it difficult to fully connect; the idiosyncratic humour, especially prevalent through aggressive editing, vanguards — here Cuarón’s distinctive visual style shines. Themes of self-discovery and moral reckoning are compelling even while maybe lacking the nuance that Cuarón would master later in his career. Overall, while Sólo con tu pareja offers glimpses of brilliance, it struggles to balance its satirical edge with emotional depth.

reviews.text: As the film opens with startling precision (a theatre filled with children screaming to 'look behind you'), as an audience, we're automatically on edge. From here, Grandrieux just keeps pushing us into a further state of disarray with layered images and decontextualized narrative curves, hitting time after time with an experimental style and a straightforward narrative; there's a reason this is Grandrieux's most well known film (and it's slightly disappointing that it's his debut because of the fact) and it's because it's startlingly clear, and the only full-on knockout in Grandrieux's time as filmmaker.

Some of it is really funny, and some of it is really sweet. Some of the jokes really didn't land for me though, and the drama gets laid on so thick for so long that it started to lose me. The performances are largely good though, and the slasher moments we get are bloody fun. As a whole it just wasn't a consistent package for me, but I can see the appeal.

reviews.text: Potentially the greatest animated film ever made. A film that exists in a place outside of time, temporally expansive and reserved simultaneously, transportive to the point of destroying one's perception of moments as they move, from one to the next, weaving in and out of worlds, destroying & creating dimensions and falling deeper into the pull of novel galaxies; a film that makes you feel like a pingpong ball, only the pingpong machine is a swirl of dreamscapes and non-space and realities and outer space and dark matter, fused into a never-ending, reddening rainbow, an arch of colors formed of folklore in the spiraling sky.

reviews.author: Eli Hayes
reviews.text: Quite simply the quintessential hyper-psychedelic animated film, more of a trip than even Pink Floyd - The Wall. Marcell Jankovics transitions through a never-ending sensory overload of stunning images with perfect fluidity and attention to detail without ever abandoning his mythologically-based narrative for too long. The battle sequences, for lack of a better word, are amazing; watching this film is like playing the most surreal, abstract Atari 5200 game that you can imagine and crossing it with a healthy dose of ancient Scythian folklore. Get to it.

reviews.text: The first time I saw this poster (LOOK AT IT), I knew I had to see this movie. Finding out that the whole thing looked like this made it irresistible. Why I waited a few months first, I don't know. This is the brightest, most beautiful animation I have ever seen. It's expressive, unique, inventive, and bizarre. There are so many little moments that just blew my mind, like when the three brothers wake up together, and it just morphs through all three of their faces waking up. The way everything just flowed through from one image to the next was also mesmerizing. It reminded me of the best moments from Prince Achmed, but far more dazzling and psychedelic.

reviews.text: Taking place in a once prosperous Ohio mining town, 'Spring Night, Summer Night' is set within the type of small community where telling the future takes no magic: A young person can look across the room while dancing at the only bar in town and glimpse the particular worn down and tired archetype they will eventually replace in the years ahead. Some may escape for a brief stretch, by joining the Army or trying their luck in a big city, but something always seems to pull them back home.

reviews.text: "Spring Night, Summer Night" is a 1967 drama directed by Joseph L. Anderson. A small an earnest production, "Spring Night, Summer Night" is really Anderson's only full-length feature in his cannon. As such, it is an underseen gem that really holds quite a bit of viewing fruition because Nicolas Winding Refn cherry picked it from obscurity to be restored. In absolution I am glad that he did, as there really isn't many films that give a raw pictorial viewpoint of midwestern atmosphere such as this.

reviews.text: This nice, obscure, low-budget passion project, shot over the course of two years by an Ohio State University film professor, J.L. Anderson, offers a beautifully shot portrait of a small Ohio town in the mid-1960s. Rescued from obscurity by Nicholas Winding Refn (Drive), of all people , the film centers on a family that has fallen on hard times, just as the town of Canaan, Ohio has. Once a thriving mining town that peaked during wartime, the mines have closed. The family at the heart of the movie runs a small, seemingly unsuccessful farm. The core relationship of the movie is between Jessica (Larue Hall) and Carl (Ted Heimerdinger), especially because it is sexual, and they are most likely (step-)siblings.…

reviews.text: The working class patriarch is bedeviled by contradictions which—barring willful consciousness-raising or the luck to suddenly be living in a nation not beholden to class stratification, each gradation-echelon boasting its unique neurosis-inducing approach to Performing Nuclear Propriety—ultimately render him ineffective. Take Virgil Royer. Scrabbling and harried at his fall from Mine To Sub-sub-sub-sistence Farming, he plays the hectoring patriarch who can never be satisfied. His wife, his blended children, even peripheral ex-lovers from decades ago, they are all failing him in some way. Within Virgil's mind palace, there is a vaunted trophy case—presently empty, cobwebbed—with lonely placards reading MOST DUTIFUL DAUGHTER and MOST RESPECTFUL SON and WIFE WHO NEVER ASKS UNCOMFORTABLE QUESTIONS. Obviously, the point of these trophies is their…

reviews.text: Spring Night, Summer Night is an unsettling, but somewhat lyrical, story of small-town life. It is full of sin, family, incest and cruelty. It is equally amateurish and breath-taking. There shots from this film that are going to linger long in my mind. Long-shots of characters in deep shadow against sunset-light, lyrical shots of loneliness; shots capturing freedom and small-town claustrophobia.

The last one he released, Spring Night, Summer Night was the only one that I found interesting/thought I would like, and so I was looking forward to that. It was okay. I don’t have much to say about it, I just wanted to get the word out if anyone cares. The website is byNWR.com.

reviews.author: Andrew Rogers
reviews.text: Deserves mention alongside The Exiles and Killer of Sheep as part of a strain of American Neorealism in the 60s and 70s. The incestuous premise may scan as exploitative and thus divorced from that disposition, yet it's in keeping with the aim of crafting honest portrayals of unexamined corners of American life—in both a societal and geographical sense. Spring Night, Summer Night's dirt-caked rurality gives way to the ethereal as J.L. Anderson wrings ecstatic moments out of remote Ohioan life. The adult members of this family try to define themselves in this town already abandoned by industrial boom and left with little but a bar and some beat-up cars, and find it an insurmountable task as values change and boundaries…

I don't know if this series can be counted as a "kids show" after this, because death, depression, and gallows humor now take center stage as the more traditional children's media themes of friendship and morals are more implied than anything, and I'm definitely not complaining about that. Star vs the Forces of Evil proves how far animated shows intended for children have come after all these years, and Battle for Mewni only further cements this. You'd be doing yourself a disservice if you missed out on this amazing show and accompanying movie.

It's intimate, careful, sensitively approaching the victims of abuse, rape, and (domestic) violence. All those girls have suffered a lot and did a lot of stupid things, were forced to do them but it's finally here - what some might call a prison - that they have the chance to be human (aka. girls) again. But that's not all. Aside from the grave topical issue, the film is beautifully shot, has a great pace and finds a very good balance of sucking the viewer in and releasing him a little bit, giving a little space. A must see, this is.
