Starless Dreams is neither. It is frighteningly realistic, a document on people far too young to be this familiar with pain and suffering, and yet are because of circumstances far beyond their control. It paints an awful picture of how abusive families are solely responsible for the children's inability to cope with life, and how this turns them into cruel, emotionless criminals themselves.…

In short; I loved every minute of this, and simply can't recommend it highly enough.

There were elements of it which interested me, and it's very much a David Cronenberg film especially in its content, but its form (no dialogue, no diegetic sound, etc.) made it a little too difficult to have fun with.

reviews.author: Evan “Raymond Gun-Virus” Pincus
reviews.text: Cronenberg begins here, both thematically and visually. The beginning of his "overlapping nervous systems" trilogy, continued with Scanners and Dead Ringers. Always a joy to see Ronald Mlodzik on the screen, especially in his bonkers Victorian getup. Ambition can occasionally outpace the budget (especially when the visual part of the story feels more traditionally narrative focused than the auditory component), but all the ideas Cronenberg would explore throughout his career are here in concentrated form. Stereo, despite being far from the heights Cronenberg would reach, is a phenomenal debut which deserves far better than the DVD bonus feature and historical curio status it is so often granted.

reviews.author: DNA cinephile🏳️‍🌈
reviews.text: Stereo (Tile 3B of a CAEE Educational Mosaic). 1969. Directed by David Cronenberg.🏳️‍🌈 In David Cronenberg’s early silent films with voice over for narration he was obsessed with science fiction, experimentation, aphrodisiacs, telepathy evolution, biology, erotica, omnisexuality, and art. Stereo (1969) is written and directed by David Cronenberg and showed his talent for upcoming sci-fi horror masterpieces. The power of Stereo lies in the dialogue as the visual imagery was not as refined as later Cronenbergian works. Considering a great deal of this was shot in a university, the cinematography and editing by Cronenberg was complex and showed signs of his talent. This was Cronenberg’s first feature film and is now showing on Criterion.

reviews.author: shookone
reviews.text: Cronenberg's first two feature films are experimental cinema constructions that thematically outline the Canadian's path. Both STEREO and CRIMES OF THE FUTURE are vaguely reminiscent of Stanley Kubrick - notably his recent masterpiece 2001 - in their focus on architecture and coldness, the two defining characteristics of Cronenberg's two 60-minute films. In both films, a kind of science diary of a narrator is superimposed on images that stand on their own.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: A manifesto on how you and your friends (with the help of some instruments, a couple of lights, a few cameras and platforms, a cartoonishly oversized suit and a standard house lamp) can see the face of god. Opens with an anxious man alone in what looks like an abandoned factory hitting play on a tape and within the span of a few songs you are watching a transcendent celebration of pure music and art and collaboration where everyone and everything in its vicinity is possessed by the experimental punk and funk and art rock sounds for 80 minutes including the camera. Byrne's body movements and vocal performance, Demme's intense close-ups and stylized lighting, the raw, off-kilter sounds and organic moments between the band members. I can't believe this was captured on film, and that I hadn't seen it yet. I will be watching this a million more times.

reviews.author: G_MOVIES
reviews.text: Mandatory viewing for any true '90s hip-hop fan. NYC's DJ Stretch Armstrong and host Bobbito Garcia had one of the most important rap radio programs to ever hit the airwaves, broadcasting from a small college radio station (WKCR 89.9FM) at Columbia University on Thursday nights. The show was so good that dedicated fans stayed up until 5 AM so as not to miss a thing. Tapes of the show circulated everywhere. Rap fans loved not just the music (Stretch and Bob often played exclusive tracks and rare demos) but the humor (co-host Lord Sear added to the comic relief). But the biggest draw was probably the chance to hear hundreds of hungry hip-hop artists appear live, many of which went…

reviews.text: Super Fuzz a.k.a. "Super Snooper" in North America, is a high concept buddy cop slapstick action comedy and inflated superhero farce by spaghetti western trailblazer Sergio Corbucci starring Terrence Hill and Ernest Borgnine. The film is a lost artifact of 80s cheese. It doesn't make a whole lot of sense as a story, or a scene by scene plot, but I can attest to the peculiar charm that this film displays. A cop stares into the blast of a nuclear explosion and gains limitless superpowers just as long as he doesn't see the color red with his eyes. If he sees red, his powers go away and so situation comedy ensues.

reviews.author: Ira Brooker
reviews.text: I woke up freezing in my father-in-law's living room at 2:30am the day after Thanksgiving. Unable to sleep, I checked Twitter and found a message from my pal Laird that Massacre Video was streaming Tales from the Quadead Zone for one day only. I cued it up, made myself a Velveeta and mustard sandwich and spent an hour sitting at the kitchen table staring in bleary-eyed awe at the singular vision of Chester N. Turner. In 2014, that's about as close as you get to stumbling upon a legendary trash film in a dusty corner of your local video store, and about as perfect a viewing experience as you could ask for this film.

reviews.author: Joshua Dysart
reviews.text: Casio Keyboard SOV macabre. Slow to get going, the first story read from the book of the quadeaD zone, an obvious allegory for capitalism, is rough when it comes to its shot-to-shot construction, but the filmmaking (VHSmaking) kicks it up around the 35 min mark and there starts to be some legitimate 80s video artifact gold here. An undead clown attack, Bobby’s Mother stabbing her husband Daryl as he physically assaults her, Bobby’s Mother contemplating the razor blade in her hand while thinking back on fond memories of her own dead child, chroma-key ghosts (is that what that effect is?). All done with real hypnotic droning intensity.

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: "TALES FROM THE QUADEAD ZONE, a three-story anthology, is Chester N. Turner’s second and final dig into self-released, SOV sludge. Following up the exhausting-yet-hilarious filth of BLACK DEVIL DOLL FROM HELL (1984), Turner and friends are in a very distinctive place. They honed the skillz, cut the sex, and unwittingly churned out the greatest SOV trash film of all time. No exceptions. Logic, be it godly or mortal, has gone missing during QUADEAD’s 62 deranged minutes. Therefore, we must be prepared for anything. Don’t knock ‘em for the plastic Casiotone; take heed of the ceramic titty-mug. In the mind of Chester Turner, these things may be the substance of life."

reviews.text: Man, I'm conflicted. This is so much more competent when compared to Black Devil Doll, but I'm not sure if competency is what I'm looking for? This feels like a movie, not just some transmission from the darkest depths of a scarred mind. Now don't get me wrong, it's still a REAL weird watch, definitely not normal, but the insanity has been toned down a notch.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: This film is rarely mentioned on lists of best Spaghetti Westerns, and there's a good reason for that! Texas, Adios is a rather pedestrian western, with an unremarkable plot and lack of memorable moments. The story focuses on a sheriff who heads to Mexico with his brother, in search of the man who killed his father. Franco Nero takes the lead role and delivers his usual swagger but there isn't a whole to the character. The action is rather turgid but there's a peppering of shootouts which provide some entertainment. Much of the film takes place outside and director Ferdinando Baldi captures some nice desert scenary. I'm struggling to think of much more to say and really I would say that this one is for completists only! Everyone else needn't go out of their way to see it.

reviews.author: nick
reviews.text: That Obscure Object of Desire is simply sexy and entertaining. Depicting a cat-and-mouse romance between an older bourgeois man and a young lower class woman, it's a ride filled with lies, erotic frustrations, and abundant symbolism as you would expect from a Bunuel feature. It's an extremely captivating tale reflective on the truth of love and the fallibility of human nature, with occasional gags and heavy political undertone throughout. It's purely conventional narration until the very end, where Bunuel's trademark surreal elements finally creep in and give the story a whole new sinister twist. The acting deliveries are also top-notch, with Fernando Rey being the absolute standout, playing an older naive romantic with absolute conviction. Highly recommended.

reviews.text: I found it disappointing that the casting of two actresses for one role was done to get around a problem in filming and not as an intentional statement. reviews.author: Auteur
reviews.text: I was planning on watching all of Charles Band's Full Moon Productions by the end of next year, and I thought, while I'm at it why not start at the beginning with Empire Pictures. The Alchemist was the distributor's first feature, and Band's first time directing as alias James Amante, and it proves a pretty accurate precursor to the Full Moon blueprint. It's low budget, with cheesy acting and dialogue, but the special effects are good and at a certain point the film actually surrenders to its story of a centuries long battle between a magician and an alchemist over the latter's daughter, reincarnated as our modern day heroine. It doesn't make much sense but the film believes in itself enough to provide a satisfying finish. You can tell these films were true labors of love for Band and sometimes that passion bleeding through is all a film like this needs in order to be recommended.

reviews.text: Neat to see Morris dial down his muscular tendencies and extreme organization. I can't recall another time he's essentially handed off authorship to a subject like this. Sometimes this feels like this should be cut between two or three other subjects like Dorfman, but then it'll remind you that there is nobody quite like Dorfman which is pretty much an unbeatable defense for this being a stand-alone work. Spread pretty thin, even at eighty minutes, but it's intimate like most of Morris' works, fuzzy and warm like few of them, and melancholic in all the right spots, mourning how past modes of expression can be left frozen in time. Viewed this as warm-up for Wormwood and was pleasantly surprised by its comfy charms.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: Peter Greenaway's *The Baby of Macon* is a pretty polarizing and audacious piece of work, down to its shock value and presentation, but with most of his works, it offers a stark beauty and an uncompromising take with his views plastered all over. The film, set in the 17th century and staged within a theatrical performance, often challenges the viewer to decide what's real and what is actually being experienced. The story follows a miraculous birth by an old woman in the plague-ravaged city of Macon, and the baby is immediately hailed as a divine gift, but that doesn't stop people from taking advantage of the situation and highlights some of the worst of human greed.

reviews.text: High art achieved through disgusting and decadent cinematic artifice. Peter Greenaway’s The Baby of Mâcon is a damning, unflinching indictment of humanity. Made in the style of a stage play in mid-17th century France in the court of Cosimo Medici; the film tells the story of a baby born of an old, hideous and plague-ridden woman in the barren village of Mâcon. Thought to be a divine miracle due to the circumstances in which he was born, the child is thought of as a saint by the commoners and exploited by everyone except its birth mother, who has been locked away in exile. Church and state work together to profit and gain favor at the expense of the child, while the…

Peter Greenaway conjures a twisted theatrical spectacle, exposing the murky depths of religious hysteria and human depravity, and breathes into something alive, unbridled, boisterous, and chaotically magnificent.

reviews.author: Jim Beaver
reviews.text: On one hand, the battle sequences (95% of the film) are staggering in size and scope, a truly magnificent achievement. On the other hand, except for a few cameos (Yul Brynner, Orson Welles, Hardy Kruger, Curt Jürgens, etc.), most of the characters are hard to keep straight, and their relationships are extremely muddled, at least in the 144-minute version I saw, with occasionally sloppy subtitles. The long version (175 minutes) was nominated for the Oscar for Best Foreign Film, and perhaps it is a little more coherent. This is a visual and logistical masterpiece, but so much was either missing or confusing about the connections between characters that the film suffers immensely in that department. Of the celebrity roles, only Yul Brynner's and Sergey Bondarchuk's are of special interest, though Kruger does well as a slightly reluctant German officer. Well worth seeing for the spectacle, which is deeply impressive.

Leo’s willowy beauty, Boyle’s twitchy Y2K electronica style, the gorgeous reveal of the beach set to Moby’s “Porcelain.” It’s all etched into my memory, a teenage dream. There’s something valuable about a time capsule that accurately recreates a recognizable strain of experience—what it felt like to listen to people talk, the music you heard in commercials, the visual cues of a filmmaking generation. reviews.author: MushiMinion
reviews.text: The Black Castle sets itself up with everything a Gothic horror could possibly need to succeed: a gloomy hillside castle that belongs to a cruel and malevolent host with a crocodile pit. Sadly, it fumbles where it counts most. Our young leads are the very definition of "bland", including the foppish Count with an eye-patch and murderous intent. Oh sure, it says Boris Karloff and Lon Chaney Jr. are in the film, but Chaney is relegated to only a few scenes with no dialogue and Karloff doesn't fare much better. Where's Vincent Price and Roger Corman when you need them? The director, Nathan H. Juran, has some classic B-material listed on his résumé, but here - his first time in the director's seat - he failed to illicit much of interest out of a slipshod script and was lacking a cast who could elevate the material without him.

reviews.text: A storm is raging near the Canadian border which washes the bridges out. A rag tag group of characters take refuge in the closest hotel, the Black Raven. We have a couple eloping away from the woman's rich controlling father, a bank employee who just stole $50,000, and an escaped prisoner who has come to kill the hotel's proprietor (George Zucco) who he feels wronged him. Soon the angry father arrives and is quickly found dead. The police are summoned and everyone is trying to figure out what is going on and where that $50,000 the bank employee had has gone. At sixty one minutes this clips along and is super fun. Zucco is great as always and gets some amazing quips in along the way.

reviews.author: PapaMayhem
reviews.text: I loved the disappearing raincoat and hat in one scene. I guess there weren’t continuity people on films at this time? So this is a murder mystery with a decent atmosphere to it. I quite like the role George Zucco does in this one. The mild mannered inn keeper who is also “The Black Raven”, a former big time criminal who now quietly makes some side money by smuggling people across the Canadian border. It occurs to me that in the 1940s it wasn’t really a big deal to go across the Canadian-US border, but ok. It’s not an amazing mystery, but it’s a fun little film from this era of the industry.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: The Blancheville Monster opens with a typically Gothic pre-credits scene; introducing the central castle and grounds; everything overlaid with heavy rain and a thunderous score. Indeed, this is a film that goes all in with the atmosphere - checking off the various Gothic horror tropes as it goes. The plot takes obvious influence from Edgar Allen Poe (specifically House of Usher) and focuses on a young woman who returns to her ancestral home after some time, only to find that everything has changed and apparently her family is afflicted by some prophecy that threatens her life. The opening twenty minutes or so are really quite effective; culminating in a lovely twist that just begs to be explored.... just as the…

reviews.text: The Blancheville Monster also simply called “Horror” is an Italian Gothic Horror movie clearly inspired by Edgar Allen Poe’s House of Usher. It’s a slow paced movie but man oh man does it look beautiful. I am a sucker for this kind of b/w atmospheric spooky movies. And the Italians made some of the best ones. I don’t think this one quite reaches the heights of the best of them like Mario Bavas Gothic Horror movies or Roger Corman’s Poe adaptations but it stands as a pretty solid little example of the genre.

The last act is easily the most entertaining, which isn't at all unique, but it does reward a bit for sticking around through the first two acts. Yet honestly the few mild action sequences it has really didn't do it for me. The gothic sets and costumes and score were entertaining, but honestly those the best parts of the feature, which to me fell short in creating the suspense needed for a good horror flick.

reviews.text: THE BLANCHEVILLE MONSTER is an Italian Gothic horror movie from the early 1960’s that has elements from a number of films. The most prominent ones that I noted were James Whale’s THE OLD DARK HOUSE, 1960’s HOUSE OF USHER, THE PREMATURE BURIAL (just a year before this one) and a touch of Hitchcock’s REBECCA in the dark and ominous housekeeper, Miss Eleonore. Surprisingly, even though there is a fair amount of screaming, THE BLANCHEVILLE MONSTER felt more like the atmospheric JANE EYRE than it did a horror movie. The look sometimes the movie reminded me of Horror films from the silent era like The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari. Not a great movie, but an interesting and enjoyable one to watch.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Blood on Satan's Claw is folk horror done right! Set in 17th century England, Piers Haggard's film begins with the accidental unearthing of an ancient skull. This is followed by a series of strange events affecting the villagers - madness, possession, weird skin growth and more. The film was originally conceived as three separate stories before being merged into one narrative. The fractured plot actually works to the film's credit - as we see the effects of the unleashed evil spreading across the village population. It's all set off by a brilliantly realised surreal atmosphere; braced by an inventive and off kilter score by Marc Wilkinson. This lends the film a real imposing aura of suspense - it's never clear…

reviews.author: Rafael "Mister Movie" Jovine
reviews.text: A vampire film drenched in eroticism and, above all, atmosphere, this one leans heavily into mood over narrative. It often plays like a hazy giallo, unfolding with a dreamlike logic where everything feels slightly off-kilter. That tone is beautifully realized through Fernando Arribas’ glossy, almost hypnotic cinematography, which gives the film a surreal, otherworldly sheen. At its center is a predatory presence—a roaming vampire whose encounters blur desire and danger—set against a backdrop of strange occurrences and a long-buried act of violence slowly coming to light.

reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: The title seems to suggest that for the bride, there's something violent and bloody about marriage. Or it could suggest that the bride is insane. But this doesn't seem to be an exploitation film so I'd go for it being an allegory about a young woman entering into an institution that will make her the slave of her new husband, and then set it in a Gothic mansion where the bride discovers a mysterious woman who can rescue her from this bourgeois middle class patriarchal hell. Its subversive theme works well as a horror film once the two women become lesbian vampire Gore Gore girls with a bitchin dagger with a twisted blade and a handle that looks like carved ivory. However, to drive the point home, the established order gets its reckoning in this Spanish art horror beatdown.

reviews.text: Death by hamburger. And a friendly reminder: Non-conformity can lead to 'killin' for kicks.' The local beatnik hangout is ground zero, and strangely, Roffman can barely hide his disdain for this peculiar subculture. Of course, that's the best part and a font of unintentional hilarity. But he's also a visual stylist: choreographed moving pieces fill every corner of the frame, and it's fun watching these cartoony jazzniks in their natural habitat. In fact, Peter Falk's low-key villainy brings it down a notch, a classic bit of cinematic irony.

reviews.author: Michael Wilson
reviews.text: This fast-paced, well acted, low budget Canadian film has a similar premise as Alfred Hitchcock's ROPE, with two beatniks deciding to kill a young stranger at a party just for kicks. The youth's older brother, frustrated by the inability of the police to solve the crime, investigates the boy's death and finds himself pulled into the beatnik underground. One of the killers, Nico, is played by Peter Falk in one of his earliest film roles. The film makes good use of a jazz-oriented soundtrack and the typical cinematic version of a beatnik coffee house filled with women in leotards and spaced out characters spouting poetry and existential one liners. Great fun to watch. Featuring Jack Betts, Barbara Lord and Ron Hartman. Produced and directed by Julian Roffman.

reviews.author: Michael Wilson
reviews.text: Like most of the Mexican vampire films from the late 1950s and into the early 60s, this movie is full of dark atmosphere and some very striking sets and cinematography. It opens with a carriage being driven slowly across a barren landscape, accompanied by the sound of howling winds and bursts of blowing sand and fog. When the carriage reaches its destination, a mysterious castle, we learn that the driver is a moldy skeleton in a black hooded robe. This scene is reminiscent of the slow-motion carriage scene in Mario Bava's BLACK SUNDAY (1960). After this auspicious beginning, the film turns into a talk fest until the last fifteen minutes when actual vampire stuff starts happening, complete with fangs and flying rubber bats. My DVD is the K. Gordon Murray version that was dubbed into English and released to television by American-International Pictures in the 1960s. I'd love to see the original Spanish-language version, if it's available anywhere.

With telekinetic gore-slayings and surprisingly perverted twists, the movie plays out like AMITYVILLE HORROR meets HALLOWEEN as directed by Lucio Fulci’s third cousin who never graduated high school. Add the finest bedroom synthesizer soundtrack of all time and you’re guaranteed 80 minutes of gentle slasher angst. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: A horror pastiche, taking everything they could from popular horror films from the previous decade to create a solid and surreal slasher. The soundtrack immediately tells you in the opening that this film is going to be a rip-off, but then it surprises you by ripping off multiple films in order to get to its bizarre climax. If it were made 40 years later, it would be hailed for its classic horror references; being made a year after at least one of the films it's taking from, it's clearly an attempted cash-in. That said, I enjoyed it in part because its storytelling was decent for a lower budget horror flick and in part because of that sense of trend-exploitation. Thank you for being shameless, filmmakers.

reviews.text: There's something especially charming about 1973's THE BOY WHO CRIED WEREWOLF, which brought director Nathan H. Juran out of retirement from a favour to producer Aaron Rosenberg, as a horror adaptation of the classical The Boy Who Cried Werewolf from Aesop's Fables, and something especially weird about the the whole thing dealing with local hippie Jesus Freaks. On one hand, it's enduring for little Richie (Scott Sealey) who just wants his father Robert Bridgestone (Kerwin Mathews) to get back with his mother, after their divorce. This is the element of the film that really works, but the inclusion of the Jesus Freaks creates an uneasy counterpoint that just is at odds with everything.

reviews.text: I have some issues with this; the logic and unnecessary red herrings, some cheesy jumps and editing, but I still found it to be rather entertaining. Some interesting concepts and twists, a few good reveals and really intense sequences. I think that, even though it isn't terribly long, this has a solid short story sort of core, could've made for a tight 1 hour segment by cutting out the excess; something like a Masters of Horror entry. It came a while after that ship had sailed, but still very much resembled the aesthetic. So maybe I forgive the flaws a bit more, because I think it's working with something pretty cool.

reviews.author: CJ
reviews.text: There's a brilliant concept here but one that's tough to sell to an audience and it takes The Caller a loooong time before it becomes convincing. However, when it does, the weird mix of classic homicidal stalker movie and time-travel mind-bender is surprisingly clever and effective. The main arc of the plot is brilliant. It feels totally original and follows through to a strong climax. There are a few red herrings, some clunky dialogue and some confusion in the first half that feels like padding (ideally, this would've made a perfect 30 minute Twilight Zone episode) but when it pulls itself together, it's great.

reviews.author: Chico Fireman
reviews.text: Muito mais barato de ser realizado do que um filme de ficção, o documentário se tornou, mais do que um destino em si, um caminho para que os jovens diretores brasileiros pudessem começar suas carreiras. O cinema documental cresceu em quantidade e qualidade e possibilitou uma série de experiências que promoveu encontros das mais variadas formas com os filmes de ficção. Colocar pessoas "reais" para interpretar a si mesmas ou até viver outros personagens se tornou um modelo bastante comum no recente cinema brasileiro, com resultados impressionantes, como em "Girimunho", "O Céu Sobre os Ombros", "Histórias que Só Existem Quando Lembradas".

But in Max Kalmanowicz's film, these gases leaked and the radiation levels sparked these little buggers of the title to become walking, hugging nuclear weapons that microwave anyone on touch. Shot and scored by the same duo who did Friday the 13th this is a FUCK THEM KIDS classic that's mostly a sleepy, all-night hangout movie with the local sheriff & a couple of the townsfolk as they slowly realize it's the creepy little kids that are brutally picking them off one by…

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: THE CHILDREN might be aging out due to its stoned pace and anemic energy, but I'll always love it. After exposure to toxic waste, killer kids with black fingernails wipe out a small rural town named Ravensback. And they do it with hugs—radioactive, skin-melting hugs. Simple, uncluttered, and careless in all the right places, THE CHILDREN is the type of modest trash-horror that is often idealized, but rarely actualized. No effort is made to convey relatable emotions or experiences, and there’s no heaviness to sort through. This is where high camp meets taboo violence and we all win. Also: don’t miss the ending, which involves a samurai sword. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

I appreciate the mean spirited nature too as there's no shortage of zombie children massacres and even an innocent melting of a regular ol kid! That's some dark stuff! A film that hits just right this time of year.

reviews.author: shookone
reviews.text: Cannes golden palm 2008 Entre les murs paints a realistic picture of the social microcosm of a suburban Parisian high school. Its lively fragmentary nature predominates, with a multitude of characters whose position in the narrative sometimes only becomes clear halfway through the film. The actors are amateurs and were actually "cast" from the same school. While the interesting concept works surprisingly well as an authentic insight, the gentle handling of the characters leaves much of it shallow. The film doesn't reveal any real potential for conflict, and thus the tour through the milieu is a watered-down, almost somewhat sugarcoated look at a popularly discussed problem area. A film whose subject matter apparently played the key role in winning the top prize at Cannes.

reviews.author: Daniel88
reviews.text: Admittedly, Cecil B. DeMille’s style probably suit his Roman and Biblical epics better, but even so, The Crusades works as a fun proto-companion to Kingdom of Heaven – chronologically, it even is a direct ‘sequel’. And while the portrayals of Richard the Lionheart and Saladin are rather comical and acted as if this was still a silent film, I love that DeMille – even in this Medieval setting – just goes all in on the spectacle. Particularly the battle scenes are genuinely well directed and the practical effects hold up surprisingly well. At moments, you can’t help but wonder if these scenes somehow influenced Eisenstein’s Alexander Nevsky a couple of years later.

reviews.author: Dale Nauertz
reviews.text: Cecil B. DeMille had already established his brand quite well by 1935, having directed "Sign of the Cross" and "Cleopatra". He's still famous, 90 years later, for his lavish historical sagas teeming with casts of thousands and bursting with spectacle. His ability to stage spectacular sights involving huge sets, thousands of extras, incredibly choreographed battles, and melodrama big enough to match it all remains impressive nearly a century later...probably because modern blockbuster spectacle is rarely as awe-inspiring.

reviews.author: Michael Shawn
reviews.text: A largely historically-inaccurate account of Richard the Lionheart's Holy Crusade against Islam to take back Jerusalem, Cecil B. deMille's epic is still spectacularly staged and narratively compelling. Of course, though it may seem silly to make such a statement against a film about the Crusades, it's also oppressively religious and propagandistic in parts. It seems it was primed to appease the newly-instated Hays Code authorities. But the grandeur of it impresses and the cast are all well-suited to their roles. None moreso than Loretta Young, who shines whenever she's on the screen. DeMille does have a tendency to oversell everything, so the pomp and circumstance may irk some viewers. And the subject matter isn't the most interesting of the many films he made. But it's a minor triumph, taking the caveats into account.

reviews.text: In cinema, the difference of making something visually excellent to something that isn't, hinges on one true trait. Filmmakers who understand the material use the camera as a tool with energy and weight, that carries energy and weight to its subject. It sounds simple but it becomes an exercise on knowing how to employ that technique as well as the volume in which it is employed. Horizontal and vertical movement are basic signifiers of plot progression or time, and sometimes, when the camera moves it showcases specific items or places to render its subject important. In Damiano Damiani's The Day of the Owl, the camera showcases plot progression, time, character entrances and departures, and themes via roads. Roads are symbolic…

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Early crime drama from Damiano DamianI. The tone is far more serious than the bulk of the films that Eurocrime would come to be known for. There's not a lot of action and the film is rather talky - but the story is involving and the overarching plot which focuses on a police captain trying in vain to bring a suspected mob boss to justice, is well done. The film features a trio of standout performances; a young Franco Nero in the lead, and great support from Lee J Cobb and Claudia Cardinale. The film is set in a small town in Scicily and the director makes the best of this as everything is very claustrophobic, building to something of a pressure cooker at the end. The ending itself is satisfying, if not exactly conclusive!

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: It’s a slow and fairly realistic police procedural movie. But director Damiano Damiani knows how to keep things interesting and engaging. The three stars, Franco Nero, Claudia Cardinale and Lee J. Cobb also give excellent performances and provide the film with some potent star power. The Day of the Owl isn’t the most flashy Italian crime thriller ever made. In fact, it works much more as a character focused drama with a strong social component. So don’t expects much action, sex and thrills. But it is a well-made, written and acted film absolutely worth your time of you like the Italian crime genre.

reviews.text: Perhaps the most likable horror protagonist I can think of is young Charles, the horror-enthusiast who is a stand-in for every horror fan ever looked at funny for their enthusiasm. He's smart. He's calm. He's resourceful. And he isn't pompous or disingenuous. He's just a normal kid with an active imagination, as his aunt says, who shows remarkable poise in the face of gruesome horror. It makes it clear that the people making this film love horror just as much as the people watching, that we are among friends here. They do not condescend to the audience, and that is worth quite a bit.

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: GAKIDAMA, aka DEMON WITHIN, is a delightfully stunning exercise in body-horror that proves, once again, that you don’t need billion-dollar CGI to execute something horrifying and affecting. There are simple camera and lighting tricks, stop-motion animation, puppetry, a respectable amount of goop, light aerobics, a candlelit dinner, and a dead parakeet that probably had it coming. The creature is an absolute rip-off of one of the GHOULIES, but because it’s Japanese, there’s better craft, execution, attention to detail, and, of course, it goes a step further. This is absolutely a dig at America. GAKIDAMA delivers on pretty much every level—gore, exploitation, cannibalism, even runtime. It’s a lean, mean 50 minutes where we get to witness a larva transform into a beautiful butterfly. A dazzling, exquisite butterfly that totally destroys a kitchen.

It's not his best film, but it still feels like his magnum opus, the single project that includes all of the things he was most uniquely interested in and most uniquely able to execute: it's an unclassifiable mixture of the purest possible limited animation (the "characters" are unyielding geometric shapes) with exceptionally smooth movement at a high frame rate, so that every beat is gracefully and precisely executed. He was always the mathematician at Termite Terrace, so making a short about the inherent beauty in fractal forms and linear visualizations of numerical…

reviews.author: TajLV
reviews.text: Animated Short - I was in high school by the time this came out, and I don't recall ever having seen it before, but it's just the type of short film math teachers love to show to elementary level students to get them interested in geometry. It's about a straight blue line that falls in love with a lively red female dot. But she's infatuated with a free-spirited squiggle that causes her to laugh and play. We watch with wonder as the line discovers how to transform himself into shapes and intricate patterns to woo her. The narration by Robert Morley is a delight, even for writer Norton Juster couldn't resist dropping in the occasion bad pun or two. Directed by Chuck Jones & Maurice Noble, this 10-minute animation won the Oscar for Best Short Subject, Cartoons, while earning a nomination for the Palme d'Or - Best Short Film at Cannes. Worth a look, for sure.

reviews.text: Greenaway's Thanatos and Eros are always entwined, the eroticism as muted as the threats of violence until both explode. As usual, he crafts each image with his own painter's eye, everything perfectly placed and angled and lit, lending baroque beauty to an amusing travesty of sexual games between the idle rich. Fundamentally, this boils down to a film noir set in the imperial era, one where courtly intrigues and the inherent power of sex for producing heirs makes femmes fatales out of seemingly listless and easily controlled women.

reviews.text: War movies, whether narrative or nonfiction, are necessarily limited by the perspective of those who make them. The Emperor’s Naked Army Marches On is what happens when this fundamentally selfish framing is pushed by sheer force of will to such an extreme that it actually becomes a true reckoning with the forces of one’s own homeland because one man’s grief is so profound it escapes the limits of his body and soul. Okuzaki Kenzo is just about the least likable protagonist in the history of cinema; from the moment we meet him derailing a wedding to soapbox about Emperor Hirohito’s crimes (and, wildly, his own), the WWII veteran is obviously still trapped in that war in some catastrophic way. reviews.author: Halcyon
reviews.text: The Fake is an unremitting anti-religion statement. Religion itself thrives upon transcendental beliefs and optimistic human nature. Extorting money from devoted believers is all too common, especially from people who see faith as their last source of hope. The film gradually develops into an intricate thriller where egos collide. One man is outcasted by society but he perseveres in his own way, in order to divulge the truth behind the church in his village. Conmen have strategically manipulated the villagers which include his family. The inept handling of this scheme by the authorities only encourages both sides to take matters into their own hands. The Fake delicately weaves a narrative that reflects the harsh reality of human credulousness. The thrilling film forces us to question the purpose of religion and differentiate fabrications from the truth. Yeon Sang-ho's second feature film is brutal, the anxiety is palpable and it's nothing short of brilliant.

Taking a formalist approach to absurdism, this 3-hour mammouth chronicles 92 subjects who have been affected by a fictitious phenomenon known as the VUE (or the Violent Unknown Event) in painstaking detail. Equal parts dry mirth as it is stupefying morbidity, The Falls challenges its audience by flooding them with information, daring you to keep up. But this is by meticulous design and upon seeing the film a second time, I realized how much you will soak in with every viewing. reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Aside from featuring the most spiral staircases in any film ever, this is surely one of the most underrated films of the Giallo genre! Luigi Bazzoni's The Fifth Cord begins with a creepy monologue from a killer promising to kill five people. We then move into a tightly constructed but labyrinthine plot that focuses on a journalist who begins to investigate the murders and finds himself chief suspect as they are all people he knows! The film features a standout performance from the great Franco Nero, whose alcoholic journalist makes for an interesting and complex lead character. It's not the bloodiest Giallo but there's a few murders and the killers pov shots give it a real voyeuristic feel. It's stylishly shot throughout and the plot moves quickly, which helps to ensure that the film is always interesting. There's all the red herrings you would expect and the mystery boils down to a satisfying conclusion.

reviews.text: What gravitated me towards this film was seeing the incredible mix of cast it has, and honestly, all are absolutely thrilling in this slow-burn drama, which uses minimal action but through dramatic tension makes it a very compelling watch. There's basically no action here, but it didn't need it since the psychological tension between the cast is immense. Stewart, Attenborough, and Kruger all bring different elements to their characters, which do clash at parts, but this clashing for the sake of saving their lives becomes the emotional power of the film. The desert setting is much a character itself since it feels harsh and claustrophobic, and even if I'm pretty sure it was a set, it just never feels fake…

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: Robert Aldrich's Flight of the Phoenix has one really heavyweight cast to call upon. James Stewart, Richard Attenborough, Peter Finch, Ernest Borgnine, Hardy Kruger, George Kennedy, Christian Marquand, Ronald Fraser, and one of my Western favourites, Dan Duryea, all fight for survival in the Sahara Desert when their plane is forced down during a sandstorm. Heading for Benghazi, the plane is carrying oil workers, a French doctor, a British Army officer and his sergeant, a company accountant, and a German Aeronautical Engineer. The crash sees two dead, and one seriously injured, and with the plane badly damaged in the crash-landing, they are soon in a perilous position in an environment where the heat and a lack of water will soon…

reviews.text: Welcome to The Forbidden Room, an exhilarating slipstream of two-strip technicolor havoc that feels like an exquisite corpse assembled from every leftover idea that filmmaker Guy Maddin has ever had. A dense quilt of nested scenes that were allegedly pulled from the cinema’s great abandoned films, The Forbidden Room never proves that Maddin is reanimating “real” lost projects, but how real can a film be if it was never shot?

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: Wormholes of absurdism. Layers upon layers of abstraction. The Forbidden Room was my first journey into the zonked out, chimerical mind of Guy Maddin—a supreme exhibition in color and design, hypogenic visuals, risible (whether intentional or not) dialogue and nesting doll narrative style—the film combines avant-garde surrealism with silent film techniques and experimental montage, lighting and editing styles to form a nearly-incomprehensible, yet imposingly bizarre piece of fantastical cinema that defies traditional definition or dissection. There were moments that I really enjoyed like the bookending (and occasionally recurring) ‘bathtub man’ bits, the Udo Kier derrière song and dance number and a few other random instances of comedic or oddly dramatic mania. Unfortunately, as a whole, I couldn’t really get into this…

reviews.text: Peter Jackson's "The Frighteners" is full of so much over-the-top, wam-bam energy that it is hard to be able to latch on to anything with meaning or value. Not that the film is made to be deep or meaningful. It is the kind of full-speed horror-comedy-adventure where everything is played at high volumes for maximum enjoyment. Still, it is nice when a film slows down and lets its audience connect with something. This eventually happens in "The Frighteners," turning it from ghost adventure bore to engaging thrill ride; but it is almost too late to make the experience anything beyond fleeting fun.

Like Weiner and Clinton (but more charismatic than both of them combined), Hart was a passionate statesman motivated by a genuine desire to better the lives of his constituents. And, like Weiner and Clinton, none of that seemed to matter from the moment Hart was caught with his pants around his ankles.

reviews.text: Since it's technically six days older than The Red Turtle (both premiered at the 2016 Cannes Film Festival), I can't in good faith call it "the most X film since" anything. That being said, the mixture of unapologetic fairy tale narrative rhythms with artwork that's both quintessentially digital and mired in traditional forms (Chinese ink wash painting, in this case) scratches nearly the same itch that film scratched. It's too emotionally remote for that last half-star, but it's easily the most exciting animated film of the year, and I look forward to yammering on about it until I've alienated all my friends and loved ones. Incredibly beautiful minimalism in the imagery, the characterisations, the score, the overall weight.

Anna May Wong, one of Hollywood’s first big Asian actresses, desperately wanted to play O-Lan in the movie. She got the chance to even test for the part but ultimately produced went in a different direction and cast Caucasian actress Luise Rainer in the role instead. Rainer would later go on to win an Oscar for this role. Whitewashing was pretty common back in those days. There was also apparently a written law back then that prevented two different races to play a married couple. Paul Muni played O-Lan’s love interest so that also laid some influence in Wong not getting the part. …

reviews.text: The Good, the Bad, the Weird is one of the best westerns ever made. What a stylish, badass and splendidly entertaining - riff on Sergio Leone's The Good, the Bad & the Ugly. Song Kang Ho, Lee Byung Heon and Jung Woo Seong brought their A game here!It's hard to do justice in words to it's wall-to-wall visceral action, insane practical stunts and brilliantly composed sequences. The camera movement and shot compositions are amazing, Kim Jee-won puts most Hollywood filmmakers working on much bigger scale to shame.

His out-of-place clownish behavior serves as the movie's main source of comedic energy, almost effortlessly propelling the story forward ever since his first appearance during a crazy train heist. The director Kim Jee Woon made it obvious that the ultimate goal of the film is to be as silly as possible, and he had achieved it with Song alone, who, surprisingly now that I've checked, has only a handful of comedic roles in his career so far.

reviews.text: Guilt Trip is entertaining enough to keep you interested, but not engaging enough to keep your attention from wandering. It is a ferociously funny comedy that takes a lot of risks and connects just enough, and it's a step above the normal comedies thanks to its innovative idea and quartet of charming comedic star turns. The entire ensemble does an outstanding job with their roles, and they all carry the film with such a strong feeling of charisma and flattery. While the plot may be a little too conventional and the story may not be particularly memorable, it is nonetheless a family-friendly comedy with some belly laughs and a loving message that takes unexpected turns. In many ways, it exceeded my expectations, and I must say, I enjoyed it!

reviews.author: Blake VP
reviews.text: A small, simple film shows us the pride behind the Globetrotters and the importance of winning for the community that takes away hope from watching them play. It's thematically present too, emphasizing the idea of forgoing schooling to play a professional sport and the benefits of earning game checks. On the surface, it's a breezy human story about the fun-loving Trotters, but at its core, there's a familiar story about following our passions and doing the sensible thing for our lives.

reviews.author: ChrisInJax
reviews.text: If this story had been fiction, it would have been deemed over-the-top. But this story, which spans five seasons of a Washington state high school girls' basketball team, not only is true, but the filmmakers were extremely fortunate enough to have cameras film the team's highs and lows over those years. As is the case with this kind of doc, the filmmakers clearly started filming with one thing in mind (an off-the-wall coach who makes the team competitive) and being able to make a very powerful teenage drama about civil rights, teenage insecurities, and of course, deeply passionate sports competition.

reviews.text: I used to live on Smith Street, two blocks from Carroll Street in the Carroll Gardens neighborhood of Brooklyn. Despite having an Irish surname, in recent times it’s become an Italian American neighborhood. But in the last ten years, it’s barely been Italian American, completely gentrified by the likes of Starbucks and Park Natural Foods. All the remaining traces of the Italian American community I saw when I moved in were all but gone when I moved out four years later.

reviews.text: This mystery set in 1950’s Red Scare era is pretty average fare from director Peter Yates, with the stakes never feeling all that high, except towards the end when the Hitchcock homage becomes pretty overt albeit effective. Kelly McGillis is fired for not naming names and becomes caught up in uncovering a conspiracy to smuggle in Nazi doctors to America led by a sneaky, snarky politician (Mandy Patinkin). She is aided in her efforts by a country bumpkin do-gooder Fed (Jeff Daniels), who wants to see justice done but who would also love to ride off into the sunset with McGillis. The main issue is the screenplay and the film’s pacing/lack of urgency and suspense. There’s so much talent involved…

reviews.text: Peter Yates proves he can direct a foot chase as well as he did car chases in Bullitt and Robbery, with two excellent examples in this stylish McCarthy-era drama written by one of the guys who were blacklisted alongside the more famous Trumbo. Kelly McGillis is a strong lead as the journalist fired for refusing to name names, and together with an excellent Jeff Daniels they "uncover" the two-faced nature of the committee who are helping to hide Nazi war criminals. And really Daniels is worth watching for his reaction shots alone, he really sells his character, especially with the most realistic representation of what happens to a man when he is kicked in the balls that you will see in cinema. There's some really good stuff shot on location at Grand Central station too.

reviews.author: Optical Noise
reviews.text: In her recognisable style of which I've become a big fan, Deborah Stratman composes an eleven segment compilation of history in Illinois, using voice accounts, archival footage, and official writings to witness white supremacy's suspicions toward and eviction of Native Americans, Mormons, Black Panthers, or really, anyone not enough like them. Like in O'er the Land, thoughtfully edited visuals create so much of the effect, without needing commentary at all. The use of geography and location is great, with mounds bridging time and place of burial from different perspectives. Frigid cold of icy lands symbolize dualities then and now. The sound is wonderfully arresting too.

reviews.text: Começa a projeção. Imagens em tela enquanto se desenrola o voiceover suave de Antônio Fagundes. Após alguns minutos de ação, a revelação: na tela, o filme dentro do filme, que Fagundes assiste em um dia de calor. O filme dentro do filme é um noir, amparado nos signos visuais mais reconhecíveis do gênero. Ao sair do cinema, Fagundes entra em seu próprio noir (e como regra obrigatória do gênero, começa a fumar, tornando-se rapidamente um assíduo). Guilherme de Almeida Prado é fascinado pelos signos das imagens.

reviews.author: caio
reviews.text: Um imaginário popular tomado por filmes estrangeiros que nos fazem reproduzir e idealizar os seus códigos. Obcecado por cinema noir, Guilherme de Almeida Prado mistura o real com o imaginário em um suspense bastante autoconsciente. Cheio de neon, jazz e fumaça de cigarro. O filme replica todo tipo de tropo que se espera de um noir e comenta, principalmente por meio da figura idealizada da femme fatale, a relação fantasiosa que temos não só com o cinema de Hollywood mas também com o cinema em geral.

reviews.text: As far as San Francisco 1973 time capsules go, The Laughing Policeman is a good 'un. It’s no lost classic, but it has some charm. The title sucks. The moody banality of the Scandi-noir source doesn’t really translate. It's slow, meandering, and I'm still unsold on Matthau as a dramatic lead (It’s like a cartoon basset hound playing a grizzled cop) But it's full of great details and great scenes. A step-by-sometimes-plodding-step procedural cross section of the city, cross-hatched with that inimitable 70s texture. Lou Gosset has some sweet sunnies and Bruce Dern is great as a twitchy racist creep who gets all the best lines and rocks an all-timer mustache.

reviews.text: Teenage Nathan Schiff created a more complex piece of trash horror here than most sludge slingers twice his age. The Long Island Cannibal Massacre is not just a stalk-and-slasher with a bag-headed killer and cannibalism. Those elements are here, but that doesn’t begin to touch what TLICM is in its entirety. No, this is a sprawling, super8, no-fi epic. With black-market human flesh trafficking, a tribe of leprous, forest-dwelling cannibals, an ex-cop waxing poetic about the human condition, intentional, psychological plot-twists, a chainsaw fight and one of the strangest father/son relationships ever vomited onto film.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: An incoherent nightmare that propels through flashes of narrative but obeys few of its basic laws, instead simply escalating by quasi-non sequiturs and lateral leaps, adding new layers that simultaneously defy your ability to comprehend the scale of what is going on and expand the strangeness of the setting. This is a film caked in the grime of 1980, the remnants of hippie chic dying in the mustaches and ugly vans of 1970s malaise and the genesis of yuppie cocaine decadence budding in every sleazy cop cliche. This is a film that owes everything to the grindhouse, video nasty, exploitation ouevre, from Texas Chain Saw to The Town That Dreaded Sundown to the Manson family. A vague (and racist) origin story hints at some flavoring from the cannibal boom as well. This is someone's passion.

reviews.text: One of my generally unspoken (til now!) fears is that I'll never see the world. I don't make a lot of money, and I'm not particularly adventurous when it comes down to it. But I have a short list of places and things I want to see one day (the Grand Canyon, the Redwoods, the cherry blossoms in Japan, Carnival in Trinidad, Ireland, the Serengeti, those lightning storms in Venezuela), even if I don't really make an effort to realize those idle dreams. I sometimes think a lot of people are probably like me, in that they have dreams of seeing far away places they'll never get to.

reviews.text: To say Anthony Mann and James Stewart end their run of Western films on a high note might be an understatement: "The Man from Laramie" is likely one of the finest Westerns ever made. Mann takes to the CinemaScope format with zeal—the visual canvas here is impossibly wide, looking ahead to the Sergio Leone epics, and the shots of Jimmy Stewart's silhouette set against the New Mexico sky are as dream-like and iconic as movies get.

reviews.text: "Nail Gun Massacre" is a 1985 slasher directed by Bill Leslie and Terry Lofton. Very much a low budget project with a can-do attitude, Leslie and Lofton took on much of the other traditional crew roles for the film. With that being said, it should be very apparent that is has every bit the feel of a regional horror display, something than could turn out be of a good result or a bad. "Nail Gun Massacre" is easily in the good if not great category of things, a gem of not only traditional horror elements but also cheesy small-town charm on display as well.

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: If all you have is a nail gun, a motorcycle helmet, a bottle of fake blood, and people willing to take off their clothes, then I guarantee that you will have yourself a good time and a great horror movie. NAIL GUN MASSACRE gets a ton of mileage out of its titular weapon and every kill is a triumph in low-budget filmmaking. Heads, hands, chests, and eyes get nailed. Even a woman’s boob gets nailed. As does a man’s crotch. No body part is safe here. NAIL GUN MASSACRE is sleazy and violent, and it’s a document of the 1980s when sordid exploitation ran freely along with the fake blood. While it may not be the goriest film ever shot in Texas, it is the best one that features an actual gun that shoots actual nails. And for one hot second, it’ll make you consider taking up carpentry. (Annie Choi)

reviews.text: John Saxon out of his depth among some of Britain's most reliable character-actors (especially Alfred Burke, one of TV's great private eyes). The type of actors who looked 50 their entire life so were never out of work. It's not great but surprisingly mature and well-made given the material. Director John Gilling was as reliable as his cast was for granting B-movies more class than usual. With more focus on grumpy police procedural than sci-fi sensationalism, his approach brings a realistic, tragic eeriness to it. Like an unsolved cold-case you'd read about in a newspaper supplement. I see a lot of comparisons with Quatermass here, but if anything it's a direct progenitor of Under the Skin, which was really a sombre remake of Lifeforce, which itself was a sensationalist remake of... oh never mind...

reviews.text: at many points, The Old Man and the Gun seems more like a love letter than a film. it’s a love letter dedicated, of course, to Robert Redford, and this is most apparent in a warm montage that is both about Forrest Tucker and Redford. it is charming in the way it both marvels and mourns the passing of time. there’s no obvious sadness, but surely there’s a quiet resistance, opposing the inevitable valiantly yet futilely.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: The most impressive feat Lowery manages with Old Man is just how little of it feels like embarrassingly overt pastiche. It’s all there, of course; the Butch Cassidy font, the 70s pans/zooms, and the lush 16mm film. Yet the writing is delightfully laid-back and beyond a few saccharine miscalculations (a wistful Spacek looking over her farm at sunset and saying “keep on keeping on” comes to mind) is free from the kind of winking that would sink a worse version of this. Instead we’re treated to a series of breezy heist/cat-and-mouse montages and a lowkey, conversational charm that are combined to hammer home the idea of how great a feeling it is to love what you do.

reviews.text: I don't like it when characters in a movie are so stupid and don't check any signs of danger, even though you as a viewer know the resolution long ago. So The Ones Below is actually my nightmare. However, this psychological thriller manages to deliver a crisp movie night with clean staging, okay suspense and good casting, which definitely has its moments again and again and keeps you interested. Especially the imagery and some nice details are convincing, while other levels are completely dropped at some point. You can't continue thinking about the film after the credits, because then it doesn't make sense after only 5 minutes.

This is mostly due to Jennifer’s character arc, some gloopy practical effects, and dream sequences that are bathed in green and pink lights. Like the character of Cathy in Findlay’s LURKERS, Jennifer spends the film battling demons of all kinds. Her husband is dismissive and demeaning (“Boy, you look terrible. reviews.author: Stephen Furda
reviews.text: A well-made documentary about Lithuanian basketball culture and their 1992 Olympics team, whose participation in the Olympics was famously funded by The Grateful Dead. Like many documentaries of its type, your level of interest in the subject will help dictate how much you get out of it. Basketball and the Dead are two of my favorite things and this is an inspiring story, so it was easy for me to enjoy. I was hoping for a bit more Grateful Dead talk, but it was funny to hear Bob Weir tell Sarunas Marciulionis that he can’t shoot but he can rebound. Best moment of archival footage: Portland citizens being outraged when the Trail Blazers drafted the “Soviet” Arvydas Sabonis in 1984.

reviews.author: Jacob Juenger
reviews.text: Hindsight can be a crazy thing sometimes. Just look at what 20th Century Fox was trying to pull in 1977. It's a tale of two movies, one an adaptation of a runaway bestseller that was expected to be as successful as the book. The other was a piece of science fiction that everyone had already written off as a flop. Fox was desperate to get what they could out of the sci-fi movie, so they used the literary adaptation, which was highly anticipated, as leverage to force theaters into booking the other movie.

reviews.text: In its own bizarre way “The Other Side Of Midnight” marked the beginning and the end of an era. Released in 1977 when 20th Century Fox had little faith in another film on the roster, there were at that time considerable hopes placed on this 165 minute soaper. Based on the book by Sidney Sheldon, a sprawling “woman’s picture ” equivalent to an extended “Dallas” episode albeit with an international flavor. The rags to riches to rags story of Noelle Page (Marie-France Pisier) in a give it all you got performance that is hypnotically interesting. Sold essentially by her father into the fashion industry and taken advantage of by her employer she meets by accident Larry Douglas (John Beck), the…

reviews.text: Dreams that make you feel alive. The Passionate Friends is a story of love across years, always struggling, and told with a fragmented narrative. This is cinema made with emotion and edited in a dreamlike manner. David Lean tackles similar topics to Brief Encounter - a married woman loves another man - but goes further and uses less subtlety in The Passionate Friends. It is a film of indecision, of romance vs pragmatism, disguised as a loving friend and a cold husband. She wants love and security, even if she can't have both. She wants to live her own life, independent of anyone else, but also wants to love and share that with someone. The three respectable leads are all…

reviews.text: What sort of film starts off by informing you that an invasive chemical compound from space has now absorbed the overwhelming majority of our planet? The most paranoid post-apocalyptic sci-fi B-movie imaginable, I'd have said, before I saw Patricio Guzmán's mind-altering new documentary. Guzmán believes the chemical has already taken Earth, and it will only claim more of our land in the future. It's water, which he suggests may have reached Earth by comet. This is an incredible enough idea, but it's just the beginning of an extraordinary transportation of the audience through space, time, matter, memory, humanity, history and art - all in 82 minutes.

Powerful forces spawning fear within the masses that creates the acceptance of a backsliding away from democratic norms and principals. Weaving back and forth between anti-globalism ideas but talking about problems that seem to only have global solutions. Or do they have global solutions at all?

reviews.text: The theatrical shorts/featurettes that Disney produced during their '90s Renaissance for whatever reason never get discussed as PART of said Renaissance. This is baffling to me, as many of those shorts are actually better than some of the features. This one is no exception, as it has everything you could want out of a 2D Pauper adaptation. Somehow manages to condense the story into only 22 minutes while still recapturing what makes it such a timeless tale. Sweeping backgrounds and music truly add to the sense that this featurette was as ambitious as any of the traditional Disney films. Throw one of the best climaxes in the studio's history on top, and you've got a truly great Mickey Mouse cartoon.

reviews.text: I'm a sucker for Chaplin/Pickford style comedies and here Marion Davies stars in a excellent comedy of that mold. She's like a second generation Pickford with exceptional comic timing. Sometimes a little light, but I thoroughly enjoyed this and it's cool seeing 'Fatty' Arbuckle direct such a detailed feature film! So many characters, mostly fat, and who better to capture how awesome fat people are then Fatty himself! In another Pickford link. Her romantic lead was Mary's ex-husband Owen Moore. He was a little bland, but he always had Snitz Edwards by his side to give some color to his scenes. And the other romance was also sweet as Karl Dane found his dream girl - Louise Fazenda! On the other side. The bad side. George Siegmann was a great baddie! Mean and vicious! And combine it all with a frosty smile, I'm super happy with this Marion Davis film!

reviews.author: Scott Kelly
reviews.text: If you scroll down the Wikipedia page for Marion Davies there is eventually a “Critical Reassessment” section, but the bottom line is the lead is still focused on her status as William Randolph Hearst’s mistress and inspiration for the talent-challenged Susan Alexander in Citizen Kane (notwithstanding Welles own efforts to set the record straight). The more Davies I see, specifically the comedies (see The Patsy and Show People), the more impressed I am and more skeptical I become of relying on easily digested shorthand “best remembered for” assessments. Of course, the director of this film, Roscoe “Fatty” Arbuckle, has his own “best remembered for” problems.

reviews.text: I've always loved this Giallo and easily consider it to be one of the best of the genre; but for some reason it always seems to be absent in discussions about the best Giallo. The plot is a mix of murder mystery and gothic fairytale and focuses on the Wildebrook household and in particular two sisters plagued by an ancient legend concerning a murderous "red queen". This one really has it all - gory murders, beautiful women, atmospheric locations and an intriguing mystery plot. The 100 minute runtime is very well used, the story moves along briskly and there's always another blood splattered murder scene just around the corner. The plot itself is well worked and while the identity of the main villain is not too difficult to guess, the film still has time to deliver a hilariously unlikely resolution to the mystery. Overall, this is great stuff and comes highly recommended to all Giallo fans!

And it does all of this under beautifully immersive animation and a runtime of only an hour and 20 minutes.

reviews.text: As someone who has relatively recently lost a loved one, the idea of this resonated deeply with me. Of course you want not to have had a close relative die, but the "returned" here aren't jumping back to a time pre-death; this plot deals with them coming back after the terrible event, after their relatives have grieved and gone some way to reconcile the death and move on. And these aren't violent zombies, they are recognisable enough as their old selves, and yet they aren't the same as before. Something is... off. How much do you want them back? Would you want that person returned to you, if they weren't as before, as you remember and love them? It's a heartbreaking and terrifying thought. The ending is a little flat, considering the eerie and atmospheric build up. However, I would recommend this to anyone in the mood for a very still, thought-provoking film.

reviews.text: Boasts the best cinematography of the year thus far and a quietly beautiful authenticity that allows the story to resonate. Zhao embraces the landscape and her main character’s place in it, drawing on the central contradiction constantly weighing him down: namely, the idea that embracing the thing that defines him could end up being his most fatal decision. Zhao doesn’t idealize the situation through a macho “fight through it” lens, nor does she wallow in misery and fatalism. Instead, she appreciates and respects the highs and lows of the human experience, finding a glimmer of hope in the loss of a dream and the long, arduous, and yet rewarding walk toward the future.

reviews.text: This tells a far different Holocaust story than we are used to- children having to live with the PTSD of what they experienced, and doing so as orphans. It is a painful watch but such an emotionally raw and exceptionally important one. In addition to casting Ivan Jandl as the young boy, putting Montgomery Clift alongside him was genius. Clift has such gentility, but such a deep capacity for conveying profound emotion that he complements Jandl's own pain perfectly. What an actor Clift is, too, that through this he never once overpowers or overshadows Jandl. He lets him have the film, and that is what makes it so exceptionally powerful. It is the child's story and we grieve alongside him, while also feeling helpless alongside Clift.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: This Czechoslovakian movie, written by Ladislav Grosman and directed by Ján Kadár and Elmar Klos, grapples with the forced deportation of Jews from employed existence in the Slovak State. It encompasses the context of broader societal issues through individual morality and responsibility, and when the sadness of reality arrives in the tale, it’s not in a manipulative way possibly foreseen. The performances convey tenseness and emotional brutality, with Jozef Kroner as carpenter Tóno Brtko and Ida Kamińska as the Jewish widow Rozália Lautmannová delivering especially charged portrayals. The Shop on Main Street is one of the most emotional movies ever made about the Holocaust and earned its best foreign-language Oscar at the 38th academy awards.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: In the mirror, he stands up slowly from his chair. Some object rests beneath his feet, making it look in the reflection as if he is floating somehow. As he stands, his head is bent down, giving it an odd, limp look. For a moment, it appears as if he has hung himself. It's a startling image because it makes no sense in that moment, but later, this brief moment, seemingly accidental, is revealed as prophetic. When Tono finally hangs himself, we never see his body. The chair falls, the noose is tied, and so on, but no, no body is shown. It cuts to a dream fantasy to end things. That earlier image serves as our warning, our visual cue, our sight of his death, subtly inserted into one of the many conversations that forewarn us of doom, that tell us the Nazis will not be stopped and no one we see here will be saved.

reviews.author: Hutch
reviews.text: I’d put off watching this film for yonks because I imagined it to be a sombre examination of national guilt over Slovakia’s collaboration with the Nazi’s in WWII, and somehow, I just never felt in the mood. It’s an examination of Slovakian guilt alright, but I was pleasantly surprised how even-handed it is in loving and condemning its countrymen and women, and how finely it balances the tragic with the comic, and the insidious with the bucolic. I knew it was made during the Czechoslovakian New Wave, but I couldn’t imagine the stylish playfulness that is so characteristic of the films of that era being translated into a story about the Holocaust. But how brilliantly it succeeds!

reviews.author: Ford H
reviews.text: This is CINEMA. Deeply profound and meaningful on so many levels, and beautifully devastating, like most Eastern European films. For a film about the Holocaust, The Shop on Main Street is also quite personal and small scale. Just proof that you don't need violence or an overwhelming shock factor to get us all riled up. It's affecting in an organic way, even as it blends fantastical elements into the narrative. Today's film landscape could probably learn something from going back to the 1960s, which to me has been the most consistent for quality storytelling. The acting is some of the best, particularly from Ida Kaminska, who was nominated for Best Actress at the Academy Awards. The cinematography is gorgeous and the themes are tackled with the utmost care. There is some humor and mad drunkenness, but these aspects don’t take anything away from this powerful film.

However, Lautmannova is a bit, shall we say, senile? She's complete oblivious to whats happening in the world. As Tono tries to get ahold of the store, hilarity ensue, that is, until reality strikes and things get bleak very quick.

reviews.author: teamgal
reviews.text: There's a lot to value here, particularly the cinematography of Wolfgang Suschitzky, who also shot the incredible GET CARTER. If you want to see stunning images of 1960s Soho you won't find better. Unfortunately, although it has much of the nasty grit one associates with kitchen sink realism, lead Anthony Newley simply doesn't have the gravitas to pull this off. He's only playing at sleaze and serves merely to remind one of the magnificent, charismatic performances that drive much of the British New Wave: Albert Finney, Rachel Roberts, Richard Burton, Tom Courtenay, Lawrence Olivier, Richard Harris, Rita Tushingham, chief among them.

reviews.author: Puffin
reviews.text: Sharp in its wit and biting in its commentary, The Teacher from Vigevano is a clear example of Elio Petri's brilliance pre-dating his more popular and acclaimed work (Investigation of a Citizen Above Suspicion, The 10th Victim, The Working Class Goes to Heaven, A Quiet Place in the Country, etc.) Some brilliant cinematic tricks play out here, whether that be with comedic intention, more sombre drama, or somewhere in-between. And even when the jokes miss the mark, the point of the joke is sharp and persistent, emphasizing a comradery with the societal underdog that seemed to interest Petri throughout his filmmaking career. An obvious sense of humor doesn't neglect the darker themes and attitudes carrying so much weight. Instead, they serve to emphasize such power dynamics that pursue Alberto Sordi's character to madness. Comedy is used for empathy, and more importantly, comedy is used to complicate a growing tragedy.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Horst Wendlandt's Rialto Film was the company behind much of what drove the West Germany box office in the 1960s, specifically both the Winnetou series and many of the Edgar Wallace adaptations that shaped the krimi genre. When Winnetou and Old Firehand flopped at the box office, Wendlandt immediately began casting about for his next success — the next genre into which he could inject his magical energy.

reviews.author: Jeff Sexton
reviews.text: "The Torture Chamber of Dr. Sadism" is an overly dramatic translation of the German title. The film is a '60s gothic horror, and something of an outlier. Despite its lurid English title, the film has very little to do with a "Dr. Sadism," a character that doesn't exist. Instead, it is a lavish, Technicolor poece that feels like a German attempt to out-Hammer Hammer Films, using Christopher Lee as its anchor.

This is the worst film I’ve seen him in by far. It’s supposed to work as a suspense thriller but apart from one scene that was a bit creepy, nothing is remotely convincing or intriguing. The constant use of flashbacks was annoying and the hallucination sequences turned to be funny instead of disturbing. The performances were horrendous all around and Cage hit another really low point in his career with this work. For the most part, The Wicker Man is boring and just plain terrible, but at least the last portion presents us with some of the most outrageously funny sequences in the history of cinema.

reviews.author: Rodman Flender
reviews.text: From the co-director of Mondo Cane. Wild Eye is a fiction film about a nihilistic Italian filmmaker who trots the globe and pays off poor and desperate locals to enact scenes of violence, cruelty and humiliation for his “documentary.” A beautiful married woman in some kind of open relationship tags along with the creep for no plausible reason. That’s pretty much it. Unevenly paced but the last sequence was kinda gripping. As a long-time fan of Cane, I found this super-interesting but I’m not sure how well it would play to people unfamiliar with that film. I appreciated a scene where the filmmaker burns through film waiting for something to happen - and it never does. That’s real documentary filmmaking. The photography is good, the syrupy music isn't as catchy as “More” from Cane. The 2K transfer on the Scorpion blu ray was top-notch.

Sometimes he gets in real trouble. This movie didn't work for me. There's a romance that is not believable and it takes quite a…

The film equates the rush of capturing real life horrors on camera to drug addiction. One shock leads to another and in the absence of real life horrors how many liberties can a journalist take with reality before distorting the truth? Before the facts of the matter become irrelevant and only the RUSH remains. Friends, lovers, family — nothing else matters.

reviews.author: Adam Kempenaar

reviews.author: Scumbalina
reviews.text: I loved how much of Kitty's life was shown. She was so cool, like a movie star. She did whatever the fuck she wanted. Her little brother looked up to her, everyone did. The crime was fucking horrible, and her killer was next level sociopath. He's fascinating in a way too, I suppose. I loved watching her brother obsessively parse this case fifty years later, unhealthy as it may be. She shaped him. Her death set in motion his decision to join the army where he would lose his legs in Vietnam. There's a beauty here that I'm not used to seeing in grisly crime documentaries. Something oddly refreshing. It's Kitty, and Bill. Their family, their love, their intellect and sense of adventure. It surpasses the death and for this viewer it overshadows the questionable silent witnesses.

reviews.text: Besides me a devastating case of murder and supposed apathy, in The Witness you're essentially watching a heavily researched therapy session play out as Kitty Genovese's brother William over analysis, breaks down and relives his sister's last 32 minutes. There's no real goal for William besides closure of trying to understand why supposedly know one helped is dying sister on that night in 1964. While I do think progress is reached by interviewing some of those who knew his sister and getting closer to this family member he lost too young, at other times it seems to be opening up old wounds and damaging relationships with those he loves. Some interviews and revelations feel forced in a way that I can't tell if it's being pushed by the filmmaker or William but it is an interesting dive into an infamous piece of New York history and media's sometimes negative involvement with high profile stories.

reviews.text: It seems a cruel trick of evolution that our worst experiences store themselves in uniquely painful, seemingly tyrannical ways. Unlike memories of a birthday party or what you had for breakfast, traumatic memories can seep into our very bodies, souls, and color our perceptions. Even with an amount of time and distance that one would think would be enough for layers of scar tissue to form, a mere smell or sound can seize one back to the initial terrorizing event. Filmmakers Joaquín Cociña and Cristóbal León explore this concept on micro and macro levels in their stop-motion masterpiece and obvious labor of love “The Wolf House.”
