reviews.text: Exorcistic by nature, as I discuss on my Top 5 of 2017 podcast here. To fight back against one criticism I saw elsewhere, this is of course not a film filled with neatly framed images, but it does what cinema is supposed to do: capture bodies in all their emotions. We don't live in a world of #OnePerfectShots; we should not ask our documentaries to do so. We do live in one in which bodies are continually moving, breathing, expanding, closing, touching, releasing—and the cameras capture that to their full extent here.

Red hot agitkino, loud and ferocious; even in the quiet domestic moments in the first scenes of the movie, Godardian decoupage imbues all the consumer commodities in a comfortable working class household with a malign, toxic quality that makes one fear the worst... and then at the factory where most of the movie takes place, all hell breaks loose. Over and over and over again.

reviews.text: I have a lot of problems with this as history. Neville is honest enough to start the movie by question if Welles said or not the film's title, and making clear he is more interested in exploring mythmaking and playing at Welles. It is very well put together, but most in the level of a solid researched but shallow magazine piece. The kind that has no time to mention that Welles did F for Fake in the middle of shooting Other Side, but does find a minute for Huston doing The Man Who Would Be King. There's a lot of great footage from the shooting that more than justifies this movie existence and some good interviews, particular Bogdanovich. Also, as a good hardcore Welles buff I'm always a sucker for Gary Graver stories and this rightfully give him a lot of screen time.

reviews.text: Listening to an aged and exhausted Orson Welles talk about filmmaking in this documentary is downright depressing. One gets the feeling that he is creatively stifled — both fiscally strained and intellectually arrested — and that the stagnation is tormenting him endlessly. His anguished disposition is almost unbearable to watch, even as he boasts in blustery terms about directorial detours and on set experimentation, such as a decision to shoot with a passive, improvisational, Beatnik-adjacent approach — ‘presiding over divine accidents.’ To say Welles became stuck in a rut is both an understatement and somewhat misses the mark. His creativity never ceased; he merely lost its linearity and capacity to finalize endeavors with architectural integrity. Welles’ aesthetic and perhaps existential…

reviews.author: Kyle Turner
reviews.text: The exploitation of the story, and its baggage, feels especially gross because it’s a film that pretends to be about humanity. At the very end of the film, the editor of the original Newsday article offers platitudes about how everyone else was looking for how similar they were and that we should be looking for their differences. And finally, the boys also admit they played up their similarities, wanted to be similar. But it’s a crock of shit when the last 80 minutes have done little to explore those differences — cultural, emotional, psychological. David Cronenberg and Charlie Kaufman are more thoughtful about twins than Wardle is. Wardle reveals himself as interested in nothing, not even the human condition to this story, but cheap tabloid drama, and, worse, doesn’t have the self awareness to explore the meta, postmodern implications of that modern mythologization. “Truth is stranger than fiction” is just a marketing strategy.

The script is wonky as hell but it makes up for it with its gold-star atmosphere and jaw-removing location shots. I could have done without the lengthy sexual assault scene towards the end, its bizarre aftermath is far more uncomfortable than any tit-gore or depiction of SA that came before it. Sure, it's a snapshot of that era's social norms and audience expectations, but that doesn't mean it's easy to ignore or doesn't completely take you out of the movie during the height of its 3rd act.

reviews.author: Digital Press
reviews.text: This series is criminally underrated and mistakenly left out of “best horror franchises”. These blind dead aren’t traditional zombies, they’re skeletal, wrapped like mummies and seeking blood like vampires, yet they are skillful and behave more like ghosts. The precise term for these guys are “revenants” - animated corpses revived specifically to haunt the living. As it is also MY job to haunt the living, I thought I’d revisit all four films again and report back how they’re holding up in 2024.

reviews.author: Ed Küpfer
reviews.text: There are two kinds of great direct to video action movies. There are the kind that transcend the genre by defying their budgets and limitations to become something else entirely—John Hyams' Universal Soldier sequels are a good example. Then there are the kind of direct to video action movies that are just direct to video action movies, but more of it. Tough and Deadly is one of these, giving you everything you expect from a DTV flick, with just so much more of it.

reviews.author: Saint_Hooligan
reviews.text: Firmly located in classic buddy movie territory, Tough and Deadly is an entertaining bit of straight-to-video action. The storyline is hardly original but the writers know exactly what fans want and provide fight scenes, both with martial arts and guns, on a frequent basis. Swift-paced, ripe with hand-to-hand fights, and never taking itself too seriously, the film is a great example of how to achieve a fun time with only minimal resources and two talented, underrated stars. Piper and Blanks have great chemistry together and bring the fun to all the action. A brawling mess of fun and one of Pipers better films.

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: Somehow even more jam packed with explosive incident (not to mention just plan explosions) than previous Shapiro-Glickenhaus Piper/Blanks fight song BACK IN ACTION. Owns way more of a Shane Black knock-off vibe, as Rowdy's disheveled bounty hunter takes Billy's amnesiac CIA assassin under his wing, only to be pursued by a legion of stunt men dressed in grey suits looking to get tossed through every window or piece of furniture in the vicinity. Call it "The Long Fist Bump Goodnight"; a total dude fest for dudes just looking to be dudes, eating ice cream in the middle of a run through the park, before another fight you're destined to decisively win breaks out. How these haven't been rescued from VHS purgatory remains a complete mystery, unless it's the Uni/MCA co-distribution holding them hostage in some anonymous content library somewhere.

Good use of thick lines to emphasise shapes.

reviews.text: The last Chuck Jones/Bugs Bunny short released (though Mad as a Mars Hare was produced last) is a good example of how much he was "over" the character by this late point: Bugs feels like an unwelcome imposition on the cartoon, and the overall construction of gags feels ill-tailored to the character: until very late in the short, he's never outwitting the vampire, he's just falling ass-backwards into tormenting the vampire through sheer luck. Not that this was ever going to happen and probably it wasn't even briefly considered as an option, but this feels like it wants to be a Porky short (maybe even a fourth Porky/Sylvester short).

reviews.author: Alice Stoehr
reviews.text: Given Buñuel's knack for getting inside bourgeois "normal" and revealing it as perverse, I wasn't too surprised by the film's immersion in aristocratic decorum, and the story's quasi-gothic intricacies do leave some striking impressions: There's a nightmare in which Fernando Rey's head acts as a bell clapper, for example, and late in the film we hear the sound of Catherine Deneuve's crutches thudding across a hallway. But despite these sensory morsels, so much of Tristana is disappointingly dry. It seems for all the world like a relatively uninflected transposition of the same-named Galdós novel to the screen.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Luis Buñuel's story of a relationship between a wealthy upper class man and the young woman who came under his guardianship after being orphaned as a child. Tristana is an oddly surreal and very bleak black comedy, which offers criticism of the church, the bourgeois and society. Fernando Rey stars as Don Lope; a man respected by society despite his dubious moral compass. Catherine Deneuve is the young woman under his charge. He seeks to act as both father and lover; possessing her entirely while also claiming that freedom is a fundamental aspect of their relationship. It's a film full of ridiculous absurdity, but delivered with such a straight face. A rather engaging first half, which culminates in the arrival…

reviews.text: Tristana is not one of the most beloved films by Luis Buñuel, but it depicts his ideas around bourgeois hypocrisy in a dark and compelling manner. The roles of men and women are discussed in Tristana, and shown as entirely decided by the domain of men. The titular lead grows up to want independence from her male guardian, but he treats her as both daughter and lover. She has no honour by staying with him, but he has power she does not have. Money is discussed as being nothing to the privileged, but meaning everything to the underprivileged. Tristana is a perverse movie, of a father figure who treats the lead as his wife. She is expected to stay home…

reviews.author: Channing Pomeroy
reviews.text: Watching one of Lubitsch Continental drawing room Pre-code masterpieces, like Trouble in Paradise (1932) or Design for Living (1933), feels now like witnessing a lost art. Witty, louche comedic gems where crime pays and creates sexual frisson. Theft goes unpunished and polyamory unjudged. Was the world ever this sophisticated and subtle? How did Hollywood forget how to do this?

reviews.author: Joel Haver
reviews.text: There’s something almost otherworldly about how modern pre-code Hollywood can feel. From the humor to the acting to even the technical filmmaking, there’s so much at play here that still feels “hip”. So often we forget that, even 90 years ago, people were still scandalous and perverse as ever. I was having quite an anxious night and this movie brought me back down, and for that alone I’m grateful. I’m excited to watch more Ernst Lubitsch, who one of my favorite college professors always raved about and I wish I had listened sooner!

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: This is the greatest horror movie about adultery ever made in Palm Beach. When Mike Strauber finds his wife in bed with his best friend, he dons a copper mask and takes out his psychological trauma on the world. This includes rolling over a baby with a car and rearranging a senior citizen’s face with an Uzi. reviews.text: Within 15 years of Two-Lane Blacktop’s release, three of the four principal cast members would be dead. One of them died of natural causes, the other two died before they were 40. The youngest, Laurie Bird, committed suicide by overdosing on Valium at the age of 26, after a lifetime of traumatic incidents and depression that she clearly didn’t have the right support for. The other, was Dennis Wilson, the drummer of the Beach Boys, who had notorious addiction issues with drugs and alcohol, and couldn’t heal from his disease after numerous attempts. He drowned while drunk, jumping into the ocean inebriated while trying to find things he’d thrown overboard years beforehand. He was a year out from turning 40.…

reviews.author: cuckoochanel
reviews.text: There is no end to Two-Lane Blacktop. There is no end to the restlessness of the hauntingly desolate, open road. The landscape whips by in streaks of greens, browns, and grays—a blurry rendering of pastoral America. The introspective silence, the apathy, the loneliness is echoed by the magnitude of the journey, of the winding highways—an infinite present, where “future” is a destination too abstract to anticipate and “past” a place too obscured by distance and time to seem relevant.

reviews.text: Fascinating if flawed documentary by Chris Hegedus and D.A. Pennebaker, that has most of the contours of an advocacy documentary yet plays out in a less strident register than you might expect. Following the lawyer Stephen Wise in his quest to grant legal personhood rights to great apes, it seems, from my point of view, solidly on Wise's side, but it never forces the audience onto that side. Wise gets the space to clarify and refine his theme - he's not, despite the tenor of the media coverage, saying that we should give gibbons all the rights of humans. But all of the dick-ripping and vagina-stabbing somehow feels quaint because of the sheer outrageousness of the mayhem. reviews.author: Edwin 🦦
reviews.text: It’s really no surprise that Viridiana was banned in Spain and denounced by the Vatican when it first premiered. Luis Buñuel was never shy about his anti-Catholic views, and this movie feels like a direct confrontation with the institution. He builds a world where faith is constantly tested in uncomfortable ways. You can feel how deeply he questions the idea of moral purity, especially when it’s placed into a world that doesn’t operate on fairness or grace. It’s challenging religion as a system, but also challenging the idea that goodness alone can survive in a world that doesn’t reward it.

reviews.text: Boasting an all-star cast the likes of which were par for the course in 70s disaster flicks, Stuart Rosenberg's Voyage of the Damned is an account of a different type of catastrophe: the true story of the St. Louis, an ocean liner tasked with transporting 937 German-Jewish passengers from Hamburg to Havana in May 1939. Unsurprisingly, given the film's title, the trip does not go as planned for the refugees.

reviews.author: Fint
reviews.text: A ship so overloaded by name actors that it threatens to capsize with talent, yet still manages to utterly waste the wonderful Wendy Hiller. (There was apparently a near 3-hour version so perhaps Wendy suffered in the second edit.) There is some propitious casting (Maria Schell - luminous; Max von Sydow - authoritative; Lee Grant - committed; James Mason - robust) but some head-scratchers too, mostly with the glamorous younger women: Katharine Ross doesn't convince as Maria Schell's prostitute daughter, Lynne Frederick has a cringingly gauche final scene with Malcolm McDowell, and Faye Dunaway, though she is not bad, just appears to be in the wrong film.

reviews.text: 1976 continues... Stumbled upon ‘Voyage of the Damned’ while trying to find a 1976 that pulled me in right away. ‘Voyage of the Damned’ is packed to the gills with stars, and its Social relevance is pretty high in 2020. A ship of Jewish refugees, the St Louis, leaves Germany in 1939, as a propaganda experiment, bound for Cuba. We see scenes from the lives of the crew and passengers, and the people on land trying to manipulate their fate. The best cameo in the film is Philip Stones two scenes. I love the idea that ‘The Shining’s Delbert Grady is the gatekeeper to returning jews to Europe days before World War Two breaks out.

reviews.text: Well that was a bit of a mess, wasn't it? This film just didn't know what it wanted to be. Tonally it was all over the place, it suffered from pacing issues, and the comedy didn't land at all. The script was an absolute mess and the story was quite incoherent with pointless plot threads sprouting from nowhere. I didn't buy the chemistry between Alexander Skarsgård and Michael Peña and couldn't care less about either character. The editing was atrocious, particularly at the start, and it made all the characters seem really awkward (almost like someone had removed the canned laughter from a cheesy 70's sitcom but you can still see the actors waiting before continuing their lines). And is it just me or did Alexander Skarsdård remind anyone else of Freddie Flintoff? That's all I could picture throughout the entire film. There was nothing to take away from this film but sheer disappointment.

reviews.text: John Michael McDonagh's "The War on Everyone" may be a better plot away from being great. The comedy about two cops and crime ring features smart dialogue, personality-rich characters, and appealing performances; storywise, however, the film offers little more than perfunctory crime movie threads. With Michael Peña, Alexander Skarsgård, and Tessa Thompson at his disposal, McDonagh puts something enjoyable together and builds a neatly shot, capably energetic comedy drenched in Albuquerque sunshine, dark-tinged humor, and some genuine heart. Its narrative may be soggy and routine, but the work does not fail to engage.

Intended as a commemoration of the 1965 Watts riots, one of the speakers knowingly addresses the outsiders (such as myself) who he knows will see this footage: "Some people may find it a little strange that we laugh, we sing, we joke, but we're doing our thing, the black way, to commemorate." As a document it's invaluable, as a concert film…

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: The sheer lack of concert footage from this big event quite possibly marginalizes an already-marginal get-together this film was meant to expose. Yet the footage, archival and freshly recorded, Stuart places between the songs inverts the dynamic of WOODSTOCK, MONTEREY POP and the like. Those movies showcased artists deliberately posed as anti-Establishment, given to political statements and music, playing to audiences who, for all their posturing of dropping out, are clearly there for a good show. reviews.text: "We Still Kill the Old Way" is a 1967 film directed by Elio Petri. The film stars the ever-impressive Gian Maria Volonté as Paolo Laurana, a local educated professor within rural Italy who finds himself at the center of solving a crime. The film originally sets up the crime with a ransom like death threat to a local personality who winds up killed on a hunting excursion with his hunting companion. As the town begins to automatically setup something of a convenient suspect, Laurana becomes skeptical due to their illiteracy. This leads him down a rabbit trail of build behind the crime, especially circumvented around social corruption, a dish served often by Petri in his works.

reviews.text: A naive and sheltered communist professor, Laurana (Gian Maria Volonté), lives his life in books. His nervous disposition is made apparent, as is his involuntarily celibate nature. A dolt and a creep around the ladies and without any real life skills, he is not quite the womanizer that his two friends were, who are mysteriously shot during a hunting trip. Laurana notices discrepancies in the murder investigation—call it the onset of a conspiracy. He dives headlong into an amateur sleuth investigation, surely motivated as much out of his impotence and desire for his friend’s widow as he is by genuine anger at the blatantly corrupt nature of the investigation.

reviews.text: “White Sun”, the title of Deepak Rauniyar’s sophomore Nepalese drama refers to peace. The peace that is neither as peaceful as it seems on the surface nor as easy as it is supposed to be. Balancing detailed and intimate human drama with sharply observed political delicacy, Rauniyar’s film beautifully encapsulates the post-war scenario in contemporary Nepal. Satirizing the traditions and beliefs where the old are set against the new, “White Sun” observes the dilemma of well-rounded characters and their baggage with each other through death and change. It also observes the guilt, transformations, and freedom that something as stark as war can bring into some people’s life. With a light touch and absurd comic situations, Rauniyar’s film slowly and assuredly…

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Ingmar Bergman is a famously bleak filmmaker, but Wild Strawberries stands out as different. It is Bergman at his most touching, human, loving, and emotional (even if sadness dominates many moments). Of course there are Bergman tropes but it's played at a different level to his religious or allegorical works. Wild Strawberries is a character study, dedicated entirely to dissecting the values and history of one man. Yet it is so much more as it probes the very things that make us happy.

Every shot manages to elicit the themes when dark, powerful and sorrowful. This style is definitely not for everyone, but there is just so much to appreciate.

reviews.author: sirvived
reviews.text: A lean and mean 94 minutes of animal attack horror that descends into a brutal backwoods nightmare which is completely unexpected. The backwoods dread feels very real in this one. The menace and terror are captured unbelievably well and the isolated setting made for an ideal horror film. All the deaths and traps are simply excellent. Consistently rock-solid performances and a great atmosphere, also filled with a lot of action and more than enough gore to satisfy just about any gore enthusiast, you have a film that never fails to grip the attention. That one guy with his dogs truly delivers a coldblooded, menacing, and unforgettable villain.

reviews.author: Derek
reviews.text: Wilderness is a 2006 glossy, yet slightly brutal British survival horror movie. It falls firmly under a subgenre of horror that was popular in Britain back then that they called, "hoodie horror." The most well-known example of this type of movie is Eden Lake, and it translates to all of those movies being horror and thriller films where the antagonists and sometimes the protagonists are shitty, psychopathic little teenagers. This movie kind of complicates this typical narrative by having all of the teenagers in it be awful people to varying degrees, but despite this, they are still not the antagonists.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: A halfway decent slasher is hiding underneath the generic garbage this is saddled with. There's some gore and violence in this that is artfully crafted, and the use of dogs adds a level of discomfort to the story that is much edgier than I expected. They don't manage to make the characters interesting - not always a death sentence in a slasher, but it doesn't help here - and it has an apparent military worship going on that sours the whole thing. It also squanders its premise; the exploration of trauma within a "juvenile" "criminal" facility is never done justice, probably because the filmmakers are not as sympathetic as that premise would suggest.

reviews.text: Twice over I have been that lover Stan Brakhage cuts to here ever so sparingly. I have bore witness to the human miracle of my wife's birth of our children, one cesarean and one vaginal, and there is no greater example of the seemingly unearthly strength, the gobsmacking beauty, and the sheer miracle that creating new life and bringing life into this world is. I look at my children now - seven and almost four - look back on their births, and it is as if they were out of body experiences that I somehow was vicariously privy to.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: That look on Stan’s face at the end really says it all. What I found particularly profound this time around were the cuts between the birthing and the footage from the beginning of the film with Jane sitting in the bathtub and Stan comforting her from outside it, and, to me, all the pre-birth footage symbolizes the process of gestation as a whole for the carrier and their partner—being together, with the pregnant person submerged in the experience and the other person there to offer warmth and support. The shots of water in the soft light washing over and cascading off of Jane’s stomach are unquestionably some of the most astonishing frames ever captured on film. Life is at times so tender and beautiful.

reviews.author: Joshua Dysart
reviews.text: I saw this at a Stan Brakhage retrospective in the theater. During the film a man had a stroke in the otherwise silent room. Someone began to call out for a doctor. The screening was stopped. They called an ambulance. They took the man from the theater and into the lobby and restarted the film but eventually we could hear the ambulance siren approaching out on the street and then the paramedics in the lobby. All because this film is completely silent. Silent cinema leaves space for life. Apart from that, the film itself is one of my favorite movies ever made.

Paul Newman is a radio deejay for an extreme right-wing station in New Orleans, and the movie doesn’t even show him at his damn job until the 32-minute mark. It is precious to me how much he’s photographed his brother, Diego Cataño (who later also stars in Jonas’s 2nd film, Desierto). I love the observations between awkward moments, like Molly noticing the cook (maid) for hire in the middle class Mexican family, while also being such an American about how she, theoretically wanted a working class family to host her yet even found things to complain about in the middle class house. Cuarón nailed(!) both sides completely.

reviews.text: One must possess a certain amount of fearlessness in order to subject themselves to that sort of process (committing those sides of one’s self in permanency); or, at least, a general who gives a fuck mentality has to be present and functioning at times throughout the production. Ry Russo-Young’s You Wont Miss Me has a profusion of the aforementioned qualities burrowed into the center of every aspect, huddled alongside the instances of joy found in between the vulnerability displays and the unwavering, arriving at poignancy and a version of truth with sincerity and candor.

reviews.text: A couple of great scenes revolving around the struggle of re-adapting to so-called normal life and the challenges that come with it because, unfortunately, people are assholes. However barring those scenes, You Wont Miss Me is pretty forgettable and doesn't take advantage of the great talent at it's disposal. Carlen Altman, just like in The Color Wheel, is the absolute best at spewing insults ("you're like one of these people that are going to kill themselves in five years so I don't really want to upset you any further and be implicated in anything") and has this supreme presence about her but she's underused. Not much else to say, it feels like I've forgotten most of this film already and I only finished it five minutes ago.

reviews.author: Michael Haneke Paneke
reviews.text: I was very excited for this one--I actually bought it, violating my "stop buying new movies until you watch any of the dozens of movies you already own but still haven't seen" rule--but I'm not entirely sure it works. The story itself is a great one, but the director feels unsure of its power, and tries to elevate it with self-conscious artistic flashes (flipping aspect ratios, film stock, playing with the narrative so you can't be sure in what order the events are taking place, etc). A big part of the reason I've fallen so hard for these mumblecore movies is because they eschew those stylistic excesses, just bare-bones filmmaking.

reviews.text: Another Sergio Martino sleazefest done with a style and skill that only Argento could top. This one's a bit of a trick because the giallo element only goes about halfway before Martino breaks this movie wide open into something out of Edgar Allan Poe and even Hitchcock. It's totally unexpected and keeps you guessing at what the hell he's going to show you next. Edwige Fenech plays a stronger character than she usually does and that's half the fun of the movie. Definitely one of Martino's best, if not the best of his career.

If you like laboratories full of giant, pointless electronics that are constantly blinking and beeping, this is your movie. Marine biology stock footage mixed with early synthesizer music turns this innocuous movie full on psychedelic. Droning, noodling keyboard sounds permeate everything here. Zaat is like a 1950s sci fi movie, only amped the fuck up and way better, but then turned back down again out of respect and consideration. Infinitely better than Octaman.

reviews.text: This movie scratches the nostalgia itch for me, but beyond that, Zambezia is a timeless animated classic. The film unpacks dense themes of self-identity and immigration, the busy architecture cleverly nestled inside the giant hollowed-out tree characterizing the magnificent, yet eclectic city of Zambezia. Conflict in the film spirals with the marabous. The marabous, ostracized from Zambezia, starve on the outskirts of the desolate Saharan desert. A commentary on exclusionary immigration policies, this film is a timely allegory of prejudice, the marabous on the lowest rungs of the social strata.
